fields.summary: Interactive "mcs cluster stop" command for CMAPI

issuetype.description: A new feature of the product, which has yet to be developed.
issuetype.name: New Feature

fields.description:
Right now `mcs cluster stop` command has a fixed 5 minute timeout waiting for transaction to finish/rollback, For better UX `mcs cluster stop` must interactively ask a user to initiate force shutdown after a minute of waiting for the cluster to stop. There must be parameters to the command to set the timeout and enable force shutdown w/o confirmation, e.g.

```
mcs cluster shutdown
... after a minute
There were data changing operations running on the cluster that are now rolling back. Do you want to initiate a force shutdown?
!!! Force shutdown might affect the availability of tables used by the mentioned operations !!!

comments.body:
Started testing on the following setup:
RockyLinux 8 
3-node cluster
MariaDB-columnstore-cmapi.x86_64     10.6.17_12_23.10.0-1.el8    
MariaDB-columnstore-engine.x86_64    10.6.17_12_23.10.1-1.el8
MariaDB-server.x86_64                10.6.17_12-1.el8 

I can see the new timeout options,
# mcs cluster stop --help
Usage: mcs cluster stop [OPTIONS]

  Stop the Columnstore cluster.

Options:
  -i, --interactive / -no-i, --no-interactive
                                  Use this option on active cluster as
                                  interactive stop waits for current writes to
                                  complete in DMLProc before shutting down.
                                  Ensuring consistency, preventing data loss
                                  of active writes.  [default: no-interactive]
  -t, --timeout INTEGER           Time in seconds to wait for DMLproc to
                                  gracefully stop.Warning: Low wait timeout
                                  values could result in data loss if the
                                  cluster is very active.In interactive mode
                                  means delay time between promts.  [default:
                                  15]
  --help                          Show this message and exit.

Needs more detailed testing.

mcs cluster stop -t, --timeout
It always waits for the timeout value even if there're no active writes. So, it behaves more like a wait instead of timeout. Shouldn't it check for any active writes and wait until the timeout value, otherwise just stop without waiting for the timeout value?

A sample output when there is no active writes on the cluster,
# mcs cluster stop -i -t 300
29/Mar/2024 11:44:30 [DEBUG] (mcs_cli) Called "mcs cluster stop -i -t 300"
29/Mar/2024 11:49:30 [INFO] (root) DMLProc stopped gracefully. Continue stopping other processes.
29/Mar/2024 11:49:30 [DEBUG] (mcs_cli) Cluster shutdown command called. Shutting down the cluster.
29/Mar/2024 11:49:30 [DEBUG] (root) get_module_net_address Module 1 network address 10.2.15.13
29/Mar/2024 11:49:43 [INFO] (root) Successfully pushed new config file to ['10.2.15.105', '10.2.15.109', '10.2.15.13']
29/Mar/2024 11:49:43 [DEBUG] (mcs_cli) Successfully finished shutting down the cluster.
29/Mar/2024 11:49:43 [DEBUG] (mcs_cli) Command returned: {'timestamp': '2024-03-29 11:44:30.766215'}

Now the fix in https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-columnstore-engine/pull/3150 has been merged into develop. So, I did a fresh testing. Here are some findings (potential bugs),

1. mcs cluster stop -t, --timeout behaves more like a wait instead of timeout.
The following result is on a fresh cluster where there is no active writes going on,

[root@mcs1 /]# ps aux | grep DMLProc; date; mcs cluster stop -i -t 300; date;
root      1532  0.1  0.7 456248 114668 ?       Sl   13:57   0:00 /usr/bin/DMLProc
root      1827  0.0  0.0  12128  1016 ?        S+   13:59   0:00 grep --color=auto DMLProc
Wed Apr 24 13:59:32 UTC 2024
{
  "timestamp": "2024-04-24 13:59:33.099015"
}
Wed Apr 24 14:04:37 UTC 2024

2. In interactive mode if I choose no, it continues asking the same again again.
Ideally it should exit after first No.
# mcs cluster stop -i -t 5
DMLProc is still running. Do you want to force stop? WARNING: Could cause data loss and/or broken cluster. [y/N] N
DMLProc is still running. Do you want to force stop? WARNING: Could cause data loss and/or broken cluster. [y/N] N
DMLProc is still running. Do you want to force stop? WARNING: Could cause data loss and/or broken cluster. [y/N] N
DMLProc is still running. Do you want to force stop? WARNING: Could cause data loss and/or broken cluster. [y/N] N
DMLProc is still running. Do you want to force stop? WARNING: Could cause data loss and/or broken cluster. [y/N] y
{
  "timestamp": "2024-04-24 13:21:36.284813"
} 

3. --timeout option should not be accepted in the non-interactive mode (default) 
# mcs cluster stop -t 5
{
  "timestamp": "2024-04-24 13:37:54.499705"
}

Here is the fourth problem. 
4. When there is a write going on 'mcs cluster stop -i -t' didn't prompt any warning message and went ahead and stopped the cluster.

Repro
------
Initiate a write operation which takes >10sec>
MariaDB [test]> insert into mcst2 select * from mcst2;
Query OK, 18048 rows affected (14.843 sec)
Records: 18048  Duplicates: 0  Warnings: 0

MariaDB [test]> select now(); insert into mcst2 select * from mcst2; select now();
+---------------------+
| now()               |
+---------------------+
| 2024-05-02 14:25:39 |
+---------------------+
1 row in set (0.001 sec)

ERROR 1815 (HY000): Internal error: MCS-2004: Cannot connect to ExeMgr.
+---------------------+
| now()               |
+---------------------+
| 2024-05-02 14:25:55 |
+---------------------+
1 row in set (0.000 sec)

When the above write operation is on initiate cluster stop>
# date; mcs cluster stop -i -t 5; date;
Thu May  2 14:25:42 UTC 2024
{
  "timestamp": "2024-05-02 14:25:43.164337"
}
Thu May  2 14:25:52 UTC 2024

See 'cluster stop' didn't prompt any warning message.

1. mcs cluster stop -t, --timeout behaves more like a wait instead of timeout.

In interactive mode it seems to be more like a wait but in non interactive mode it's technically timeout (yet not released).

[~alan.mologorsky] so, are we going to make the interactive mode behave the same way as in non-interactive mode? I mean in the upcoming release.
Closing this issue.

fields.summary: config upgrade helper tool

issuetype.description: A new feature of the product, which has yet to be developed.
issuetype.name: New Feature

fields.description:
A tool that helps to adjust config files after MariaDB is upgraded.

It can list all options that are no longer recognized by the server, suggest replacements, if any.
It could also edit files in place (when requested), removing, commenting out, or adding loose- prefix to such options.

Also it could check for invalid values of enum/set variables.

To parse all files it could use {{my_print_defaults}}, the list of supported options could be hard-coded or extracted from {{mariadbd --help}} and such.

perl/python or C/C++ ?  C or C++ is probably more portable for windows.

For code how to parse options like !include, check mysys/my_defaults.c

Suggested options:
- No options:  List unknown server options on stdout (those that would prevent the server from starting).
- --update
   -- Update the my.cnf file in place (and all files included with !include or !includedir)
- --backup
  --  Store modified files as backup (for example my.cnf-backup)
- --current-version=...  (for example --current-version=mysqld-5.7)
  -- Section to use for unknown options, see --mode
   --- The purpose of --current-version is to enable the tool to create a config file that will work for both MySQL and MariaDB at
     the same time.  In this case, options that works for both MySQL and MariaDB should use the section [mysqld]. MySQL unique options should be under [mysqld-5.7] and MariaDB specific options
     would be under [mariadbd].
- --edit=...
   -- Select what to do with unknown options. List of suggested mode options:
     --- remove                    Remove unoption
     --- comment                Add # before option
     --- inline-old-version  Add ['current-version'] before the option and [mysqld] afterwards.  'curent-version' is the tag specified with --current-version=...
     --- last-old-version     Move all unknown version last in the file with [old-version] before.
- --print
   -- Print converted file on stdout. In this case all !include  and !includedir files should be included.

We need both inline- and last- as some options may depend on their place in the config file.

The tool should also be prepared for special handling of some specific options.

Note that MariaDB don't have the audit_log plugin (Percona Server).
Instead MariaDB has a server_audit plugin which takes different options.
If the tool notice that 'audit_plugin' is used, it should suggest one to use the server_audit plugin instead.

--plugin-load=QUERY_RESPONSE_TIME_READ=query_response_time.so;QUERY_RESPONSE_TIME_WRITE=query_response_time.so
This is only supported in MariaDB 10.11 and above.  If used with an earlier MariaDB version it would be good to get a note that this is supported in 10.11.6 and above.

As a reference, here are some common config options found in Percona server that is not in MariaDB:
[mysqld-5.7]
--binlog-ignore-db=information_schema
--innodb_log_files_in_group=2

First concept to show incorrect options:

{{my_convert.sh}}
{code:sh}
#!/bin/bash

declare -a opts
declare -a maybebad
declare -a isbad

readarray -t opts  < <( my_print_defaults --mysqld )

while ! mariadbd --no-defaults "${opts[@]}" --help --verbose > /dev/null 2>&1 
do
	maybebad+=( "${opts[-1]}" )
	unset "opts[-1]"
done

while [ ${#maybebad[@]} -gt 0 ]
do
	opts+=( "${maybebad[-1]}" )
	unset "maybebad[-1]"
	if ! mariadbd --no-defaults "${opts[@]}" --help --verbose > /dev/null 2>&1 
	then
		isbad+=( "${opts[-1]}" )
		unset "opts[-1]"
	fi
done

echo Good options: "${opts[@]}"
echo Bad options: "${isbad[@]}"
{code}

Example:

{noformat}
 ./my_convert.sh 
Good options: --table_open_cache=17384 --max_connections=150 --datadir=/home/dan/mariadb-datadir --slow_query_log_file=/home/tom/x.slow
Bad options: --bababa=foo
{noformat}

Great first version.
Some comments:
- This will probably not work on windows (bash)
- It will not work for anyone wanting to create an automatic script that will migratate MySQL 5.7 to MariaDB.

What I would like to see in the final script/tool:
- Option to list 'bad options' (like above)
- Be able to run it on an existing config files and print the resulting config file. 
  - In this case we should move 'bad' options' in the 'server' or 'mysqld' section to [mysqld-5.7]  (user specified) to the end of the script or add a #not-in-mariadb comment before them.  The benefit of using [mysqld-5.7] is that the config files would be usable both by MariaDB and MySQL.
- Be able to run it on all config file and fix them inplace.
- When pointing to a config file for automatic conversion, support the '!include" and "!includedir" options.

When it comes to fixing things inplace, check out the replace tool. It does this and also has optimization to not change files that does not need conversion.
note  MDEV-26923 Check all invalid config options [#2935|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/2935]

mysql_upgrade_service.exe (windows upgrade tool) has edited my.ini to  remove invalid options for a while now, itself. Without suggestions, it removed known outdated options. It did not support "!include" , but neither our nor MySQL installer use any includes on Windows

As noted in MDEV-33503, replacing some parameters will involve some arithmetics. An example: If {{innodb_log_files_in_group}} was specified, then it must be removed and {{innodb_log_file_size}} be multiplied by that number. If no {{innodb_log_file_size}} had been specified but a default value was being used, then it gets trickier. I think that in that case, it would be easiest to issue a warning. In that way, the tool will not have to remember the default {{innodb_log_file_size}} in different server versions.
Another example from MDEV-33503 is that {{innodb_stats_sample_pages}} should be renamed to {{innodb_stats_transient_sample_pages}}. That we can do independent of server version.
https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/2976 has a tool created by Väinö Mäkelä that needs to be evaluated

It can be used to upgrade MariaDB.
However, that should not be needed as we should *NEVER* remove options in a way that the server will not start.
The plan is to add it to MariaDB 11.8

Things done in latest version (bb-11.8-monty):
- Added changing innodb_stats_sample_pages to innodb_stats_transient_sample_pages
- Added changing innodb_log_files_in_group and innodb_log_file_size -> innodb_log_file_size=innodb_log_file_size*innodb_log_files_in_group with proper suffix (G) handling
- Added option --add-mariadb-replication-compatibility to add section in [mysqld-XXX] to ensure MySQL can replicate to MariaDB
- Added option --add-mysql-replication-compatibility to add section in [mariadbd] to ensure MariaDB can replicate to MySQL

*{color:red}Major{color}*
The tool doesn't check the validity of string values

{noformat:title=bb-11.8-monty e98764061dedce8d2ebe747f578be906f1249018}
bb-11.8-monty-rel$ cat ../data/1st.cnf

No issues found

bb-11.8-monty-rel$ sql/mariadbd --defaults-file=../data/1st.cnf --help

{noformat}

Probably same applies to numeric values, if there are any which are strictly rejected by 11.8 server rather than just triggering an adjustment with a warning.

Backup would cause some confusing if one uses updates several times as each run uses timestamped backups.  The 'several runs' can happen when the MariaDB server is used to check the changes and caused the changes to revert if it cannot use them.  In this case you would have a backup for each run.

If the changes are safe, as they should, and are verified by mariadbd (as they are done automatically and enabled by default) the changes should be safe for the original server and for the new server;  We are not deleting anything with --edit=inline or --edit=last.
If there are cases found where the tool would cause issues for the original server, then backups should probably be enabled by default.
So far I am not aware of any case where this could happen.

error-group is to be used when making MySQL config files usable for MariaDB.  The error-group argument is expected to be mysqld-#.##, the version of MySQL that the user is migration from. All options from [mysqld] or [server] that MariaDB do not support is moved to error-group to ensure that the MySQL server can still process them.
unsupported groups is for options in [mariadb] sections that MariaDB does not support.  This is needed if a config file already contains both options for both MySQL and MariaDB.  We cannot user --error-group here as then we would move things from [mariadbd] to [mysqld-#.##] without knowing if MySQL can handle the option.

What is checked are:
- That options exists
- If the option is an enum or set the value is checked.
- For string and number options, there is no easy way that the tool can check that the option is valid.
  However, if one is using --verify (on by default) the tool will run mariadbd on the server to validate all options. This will catch the wrong option and the changes will roll back.

h3. N12
*Trivial*

{quote}
Display or change unrecognized MariaDB options in MariaDB/MySQL

At least extra period at the end; also, MySQL vs MariaDB seems to be confusing, maybe leave it to "unrecognized options" and "unsupported options".

Missing {{]}}

h3. N13
*Suggestion*

Since {{\-\-verify}} option always requires {{\-\-mariadbd=path}} and {{\-\-mariadbd=path}} is only used for verification, it would make sense to make it one option, e.g. {{--verify=path}}. 

h3. N14
*Suggestion*

In edit=last mode, if the updated file has includes at the end of the file, the new section should be inserted before the includes, to reduce the risk of overwriting the includes. Now it added at the very end of the file.

_In any case, it should be made clear that in the scenario where the updated configuration files are still supposed to be used by the old server, it is NOT recommended to use {{edit=last}} mode. As already mentioned in the JIRA description, it can cause unexpected configuration changes, and the risk is real, because while it is not a good practice to have the same variable in different config files, it happens often in real life. On the other hand, when the updated config files are only used by the new server and the error-group is kept for informational purposes, {{edit=last}} mode is better, as its outcome is much cleaner and more readable._

h3. N15
*Suggestion*

h3. N16
*Major*

{{update-paths}} only has effect when there are other modifications to the file. In {{print}} mode, the tools shows the intention to change the paths, but in {{update}} mode no changes are made. 
{noformat}
bb-11.8-monty-debug$ cat ../data/1st.cnf
[mysqld]
datadir=/var/lib/mysql
socket=/var/lib/mysql/mysql.sock
log-error=/var/log/mysql/mysqld.log
pid-file=/run/mysqld/mysqld.pid

bb-11.8-monty-debug$ extra/mariadb-migrate-config-file --edit=last ../data/1st.cnf --update-paths --print
### File ../data/1st.cnf:
[mysqld]
datadir=/var/lib/mysql
pid-file=/run/mysqld/mysqld.pid

[mariadbd]
socket=/var/lib/mariadb/mysql.sock
log-error=/var/log/mariadb/mysqld.log

[mysqld-5.7]
socket=/var/lib/mysql/mysql.sock
log-error=/var/log/mysql/mysqld.log

bb-11.8-monty-debug$ extra/mariadb-migrate-config-file --edit=last ../data/1st.cnf --update-paths --update
4 issue/issues changed

bb-11.8-monty-debug$ cat ../data/1st.cnf
[mysqld]
datadir=/var/lib/mysql
socket=/var/lib/mysql/mysql.sock
log-error=/var/log/mysql/mysqld.log
pid-file=/run/mysqld/mysqld.pid
{noformat}

If there are other issues, like an unknown variable, then all modifications -- to the variable and to the paths -- are made. See also N17 regarding the functionality of {{update-paths}}.

h3. N17
*Major*

{{update-paths}} does not reflect the real-life location changes e.g. on an RPM-based system. This is the actual contents of mysql-server.cnf which MySQL 8.0 RPM installation installs on RHEL 9:
{noformat}
[mysqld]
datadir=/var/lib/mysql
socket=/var/lib/mysql/mysql.sock
log-error=/var/log/mysql/mysqld.log
pid-file=/run/mysqld/mysqld.pid
{noformat}

This is what the tool updates it when {{update-paths}} is set (when it works, see also N16):
{noformat}
[mysqld]
datadir=/var/lib/mysql
pid-file=/run/mysqld/mysqld.pid

[mariadbd]
socket=/var/lib/mariadb/mysql.sock
log-error=/var/log/mariadb/mysqld.log

[mysqld-5.7]
socket=/var/lib/mysql/mysql.sock
log-error=/var/log/mysql/mysqld.log
{noformat}

so,
- datadir is kept as {{/var/lib/mysql}} -- correct, that's what MariaDB 11.8 installation uses;
- pid-file is kept as {{/run/mysqld/mysqld.pid}} -- wrong, {{/run/mysqld}} no longer exists after removing MySQL and installing MariaDB, only {{/run/mariadbd}} exists;
- socket is changed to {{/var/lib/mariadb/mysql.sock}} -- wrong, MariaDB 11.8 installation does not create {{/var/lib/mariadb}}, it still uses {{/var/lib/mysql}}
- log-error is changed to {{/var/log/mariadb/mysqld.log}} -- wrong, MariaDB 11.8 installation does not create {{/var/log/mariadb}}

Thus, neither the old nor the new paths work for MariaDB -- if we don't run {{update-paths}}, then the server cannot start because of the pid-file, and if we run it, because of the socket and possibly the error log.
However, I don't know what would be a good solution here, as these paths are not at all universal, I expect them to be different on different OS flavors and server versions.

h3. N18
{color:red}*Critical*{color}

{{add-mariadb-replication-compatibility}} adds options incompatible with MySQL 5.7: {{binlog_row_value_options}}, {{binlog_transaction_compression}} -- they were only added in 8.0.
If they are really needed for replication compatibility, they should probably be added with {{loose-}} prefix.

h3. N19
*Minor*

{{add-}} flags add corresponding options to every inspected file. It is not harmful, but increases noise, adding them to the topmost file should be enough.

h3. N20
*Major*
{{copy-mysqld-groups}} only works when there are other modifications to the file. Much as {{update-paths}} in N16, {{print}} shows intended changes, but in {{update}} mode the modifications aren't made. It is quite important, as it means that the valid options will be ignored.
{noformat}
bb-11.8-monty-debug$ cat ../data/1st.cnf
[mysqld-8.4]
binlog_format = row

bb-11.8-monty-debug$ extra/mariadb-migrate-config-file  /data/bld/testing/data/1st.cnf --edit=last --update --copy-mysqld-groups
1 issue/issues changed

bb-11.8-monty-debug$ cat ../data/1st.cnf
[mysqld-8.4]
binlog_format = row
{noformat}

h3. N21
*Note*

A user needs to be aware that {{open_files_limit}} and {{table_open_cache_instances}} may change after migration.
Both MySQL and MariaDB configure {{LimitNOFILE}} in the systemd service file, MySQL 8.0 sets it to 10000 and MariaDB to 32768, which should be okay.
However, MariaDB also has a logic of migrating some options from the cnf files to the systemd file, specifically {{open_files_limit}} from {{[mysqld_safe]}} section.
So, if the old MySQL config has e.g.
{noformat}
[mysqld_safe]
open_files_limit               = 8192
{noformat}
(taken from a 3rd party public example config online), then MariaDB upon installation will configure it in {{/etc/systemd/system/mariadb.service.d/migrated-from-my.cnf-settings.conf}} and the resulting MariaDB instance will in turn have open_files_limit 8192. Too low limit can in turn affect {{table_open_cache_instances}} value.

h3. N22
*Note*

A user needs to remember that the fixed and verified config files may be disabled during removal of MySQL packages and installation of MariaDB (moved to .rpmsave), and will need to be restored afterwards.

h3. N23
*Note*

A user needs to remember that while the config migration tool deals with explicitly enabled options, there are plenty of default options which are different between MySQL and MariaDB and can seriously affect the functionality of the installation. I don't suppose the tool can do much about it, as it cannot know which MySQL version it is migrating from, and the defaults are different in a different versions.
Here is an example of differences between MySQL 8.0 and MariaDB 11.8 installation on RHEL 9 (default unchanged configs), no extra plugins. The full list is attached, but here are some options which I find quite important, either from the functional or from the security point of view: 
{noformat:title=MySQL 8.0 => MariaDB 11.8}
binlog_expire_logs_seconds: 2592000 => 0
binlog_format: ROW => MIXED
binlog_row_metadata: MINIMAL => NO_LOG
disconnect_on_expired_password: ON => OFF (security)
event_scheduler: ON => OFF
innodb_adaptive_hash_index: ON => OFF
local_infile: OFF => ON
log_bin: ON => OFF
log_slave_updates: ON => OFF
max_allowed_packet: 67108864 => 16777216
max_error_count: 1024 => 64
performance_schema: ON => OFF
secure_file_priv: /var/lib/mysql-files/ => (empty)
slave_parallel_workers: 4 => 0
sql_mode: ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY,<other> => <other>
sync_binlog: 1 => 0
{noformat}

h3. N27

*Note*

This is not a config migration failure, but an {color:red}important issue a user (or the migration team) needs to be aware of{color}.
When MySQL packages are installed on Debian, they come with two top-level configuration files, one from mysql-common and one from mysql-community-server. They are both *server* configuration files, according to the comments in the files.
Upon installation, Debian alternatives pick up and use the one from mysql-community-server as my.cnf.
This file contains two includes:
{noformat}
!includedir /etc/mysql/conf.d/
!includedir /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/
{noformat}
The directory /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/ indeed exists and is not empty, it contains a configuration file too, and naturally, users can add more.

While MySQL is installed, the configuration tool expectedly finds and updates files in {{/etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/}}, since they are included by the active version of my.cnf.
However, when MySQL packages get uninstalled, the debian alternatives are updated again, and while all configuration files remain in place (since we of course don't purge them for the purpose of migration), the one provided by mysql-common becomes the active my.cnf. And this file contains only one include
{noformat}
!includedir /etc/mysql/conf.d/
{noformat}

So, any configuration files located in /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d become invisible to the server/clients, and if the user has seen previous modifications of these files by the config tool and expects them to be effective after the migration, this expectation is wrong.

Installation of MariaDB does not remedy this situation, as it installs its own config which becomes the new best alternative, and it includes
{noformat}
!includedir /etc/mysql/conf.d/
!includedir /etc/mysql/mariadb.conf.d/
{noformat}
but not {{/etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d}}, which remains invisible.

When MySQL 8.0 Oracle RPM packages are installed on RHEL 9, they create {{/etc/my.cnf}} file and an empty {{/etc/my.cnf.d}} directory. However, {{/etc/my.cnf}} does *not* include {{/etc/my.cnf.d}}. So, whatever configuration files the user may accumulate in that folder on whatever reasons, unless my.cnf is also modified, they are not visible to the config migration tool and thus are not updated, it will only adjust my.cnf itself. 
When MySQL is uninstalled, my.cnf is moved to my.cnf.rpmsave, as mentioned above. 
When MariaDB 11.8 is installed, it creates its own /etc/my.cnf file which *does* include {{/etc/my.cnf.d}} which wasn't visible before and may contain any number of still incompatible configuration files which may prevent MariaDB from running. Then, still during installation, creation of system tables fails, but at the end dnf still pretends that it succeeded.

h3. Status
as of 0d70239f4c7ef7a5b0790cc4fa77459a599cf88c, 2026-04-12.

An upgrade from MySQL 8.4 (deb packages provided by Oracle) to MariaDB on Debian 12 and from MySQL 8.0 (RPM packages provided by Oracle) on RHEL 9 has been performed according to the agreed procedure:

- install MySQL (add some non-default configuration)
- download MariaDB bintar;
- use {{mariadb-migrate-config-file}} from the bintar to update the configuration files and mariadbd from the bintar to verify the config;
- make sure that MySQL still runs with the updated config, and configuration hasn't changed;
- remove MySQL packages;
- move MySQL datadir elsewhere;
- install MariaDB packages;
- make sure that MariaDB runs.

All in all, I think that the tool is functional and useful, as long as the users and migration experts understand that it's not expected to fix everything in all circumstances, but should be used as a helper to simplify migration, and the results should be inspected and verified. I do recommend fixing at least errors in the examples in the tool's help, to minimize the confusion. However, they do not affect the functionality, unless users copy-paste the command lines.

Usage notes (some of them are my opinion which may not reflect the official position):

- special attention should be paid to the changes of configuration file structure which happens during installation/uninstallation of packages, and which depends on the OS, package provider, old a new server version, etc. There are too many permutations, it's unrealistic for a tool to predict and address each of them individually. Examples for Debian and RHEL are described above;
- I do not recommend using {{update-paths}} upon migration to existing MariaDB versions. It is good to have for future, if we ever standardize paths which MariaDB uses or make them flexible, but now it is a mix of "mysql" and "mariadb" which is partially hidden in package installation scripts, partially hardcoded, and is very different depending on OS, package manufacturer, and server version;
- if the updated config is meant to be still used by MySQL installation before switching to MariaDB:
** the value of {{error-group}} option should be set to match the existing MySQL version, rather than leaving it to a default value. By default it is {{mysql-5.7}}, which means that for MySQL 8.x and 9.x servers the options which get moved to this section will become unavailable;
** it is useful to store the output of "show variables" before the config update, and then compare it with the variables after config update and MySQL restart. They should be identical, except for the timestamp and possible thread ID changes (and replication-related changes if the config update explicitly made those);
** it makes sense to verify the updated configuration files using {{\-\-verify \-\-mariadbd=}} pointing at the MySQL server binary (even though the option is called "mariadb") before restarting MySQL.
- client configuration sections are out of the scope of the tool and may contain incompatible options which will prevent the client programs from running;
- some options (numeric and string options) may contain values incompatible with the MariaDB server, "\-\-verify \-\-mariadbd=<mariadb server>" should help to detect this, so it should always be used;
- if there is a need to compare the updated file contents to the originals, blank space changes should be ignored, it will reduce the noise.

items.fromString:
A tool that helps to adjust config files after MariaDB is upgraded.

It can list all options that are no longer recognized by the server, suggest replacements, if any. It could also edit files in place (when requested), removing, commenting out, or adding loose- prefix to such options.

For example, if it's simply run without any arguments, it'll list unknown options (those that would prevent the server from starting). If started with {{\-\-edit}}, it will edit files in place. {{\-\-backup}} will make it to create backups. {{\-\-edit-mode=\{remove|comment|loose}}} would select what to do with unknown options. And so on.

To parse all files it could use {{my_print_defaults}}, the list of supported options could be hard-coded or extracted from {{mariadbd --help}} and such.

perl/python or C/C++ ?

items.toString:
A tool that helps to adjust config files after MariaDB is upgraded.

It can list all options that are no longer recognized by the server, suggest replacements, if any.
It could also edit files in place (when requested), removing, commenting out, or adding loose- prefix to such options.

Also it could check for invalid values of enum/set variables.

To parse all files it could use {{my_print_defaults}}, the list of supported options could be hard-coded or extracted from {{mariadbd --help}} and such.

perl/python or C/C++ ?  C or C++ is probably more portable for windows.

For code how to parse options like !include, check mysys/my_defaults.c

Suggested options:
- No options:  List unknown server options on stdout (those that would prevent the server from starting).
- --update
   - Update the my.cnf file in place (and all files included with !include or !includedir)
- --backup
  -  Store modified files as backup (for example my.cnf-backup)
- --current-version=...  (for example --current-version=mysqld-5.7)
  - Section to use for unknown options, see --mode
   - The purpose of --current-version is to enable the tool to create a config file that will work for both MySQL and MariaDB at
     the same time.  In this case, options that works for both MySQL and MariaDB should use the section [mysqld]. MySQL unique options should be under [mysqld-5.7] and MariaDB specific options
     would be under [mariadbd].
-- --edit=...
   - Select what to do with unknown options. List of suggested mode options:
     - remove                    Remove unoption
     - comment                Add # before option
     - inline-old-version  Add ['current-version'] before the option and [mysqld] afterwards.  'curent-version' is the tag specified with --current-version=...
     - last-old-version     Move all unknown version last in the file with [old-version] before.
-- print
   - Print converted file on stdout. In this case all !include  and !includedir files should be included.

We need both inline- and last- as some options may depend on their place in the config file.

The tool should also be prepared for special handling of some specific options.

Note that MariaDB don't have the audit_log plugin (Percona Server).
Instead MariaDB has a server_audit plugin which takes different options.
If the tool notice that 'audit_plugin' is used, it should suggest one to use the server_audit plugin instead.

--plugin-load=QUERY_RESPONSE_TIME_READ=query_response_time.so;QUERY_RESPONSE_TIME_WRITE=query_response_time.so
This is only supported in MariaDB 10.11 and above.  If used with an earlier MariaDB version it would be good to get a note that this is supported in 10.11.6 and above.

As a reference, here are some common config options found in Percona server that is not in MariaDB:
[mysqld-5.7]
--binlog-ignore-db=information_schema
--innodb_log_files_in_group=2
--innodb_buffer_pool_instances=3
--max_binlog_files=14
--log_slow_rate_type=query
--slow_query_log_always_write_time=0.5
--slow_query_log_use_global_control=all
--plugin-load=audit_log.so

fields.description:
The current JSON_DEPTH_LIMIT is 32 as defined in include/json_lib.h
Source code:
https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/22ffe4dd227451ebd0ef842850ef57b81aa8f930/include/json_lib.h#L10

This limit is not documented.

Customer requests to make this limit configurable with a global variable.

comments.body:
[~ralf.gebhardt] [~sanja] looks like there is [hard coded limit of 100|https://github.com/mysql/mysql-server/blob/87307d4ddd88405117e3f1e51323836d57ab1f57/sql-common/json_syntax_check.cc#L82]
And AFAIK the standards don't mention the limit explicitly.
I think it is possible to have user change the limit (like adding a server variable ) but we would still like there to be a upper limit right ?

A doubt: Is that *hard coded limit of 100* https://github.com/mysql/mysql-server/blob/87307d4ddd88405117e3f1e51323836d57ab1f57/sql-common/json_syntax_check.cc#L82 the new limit? or is it a different limit? The limit we saw and was limiting our product is *limit of 32*: https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/8ad1e26b1bafa4ed9928306efc10c047f2274108/include/json_lib.h#L10

Thanks!
[~macarnero] Hi ! My comment was a reply to an internal comment about MySQL, confirming the limit of 100 for MySQL, 32 for MariaDB.

🎉 What a wonderful piece of news!  Congrats!

[~rucha174] Please let me know the following so I can document this:
1. A short description of what JSON_DEPTH_LIMIT "does". Here's a guess: _JSON_DEPTH_LIMIT limits the maximum depth of the given JSON document._ 
2. Is that an active thing, though, comparable to a function, or does it rather just display the limit that is set elsewhere? (So, e.g., SELECT JSON_DEPTH_LIMIT might return "16".)
3. What's that global variable mentioned in the task description above?
4. What it that variable's maximum value? What's the default value?

[~stefan.hinz] Hi !
1) There's no  JSON_DEPTH_LIMIT now (at least in the server). It used to be hardcoded to 32 (meaning we only allowed nesting upto 32) . That limit has been removed as a part of this MDEV and we can now have unlimited depth on the fly. 
2) Not an active thing and cannot be set/used in select. It never was. It was just an internal macro used in the code to predefine the size of relevant arrays and throw errors in case the depth of the json exceeds 32 (because the arrays were predefined). The macro still exists though because it is still in use in columnstore.
3) No variable needed. You can have any depth on the fly.
4) There is no default value and the maximum can be as much as the memory allows :)
Documented here: https://mariadb.com/docs/server/reference/sql-functions/special-functions/json-functions/json_depth

Support for Oracle-stype INDEX BY tables (associative arrays) was added in stored routines and anonymous blocks, with this declaration syntax:

{code:sql}
 TYPE type_name TABLE OF rec_type_name INDEX BY idx_type_name;
{code}

where

- type_name supports explicit and anchored data types (e.g t1.col1%TYPE).
- The INDEX BY clause supports integer and string data types.
- rec_type_name supports scalar and record data types.

The implementation supports the following associative array methods:
- FIRST
- LAST
- NEXT
- PRIOR
- COUNT
- EXISTS
- DELETE

fields.description:
In addition to MDEV-27037, which validates that a binlog coordinate or datetime based stop position actually exists within a binary log file provided to mariadb-binlog, 10.11 also supports GTID input to --stop-position, and this should also be validated that the given GTID exists within the input set of binary logs.

For more details, see the discussion on the MDEV-27037's PR [here|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/3400#discussion_r1681030120].

comments.body: https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/3600

I fell for the same trap that causes MDEV-35528.
Unless we merge my PR first and then outsource its correction to that ticket, it blocks this work.
Approved, thanks [~ParadoxV5]!
Hey [~susil.behera], can you take a quick look at this task and its predecessors, MDEV-27037 & MDEV-35528, to see if they need formal QA?

Thanks for the verification, [~susil.behera]!

About non-existent Server IDs, it is because {{mariadb-binlog}} position filters ignore them and only care about Domain IDs and Sequence Numbers.
From what I understand, GTID sequences are intended to be agnostic of servers and thus their IDs.

For your case, the 0 and the 7 already match, so the 101 didn’t matter. (And neither would it matter if those two don’t match.)
Note how yours will output no GTID events with either {{\-\-stop-position=0-100-5}} or {{\-\-stop-position=0-101-5}}.

C.C. [~bnestere]

Ignoring server_id sounds very wrong.

Sequence numbers can be assumed to be increasing within a single (domain_id, server_id) pair, but _not_ between different server_id.

So if the binlog contains:

  0-1-10 0-1-11 0-2-10 0-2-11 0-2-12 0-3-11 0-3-12

Then a starting position of 0-2-10 must start with the GTID 0-2-11, _not_ 0-1-11.
Likewise, a stop postion of 0-3-11 must stop at 0-3-11, _not_ 0-1-11 or 0-2-11.

If the mysqlbinlog GTID filters are ignoring sequence numbers, it sounds like they are simply implemented incorrectly (not surprising perhaps). The correct way involves looking at the GTID_LIST event at the start of the binlog to understand the state of sequence numbers for each (domain_id, server_id) combination, and using this to decide if a given GTID comes before this binlog, or is contained in this or a later binlog.

Possibly rewriting / fixing the GTID filter implementation of mysqlbinlog is a bit out of scope of this task. But on the other hand, is there any point in implementing a warning about stop position that is not reliable? Seems better to provide no information than incorrect/misleading information?

{quote}
So if the binlog contains:

0-1-10 0-1-11 0-2-10 0-2-11 0-2-12 0-3-11 0-3-12
{quote}
Then, {{mariadb-binlog}} would error because {{--gtid-strict-mode}} is on by default.

But, let’s suppose we’d recognize {{--skip-gtid-strict-mode}} cases.
I’m confident that it will not be difficult to add {{server_id}} to the existing implementation (that presumably can find the Domain ID from the GTID list).
It’d be a separate bugfix, of course, but that should naturally fix Susil’s case as well.

Well, the --gtid-strict-mode of mysqbinlog is just silly, it makes no sense.

In the server, we have --gtid-strict-mode, which is a tool for DBAs who prefer to get replication to fail with an error eg. to detect incorrect configuration.

But mysqlbinlog doesn't modify anything, it is just a tool to inspect the binlog. If the binlog is already written in violation of --gtid-strict-mode, what is the point of refusing to show the content?

In the example with start position 0-2-10 and binlog "0-2-10 0-1-10 0-1-11 0-1-12 ...", it will start from 0-1-10, it will not skip all future transactions. There is nothing arbitrary about this, the key to understanding GTID is to understand that GTID sequence is defined by the _binlog order_. This means that the GTID sequence is defined by how the binlog is written, not by the sequence numbers. A starting GTID of 0-2-10 means to find 0-2-10 in the binlog, wherever it is, and then start from the following GTID (in that domain).

{quote}
Well, the --gtid-strict-mode of mysqbinlog is just silly, it makes no sense.
\[…]
But mysqlbinlog doesn't modify anything, it is just a tool to inspect the binlog.
{quote}
The intent was,
bq. Though generally, I suppose it doesn't matter whether or not the logic is arbitrary or not, {{mysqlbinlog}} should behave the same as a slave. I.e. if the slave provides some GTID to start replication, mysqlbinlog should output the same transactions.
That is, A replica replicating should be analogous to {{mariadb-binlog //network/path/to/master-bin.XXXXXX | mariadb}}, as demonstrated in [Brandon’s blog|https://mariadb.com/resources/blog/build-your-own-command-line-replica-with-gtid-aware-mariadb-binlog-part-1/].

({{--gtid-strict-mode}} isn’t default on for {{mariadbd}}, though?)

Monday greetings. Since the discussion stopped for almost a week, I’m moving forward with the PR.

The conclusion so far: It’s valuable for {{mariadb-binlog}} to match a replica server, though the behaviour is questionable.

It worries me that you write "the behaviour is questionable", it sounds like you have not understood the fundamentals of how GTID lookup works?

The GTID lookup as implemented in the dump thread (ie. slave connect) is very carefully designed to work correctly. The slave specifies a GTID position to start at, and optionally one to stop at. The dump thread will, within each domain, find the specified starting GTID, and start sending events from that point. It will continue sending the domain until it sees the specified stop GTID.

If the user specified GTID 0-1-100, and mysqlbinlog instead started or stopped at GTID 0-2-100 or some other GTID not specified, that would be worse than questionable, simply wrong.

Or do you mean the default value of --gtid-strict-mode for mysqlbinlog is questionable? I still think it's silly to have it on by default, but that's less serious than wrong result, user can just change it.

bq. The dump thread will, within each domain, find the specified starting GTID, and start sending events from that point. It will continue sending the domain until it sees the specified stop GTID.
What happens if the replica specified GTID 0-1-100 but the primary’s binlog has 0-2-100? (at this time, not “should”)

I tested.
Replication doesn’t stop at 0-1-2 when specified {{UNTIL master_gtid_pos='0-9-2'}}.
But {{mariadb-binlog}} _do_ stop at 0-1-2 with {{--stop-position=0-9-2}}.

So, it’s simple: *{{mariadb-binlog --stop-position}} is +both+ wrong and inconsistent.*
Not too hard, isn’t it?
While the PR waits for the CI — dedicated bug report coming right up

Where are the fields for Bug Category and Release Note Summary?
Well, I suppose this isn’t completely a bug.

Release Notes based on [the PR|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/3600]:
* {{mariadb-binlog}} now warns about any {{--stop-position}} GTIDs that didn’t apply after reading the entire log.
Test fix for S390x: https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4200

fields.summary: Asynchronous and Buffered Logging for Audit Plugin

issuetype.description: A new feature of the product, which has yet to be developed.
issuetype.name: New Feature

fields.description:
h1. Introduction

The server_audit_plugin employs synchronous, per-event logging, causing performance bottlenecks. Individual file writes for each log entry result in significant I/O overhead, especially in large database environments.

h1. Detailed Description (Solution)

A dedicated logging thread is implemented to reduce the main audit plugin thread's wait time from synchronous write operations.The main audit plugin thread now pushes messages into a thread-safe queue, which efficiently manages concurrent access. Upon each push, it checks if the queue has reached its capacity. If the queue is full, the main thread signals the logger thread to flush and process the messages. This approach ensures efficient logging by reducing the performance hit from frequent thread creation and maintaining smooth, high-throughput operations in write-heavy applications. To further guarantee security, we introduced an additional system variable that allows users to set a log buffer time. This enhancement enables the audit plugin to periodically poll the buffer queue. If the queue is not empty, it will flush the messages at specified intervals. This approach ensures that during high throughput periods, the buffer size will be exceeded and flushed accordingly. Conversely, during low throughput periods, users are guaranteed to receive their logs after a certain period. This dual-variable system provides a more adaptive and efficient logging mechanism, accommodating fluctuations in database activity while maintaining optimal performance and security. 

h2. Summary of Changes

*Buffered Logging:*
* Implement an in-memory buffer to reduce disk I/O by batching log writes.

*Asynchronous Logging:*
* Delegate logging to a dedicated logger thread for independent log handling,
minimizing wait times for main audit threads

*Dynamic Buffer Management:*
* Add log_buffer_size and log_buffer_time system variables for user-customizable
flushing based on data volume or time, adapting to varying workloads.

*Confirm Performance Improvement:*
* An average of 15% speed improvements confirmed in benchmark tests, demonstrating the
effectiveness of these logging enhancements in high-load environments.

h1. Additional Information

h2. System Variables Added

{color:red}************
Note: this section is outdated. Ref [here|https://jira.mariadb.org/browse/MDEV-34680?focusedCommentId=306336&page=com.atlassian.jira.plugin.system.issuetabpanels:comment-tabpanel#comment-306336] and MDEV-36956 for the actual implemented variables.
************{color}

h3.  server_audit_log_buffer_size

*Description*: When server_audit_log_buffer_size is set, it determines the maximum number of log messages 
the buffer can hold. If the buffer reaches its limit, it flushes the logs and writes them to the file. The default value is 1, which means logs are directly written without buffering. Adjusting this value allows for batch logging, improving performance by reducing the overhead of writing each log message individually.     

*Commandline:* --server-audit-log-buffer-size=value

*Scope:* Global

*Dynamic:* Yes

*Data Type:* numeric

*Default Value:* 1

*Range:* 1 to 9999

h3. server_audit_log_buffer_time

*Description*: When server_audit_log_buffer_time is set, it determines how often, in milliseconds, the queue of log messages flushes itself. The default value is 1000 ms (1 second). This longer interval is due to the initial server_audit_log_buffer_size being 1, meaning logs are directly written without significant buffering. Adjusting this value allows for fine-tuning how frequently the logs are written, balancing between real-time logging and performance optimization.

*Commandline:* --server-audit-log-buffer-time=value

*Scope:* Global

*Dynamic:* Yes

*Data Type:* numeric

*Default Value:* 1000

*Range:* 1000 to 3600000 (1 hour)


h3. Results

Below are the benchmarking results comparing three implementations: the original buffer size only, the default audit plugin, and the combination of buffer size and buffer time. 

For these tests, the buffer size was set to 100, and the buffer time was set to 1000 ms (1 second).


*Benchmarking with 64 Threads: Performance Improvements Compared to Default*

| Implementation | QPS | TPS | Avg Latency (ms) | Total Transactions | QPS Improvement vs | TPS Improvement vs | Avg Latency Improve | Total Transactions Improve |
| Synchronous Direct Logging (Default) | 8182.0 | 1363.7 | 187.4 | 82011 | 0.0% | 0.0% | 0.0% | 0.0% |
| Asynchronous Logging with Buffer Size | 9535.9 | 1589.3 | 160.8 | 95561 | 16.5% | 16.5% | 14.2% | 16.5% |
| Asynchronous Logging with Buffer Size and Buffer Time | 10263.9 | 1710.6 | 149.6 | 102790 | 25.4% | 25.4% | 20.2% | 25.3% |

*Benchmarking with 256 Threads: Performance Improvements Compared to Default*

| Implementation | QPS | TPS | Avg Latency (ms) | Total Transactions | QPS Improvement vs | TPS Improvement vs | Avg Latency Improve | Total Transactions Improve |
| Synchronous Direct Logging (Default) | 2501.8 | 417.0 | 153.4 | 25116 | 0.0% | 0.0% | 0.0% | 0.0% |
| Asynchronous Logging with Buffer Size | 3225.4 | 537.6 | 118.8 | 32330 | 28.9% | 28.9% | 22.6% | 28.7% |
| Asynchronous Logging with Buffer Size and Buffer Time | 3239.9 | 540.0 | 118.2 | 32554 | 29.5% | 29.5% | 23.0% | 29.6% |


h1. Update After Feedback

After receiving feedback from Upstream, I was advised against adding additional threads since MariaDB already has built-in timer threads that can handle asynchronous time-based logging. Consequently, size-based logging will now operate synchronously. Utilizing the thr_time class, I have successfully implemented this approach. Below are the updated benchmarking results, comparing this implementation to the default audit plugin.

h3. Below are the results for New Implementation set to Default Configurations. The `log_buffer_size` is set to 1 here to mimic instant logging.

*64 Threads*
| Metric               |   Default |      New |   % Improvement |
| transactions_per_sec |     466.9 |    453.6 |            -2.8 |
| queries_per_sec      |    2801.3 |   2821.6 |             0.7 |
| total_events         |   28089   |  27271   |            -2.9 |

| total_queries        |  168534   | 163626   |            -2.9 |

*256 Threads*
| Metric               |   Default |      New |   % Improvement |

*512 Threads*

h3. Below are the results for New Implementation set to Buffered Configurations. The `log_buffer_size` is set to 1000 and `log_buffer_time` was set to 20 seconds here to mimic buffered logging.


*64 Threads*
| Metric               |   Default |      New |   % Improvement |

We observe that instant logging with this implementation performs almost as efficiently as the default implementation. However, significant performance improvements are achieved when using the buffer.

Note: We were unable to benchmark time-based buffered logging because improvements or regressions can only be detected with high throughput, which can only test size-based buffering.

Looks good to me.

I just didn't like
{code:sql}
--exec wc -l < $MYSQLD_DATADIR/server_audit.log
{code}
in the test file, better change it to something portable. E.g. {{perl}} command.

As discussed with [~holyfoot]:

* The {{\-\-server-audit-file-buffer-size}} implemented variable is what {{\-\-server-audit-log-buffer-size}} was in the description.
* The {{\-\-server-audit-sync-log-file}} was added instead, so the file buffer can be written to disk/the file when needed.

And 

* The {{\-\-server-audit-log-buffer-time}} was not implemented upon some decision.

* Created MDEV-36956 Document two new audit log variables
* Updated MDEV-36955 plugins.server_audit_buffering fails sporadically, server_audit_file_buffer_size setting not working

The latter shows an incorrect operation of the feature so I am reverting this ticket to [~holyfoot] for an updated patch. Please also merge the latest trunk (or use a new trunk clone), which will help with testing. 

[~holyfoot] when fixing this, please at the same time update the variable description for {{--server-audit-file-buffer-size}} to read:
{noformat}
From:
Size of file buffer to make logging faster
To:
Size of the audit log file buffer, in number of statements, to make logging faster. Min: 0 (Off), Max: 9999
{noformat}
Provided that the Max number still matches the original description. The "in number of statements" is however the important part, to avoid confusion with byte-sized buffers versus statement-sized buffers. Also, the original description states "messages" instead of "statements" so it would be great if this could be clarified also - i.e. does message indeed mean statement, or is it rather an '\n' terminated line (think for example stored procedures, etc.)? Finally, the default value in the description says "1" whereas it is 0. In total, perhaps it would be best to update the original description to reflect the actual implementation. Thank you

In the meantime, I will continue to test overall feature stability.

## Introduction

The server_audit_plugin employs synchronous, per-event logging, causing performance bottlenecks. Individual file writes for each log entry result in significant I/O overhead, especially in large database environments.

## Detailed Description (Solution)

A dedicated logging thread is implemented to reduce the main audit plugin thread's wait time from synchronous write operations.The main audit plugin thread now pushes messages into a thread-safe queue, which efficiently manages concurrent access. Upon each push, it checks if the queue has reached its capacity. If the queue is full, the main thread signals the logger thread to flush and process the messages. This approach ensures efficient logging by reducing the performance hit from frequent thread creation and maintaining smooth, high-throughput operations in write-heavy applications. To further guarantee security, we introduced an additional system variable that allows users to set a log buffer time. This enhancement enables the audit plugin to periodically poll the buffer queue. If the queue is not empty, it will flush the messages at specified intervals. This approach ensures that during high throughput periods, the buffer size will be exceeded and flushed accordingly. Conversely, during low throughput periods, users are guaranteed to receive their logs after a certain period. This dual-variable system provides a more adaptive and efficient logging mechanism, accommodating fluctuations in database activity while maintaining optimal performance and security. 



### Summary of Changes

***Buffered Logging***:
- Implement an in-memory buffer to reduce disk I/O by batching log writes.

***Asynchronous Logging***:
- Delegate logging to a dedicated logger thread for independent log handling,
minimizing wait times for main audit threads

***Dynamic Buffer Management***:
- Add log_buffer_size and log_buffer_time system variables for user-customizable
flushing based on data volume or time, adapting to varying workloads.

***Confirm Performance Improvement***:
- An average of 15% speed improvements confirmed in benchmark tests, demonstrating the
effectiveness of these logging enhancements in high-load environments.

## Additional Information

### System Variables Added

#### server_audit_log_buffer_size

**Description**: When server_audit_log_buffer_size is set, it determines the maximum number of log messages 
the buffer can hold. If the buffer reaches its limit, it flushes the logs and writes them to the file. The default value is 1, which means logs are directly written without buffering. Adjusting this value allows for batch logging, improving performance by reducing the overhead of writing each log message individually.     

**Commandline:** --server-audit-file-path=value

**Scope:** Global

**Dynamic:** Yes

**Data Type:** numeric

**Default Value:** 1

**Range:** 1 to 9999

#### server_audit_log_buffer_time

**Description**: When server_audit_log_buffer_time is set, it determines how often, in milliseconds, the queue of log messages flushes itself. The default value is 1000 ms (1 second). This longer interval is due to the initial server_audit_log_buffer_size being 1, meaning logs are directly written without significant buffering. Adjusting this value allows for fine-tuning how frequently the logs are written, balancing between real-time logging and performance optimization.

**Scope:** Global

**Dynamic:** Yes

**Data Type:** numeric

**Default Value:** 1000

**Range:** 1000 to 3600000 (1 hour)


### Results

Below are the benchmarking results comparing three implementations: the original buffer size only, the default audit plugin, and the combination of buffer size and buffer time. 

For these tests, the buffer size was set to 100, and the buffer time was set to 1000 ms (1 second).


**Benchmarking With 256 Threads: Performance Improvements Compared To Default**

| Implementation                                  | QPS    | TPS    | Avg Latency (ms) | Total Transactions | QPS Improvement vs | TPS Improvement vs | Avg Latency Improve | Total Transactions Improve |
|-------------------------------------------------|--------|--------|------------------|--------------------|---------------------|---------------------|---------------------|----------------------------|
| Synchronous Direct Logging (Default)            | 8182.0 | 1363.7 | 187.4            | 82011              | 0.0%                | 0.0%                | 0.0%                | 0.0%                       |
| Asynchronous Logging with Buffer Size           | 9535.9 | 1589.3 | 160.8            | 95561              | 16.5%               | 16.5%               | 14.2%               | 16.5%                      |
| Asynchronous Logging with Buffer Size and Buffer Time | 10263.9 | 1710.6 | 149.6            | 102790             | 25.4%               | 25.4%               | 20.2%               | 25.3%                      |


**Benchmarking With 64 Threads: Performance Improvements Compared To Default**

| Implementation                                  | QPS    | TPS    | Avg Latency (ms) | Total Transactions | QPS Improvement vs | TPS Improvement vs | Avg Latency Improve | Total Transactions Improve |
|-------------------------------------------------|--------|--------|------------------|--------------------|---------------------|---------------------|---------------------|----------------------------|
| Synchronous Direct Logging (Default)            | 2501.8 | 417.0  | 153.4            | 25116              | 0.0%                | 0.0%                | 0.0%                | 0.0%                       |
| Asynchronous Logging with Buffer Size           | 3225.4 | 537.6  | 118.8            | 32330              | 28.9%               | 28.9%               | 22.6%               | 28.7%                      |
| Asynchronous Logging with Buffer Size and Buffer Time | 3239.9 | 540.0  | 118.2            | 32554              | 29.5%               | 29.5%               | 23.0%               | 29.6%                      |

h2. Introduction

The server_audit_plugin employs synchronous, per-event logging, causing performance bottlenecks. Individual file writes for each log entry result in significant I/O overhead, especially in large database environments.

h2. Detailed Description (Solution)

A dedicated logging thread is implemented to reduce the main audit plugin thread's wait time from synchronous write operations.The main audit plugin thread now pushes messages into a thread-safe queue, which efficiently manages concurrent access. Upon each push, it checks if the queue has reached its capacity. If the queue is full, the main thread signals the logger thread to flush and process the messages. This approach ensures efficient logging by reducing the performance hit from frequent thread creation and maintaining smooth, high-throughput operations in write-heavy applications. To further guarantee security, we introduced an additional system variable that allows users to set a log buffer time. This enhancement enables the audit plugin to periodically poll the buffer queue. If the queue is not empty, it will flush the messages at specified intervals. This approach ensures that during high throughput periods, the buffer size will be exceeded and flushed accordingly. Conversely, during low throughput periods, users are guaranteed to receive their logs after a certain period. This dual-variable system provides a more adaptive and efficient logging mechanism, accommodating fluctuations in database activity while maintaining optimal performance and security. 

h3. Summary of Changes

*Buffered Logging:*
* Implement an in-memory buffer to reduce disk I/O by batching log writes.

*Asynchronous Logging:*
* Delegate logging to a dedicated logger thread for independent log handling,
minimizing wait times for main audit threads

*Dynamic Buffer Management:*
* Add log_buffer_size and log_buffer_time system variables for user-customizable
flushing based on data volume or time, adapting to varying workloads.

*Confirm Performance Improvement:*
* An average of 15% speed improvements confirmed in benchmark tests, demonstrating the
effectiveness of these logging enhancements in high-load environments.

h2. Additional Information

h3. System Variables Added

h4.  server_audit_log_buffer_size

*Description*: When server_audit_log_buffer_size is set, it determines the maximum number of log messages 
the buffer can hold. If the buffer reaches its limit, it flushes the logs and writes them to the file. The default value is 1, which means logs are directly written without buffering. Adjusting this value allows for batch logging, improving performance by reducing the overhead of writing each log message individually.     

*Commandline:* --server-audit-log-buffer-size=value

*Scope:* Global

*Dynamic:* Yes

*Data Type:* numeric

*Default Value:* 1

*Range:* 1 to 9999

h4. server_audit_log_buffer_time

*Description*: When server_audit_log_buffer_time is set, it determines how often, in milliseconds, the queue of log messages flushes itself. The default value is 1000 ms (1 second). This longer interval is due to the initial server_audit_log_buffer_size being 1, meaning logs are directly written without significant buffering. Adjusting this value allows for fine-tuning how frequently the logs are written, balancing between real-time logging and performance optimization.

*Commandline:* --server-audit-log-buffer-time=value

*Scope:* Global

*Dynamic:* Yes

*Data Type:* numeric

*Default Value:* 1000

*Range:* 1000 to 3600000 (1 hour)


h3. Results

h1. Introduction

The server_audit_plugin employs synchronous, per-event logging, causing performance bottlenecks. Individual file writes for each log entry result in significant I/O overhead, especially in large database environments.

h1. Detailed Description (Solution)

A dedicated logging thread is implemented to reduce the main audit plugin thread's wait time from synchronous write operations.The main audit plugin thread now pushes messages into a thread-safe queue, which efficiently manages concurrent access. Upon each push, it checks if the queue has reached its capacity. If the queue is full, the main thread signals the logger thread to flush and process the messages. This approach ensures efficient logging by reducing the performance hit from frequent thread creation and maintaining smooth, high-throughput operations in write-heavy applications. To further guarantee security, we introduced an additional system variable that allows users to set a log buffer time. This enhancement enables the audit plugin to periodically poll the buffer queue. If the queue is not empty, it will flush the messages at specified intervals. This approach ensures that during high throughput periods, the buffer size will be exceeded and flushed accordingly. Conversely, during low throughput periods, users are guaranteed to receive their logs after a certain period. This dual-variable system provides a more adaptive and efficient logging mechanism, accommodating fluctuations in database activity while maintaining optimal performance and security. 

h2. Summary of Changes

*Buffered Logging:*
* Implement an in-memory buffer to reduce disk I/O by batching log writes.

*Asynchronous Logging:*
* Delegate logging to a dedicated logger thread for independent log handling,
minimizing wait times for main audit threads

*Dynamic Buffer Management:*
* Add log_buffer_size and log_buffer_time system variables for user-customizable
flushing based on data volume or time, adapting to varying workloads.

*Confirm Performance Improvement:*
* An average of 15% speed improvements confirmed in benchmark tests, demonstrating the
effectiveness of these logging enhancements in high-load environments.

h1. Additional Information

h2. System Variables Added

h3.  server_audit_log_buffer_size

*Description*: When server_audit_log_buffer_size is set, it determines the maximum number of log messages 
the buffer can hold. If the buffer reaches its limit, it flushes the logs and writes them to the file. The default value is 1, which means logs are directly written without buffering. Adjusting this value allows for batch logging, improving performance by reducing the overhead of writing each log message individually.     

*Commandline:* --server-audit-log-buffer-size=value

*Scope:* Global

*Dynamic:* Yes

*Data Type:* numeric

*Default Value:* 1

*Range:* 1 to 9999

h3. server_audit_log_buffer_time

*Description*: When server_audit_log_buffer_time is set, it determines how often, in milliseconds, the queue of log messages flushes itself. The default value is 1000 ms (1 second). This longer interval is due to the initial server_audit_log_buffer_size being 1, meaning logs are directly written without significant buffering. Adjusting this value allows for fine-tuning how frequently the logs are written, balancing between real-time logging and performance optimization.

*Commandline:* --server-audit-log-buffer-time=value

*Scope:* Global

*Dynamic:* Yes

*Data Type:* numeric

*Default Value:* 1000

*Range:* 1000 to 3600000 (1 hour)

h1. Introduction

The server_audit_plugin employs synchronous, per-event logging, causing performance bottlenecks. Individual file writes for each log entry result in significant I/O overhead, especially in large database environments.

h1. Detailed Description (Solution)

A dedicated logging thread is implemented to reduce the main audit plugin thread's wait time from synchronous write operations.The main audit plugin thread now pushes messages into a thread-safe queue, which efficiently manages concurrent access. Upon each push, it checks if the queue has reached its capacity. If the queue is full, the main thread signals the logger thread to flush and process the messages. This approach ensures efficient logging by reducing the performance hit from frequent thread creation and maintaining smooth, high-throughput operations in write-heavy applications. To further guarantee security, we introduced an additional system variable that allows users to set a log buffer time. This enhancement enables the audit plugin to periodically poll the buffer queue. If the queue is not empty, it will flush the messages at specified intervals. This approach ensures that during high throughput periods, the buffer size will be exceeded and flushed accordingly. Conversely, during low throughput periods, users are guaranteed to receive their logs after a certain period. This dual-variable system provides a more adaptive and efficient logging mechanism, accommodating fluctuations in database activity while maintaining optimal performance and security. 

h2. Summary of Changes

*Buffered Logging:*
* Implement an in-memory buffer to reduce disk I/O by batching log writes.

*Asynchronous Logging:*
* Delegate logging to a dedicated logger thread for independent log handling,
minimizing wait times for main audit threads

*Dynamic Buffer Management:*
* Add log_buffer_size and log_buffer_time system variables for user-customizable
flushing based on data volume or time, adapting to varying workloads.

*Confirm Performance Improvement:*
* An average of 15% speed improvements confirmed in benchmark tests, demonstrating the
effectiveness of these logging enhancements in high-load environments.

h1. Additional Information

h2. System Variables Added

h3.  server_audit_log_buffer_size

*Description*: When server_audit_log_buffer_size is set, it determines the maximum number of log messages 
the buffer can hold. If the buffer reaches its limit, it flushes the logs and writes them to the file. The default value is 1, which means logs are directly written without buffering. Adjusting this value allows for batch logging, improving performance by reducing the overhead of writing each log message individually.     

*Commandline:* --server-audit-log-buffer-size=value

*Scope:* Global

*Dynamic:* Yes

*Data Type:* numeric

*Default Value:* 1

*Range:* 1 to 9999

h3. server_audit_log_buffer_time

*Description*: When server_audit_log_buffer_time is set, it determines how often, in milliseconds, the queue of log messages flushes itself. The default value is 1000 ms (1 second). This longer interval is due to the initial server_audit_log_buffer_size being 1, meaning logs are directly written without significant buffering. Adjusting this value allows for fine-tuning how frequently the logs are written, balancing between real-time logging and performance optimization.

*Commandline:* --server-audit-log-buffer-time=value

*Scope:* Global

*Dynamic:* Yes

*Data Type:* numeric

*Default Value:* 1000

*Range:* 1000 to 3600000 (1 hour)


h3. Results

Below are the benchmarking results comparing three implementations: the original buffer size only, the default audit plugin, and the combination of buffer size and buffer time.

h1. Introduction

The server_audit_plugin employs synchronous, per-event logging, causing performance bottlenecks. Individual file writes for each log entry result in significant I/O overhead, especially in large database environments.

h1. Detailed Description (Solution)

A dedicated logging thread is implemented to reduce the main audit plugin thread's wait time from synchronous write operations.The main audit plugin thread now pushes messages into a thread-safe queue, which efficiently manages concurrent access. Upon each push, it checks if the queue has reached its capacity. If the queue is full, the main thread signals the logger thread to flush and process the messages. This approach ensures efficient logging by reducing the performance hit from frequent thread creation and maintaining smooth, high-throughput operations in write-heavy applications. To further guarantee security, we introduced an additional system variable that allows users to set a log buffer time. This enhancement enables the audit plugin to periodically poll the buffer queue. If the queue is not empty, it will flush the messages at specified intervals. This approach ensures that during high throughput periods, the buffer size will be exceeded and flushed accordingly. Conversely, during low throughput periods, users are guaranteed to receive their logs after a certain period. This dual-variable system provides a more adaptive and efficient logging mechanism, accommodating fluctuations in database activity while maintaining optimal performance and security. 

h2. Summary of Changes

*Buffered Logging:*
* Implement an in-memory buffer to reduce disk I/O by batching log writes.

*Asynchronous Logging:*
* Delegate logging to a dedicated logger thread for independent log handling,
minimizing wait times for main audit threads

*Dynamic Buffer Management:*
* Add log_buffer_size and log_buffer_time system variables for user-customizable
flushing based on data volume or time, adapting to varying workloads.

*Confirm Performance Improvement:*

h1. Introduction

The server_audit_plugin employs synchronous, per-event logging, causing performance bottlenecks. Individual file writes for each log entry result in significant I/O overhead, especially in large database environments.

h1. Detailed Description (Solution)

A dedicated logging thread is implemented to reduce the main audit plugin thread's wait time from synchronous write operations.The main audit plugin thread now pushes messages into a thread-safe queue, which efficiently manages concurrent access. Upon each push, it checks if the queue has reached its capacity. If the queue is full, the main thread signals the logger thread to flush and process the messages. This approach ensures efficient logging by reducing the performance hit from frequent thread creation and maintaining smooth, high-throughput operations in write-heavy applications. To further guarantee security, we introduced an additional system variable that allows users to set a log buffer time. This enhancement enables the audit plugin to periodically poll the buffer queue. If the queue is not empty, it will flush the messages at specified intervals. This approach ensures that during high throughput periods, the buffer size will be exceeded and flushed accordingly. Conversely, during low throughput periods, users are guaranteed to receive their logs after a certain period. This dual-variable system provides a more adaptive and efficient logging mechanism, accommodating fluctuations in database activity while maintaining optimal performance and security. 

h2. Summary of Changes

*Buffered Logging:*
* Implement an in-memory buffer to reduce disk I/O by batching log writes.

*Asynchronous Logging:*
* Delegate logging to a dedicated logger thread for independent log handling,
minimizing wait times for main audit threads

*Dynamic Buffer Management:*
* Add log_buffer_size and log_buffer_time system variables for user-customizable
flushing based on data volume or time, adapting to varying workloads.

*Confirm Performance Improvement:*

effectiveness of these logging enhancements in high-load environments.

Log write buffering added to the SERVER_AUDIT plugin.
The buffering is controlled by the added variables:
server_audit_file_buffer_size  - defines the size of the buffer.
The default value is 0 meaning there's no buffering at all.
Setting non-zero value enables the buffering with the buffer of the specified size aligned by 8192. The maximum value is 65536.
server_audit_sync_log_file - flushes the buffer to the log file.
  While the log record is in the buffer, it cannot be seen in the log file. And if there are not many events to log, the time before records can be observed can be significant. So user can do 
SET GLOBAL server_audit_log_file=1
to this variable to force write the buffer to the file, to make sure he doesn't miss the recent records.

fields.description:
No need for two MSAN clang based builders.
We already have clang-16 as a Protected builder.

Will remove the clang-15 based one and prepare a clang-20 image.

Transition plan:

h1.  dev environment

The current update removes the amd64-debian-11-msan builder. This is significantly obsolete already because of the later clang-16 protected branch builder.

A amd64-msan-clang-20/amd64-msan-clang-20-debug are the replacements.

The non-debug builder is considered the primary focus. Based on discussions with Marko a RelWithDebInfo build represents a closer to production codebase and only features minor changes because of HAVE_VALGRIND (unfortunately) and narrowly scoped MSAN instrumentation. Previous debug only initialization in the server has left MSAN/Valgrind builders pleasantly green while the RelWithDebInfo builders where obvivious to the undefined behaviour they where carrying.

The updates to the msan.fragment.Dockerfile means that the clang-16 builder is no longer built by the github actions. There are incompatibilities with the way the cleaned up fragment of msan and its master.cfg file operate that render it incompatible the the clang-16 current stable protected branch builder and its configuration file.

msan-clang-16 builder, a protected branch builder, definition in master-docker-nonstandard/master.cfg because we want to keep it alive while we validate the new msan-clang-20 builder. As such this builder isn't changed at all.

Several clang major versions ago [~marko] observed some 2½ to 3½ times overhead for MSAN under Debug builds. As such MSAN debug instrumented builder some tests are more likely to time out.

h1. prod deployment

usual dev-> prod procedure.

h1. upgrade to protected builder

* The upgrade of amd64-msan-clang-20 to a protected branch builder will replace msan-clang-16.
* amd64-msan-clang-20  will become a github status builder replacing msan-clang-16
* The msan-clang-16 builder will be decommissioned
* amd64-msan-clang-20-debug because of risks and low added value will *not* become a protected branch builder.

Take into account that now f_msan_build factory in master-docker-nonstandard-2 is not equal anymore with f_msan_build factory in master-docker-nonstandard (where clang-16 builder is).

Things to note:

* a protected branches builder should have backup workers. It's OK that now these 2 builders only have apexis, they are not protected. MSAN Clang-16 for example has hz-bbw1 / 4 / 5 as worker nodes.
*  at transitioning, f_msan_build factory that clang-16 uses is no longer valid (right ?) and we can move f_msan_build from master-docker-nonstandard-2/master.cf to in common_factories.py and of course, adjust the worker pool of these the amd64-msan-clang-20 (non-debug only) builder when they become protected.

Addressed review comments, almost all accepted.

with the exception of currently failing to rebase/squash to a small number of commits (:sorry:, sad:, :pleadingforgiveness:).
rebased and commits=4 with good descriptions.

Debug builds - yes something in server needs to be corrected. Don't think a MDEV exists yet.

non-debug -  CONC-755  applies - submodule not updated.

archive.archive-big                      w16 [ fail ]  timeout after 900 seconds
- tempted to add not-msan in  the server side.

[~danblack]
I suggest removing the builders from constants.py until they are stable so we don't block any buildbot production deployment.
Or if you have an estimation on when do you think the builders are ready for prod ?

Debug fixes are in https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/3899. There is one other. So dropping debug definitely.

https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/3906 containts the archive-big unmasking.

Will ping [~serg] for a C/C update after which its just up for a merge up.

The non-debug might be stable very soon.
