comments.body:
Note that it happens with split_materialized=off, as well:
{code}
MariaDB [j1]> set optimizer_switch='split_materialized=off';
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.000 sec)

MariaDB [j1]> explain select *  from    t2, (select max(value) maxval, grp_id from t1 group by grp_id) DT where   t2.a= DT.grp_id;
+------+-------------+------------+------+---------------+------+---------+---------+--------+---------------------------------+
| id   | select_type | table      | type | possible_keys | key  | key_len | ref     | rows   | Extra                           |
+------+-------------+------------+------+---------------+------+---------+---------+--------+---------------------------------+
|    1 | PRIMARY     | t2         | ALL  | NULL          | NULL | NULL    | NULL    | 5      | Using where                     |
|    1 | PRIMARY     | <derived2> | ref  | key0          | key0 | 5       | j1.t2.a | 99     |                                 |
|    2 | DERIVED     | t1         | ALL  | NULL          | NULL | NULL    | NULL    | 998412 | Using temporary; Using filesort |
+------+-------------+------------+------+---------------+------+---------+---------+--------+---------------------------------+
3 rows in set (0.008 sec)
{code}

Analysis of 11.4 at git sha {{aa3578aa8a56b53318860c55c6f1d4163d36b069}} (for line number references) which includes the fix for MDEV-30877: "Output cardinality for derived table ignores GROUP BY"

Why do we see a 10x over-estimate in the optimizer trace output as shown in the Description above?  Where do the numbers come from which are used to compute the costs for particular join orders?  Below, we trace the provenance for "rows_for_plan", records_out, and the "rows" output for explain.

In {{best_extension_by_limited_search}}, "rows_for_plan" is computed by {{current_record_count= COST_MULT(record_count, position->records_out);}} but {{record_count}} is an argument passed to {{best_extension_by_limited_search}}.  Its caller, which is itself by recursion, computes {{partial_join_cardinality}} for the {{record_count}} argument this way:  {{partial_join_cardinality= record_count * position->records_out;}}.  This has a compounding effect on the {{record_count}} value seen by the recursively called {{best_extension_by_limited_search}}.  In the case when "rows_for_plan" is 50:  {{current_record_count= (record_count=5) * (position->records_out=10)}} and in the caller, {{partial_join_cardinality= (record_count=1) * (position->records_out=5)}}.  best_extension_by_limited_search sorts the tables to be joined by the expected number of rows found.  Again, in the case where the current_record_count ("rows_for_plan") is 50, we have one sorted join position ({{SORT_POSITION}}) whose join structure ({{pos->join_tab_0->join}}) counts two tables in the join:  DT and t2 (verifiable by inspecting {{ pos->join_tab_0->join->table_0->alias }} and {{ pos->join_tab_0->join->table_1->alias }}).  For derived table DT, during {{best_access_path}}, the position is created (around line 9887, comment 'Update the cost information for the current partial plan').  Here, the {{pos->records_init}} is copied from {{best.records_read}}, which is 10.  {{best_access_path}} was called by {{get_costs_for_tables}}, which itself is called by {{best_extension_by_limited_search}}, just before walking the sorted join positions (sorted as noted above).  During {{best_access_path}}, {{best.records_read}} is set after the {{cur_cost + COST_EPS < best.cost}} check.  Ultimately, the {{records=10 comes}} from {{best_access_path}}:  it checks {{records= keyinfo->actual_rec_per_key(key_parts-1)}} which sets {{records=0}} (see note on {{generate_derived_keys_for_table}} below), causing a different computation to derive {{records=10}}: the body of the conditional takes {{s->records}} and divides by {{rec}}, then that is scaled by a ratio of the difference of key length and max key length to the key length; essentially, scaling records by a computing the key length as percentage of the maximum key length.  {{rec}} is {{s->records/MATCHING_ROWS_IN_OTHER_TABLE}} and {{MATCHING_ROWS_IN_OTHER_TABLE}} is 10 by definition.  {{TABLE SHARE s}} refers to a join table whose corresponding join member indicates two tables in the join, again DT and t2.  {{s->records}} is 100 and was computed during {{JOIN_TAB::choose_best_splitting}} by this formula:  {{records= (ha_rows) (spl_opt_info->unsplit_card * spl_plan->split_sel)}} after a partial join plan is chosen.  In our case, {{spl_opt_info->unsplit_card}} is 9984 and {{spl_plan->split_sel}} is 0.010016025641025642, and their product is 100.00000000000001 which is cast to type {{ha_rows}} (integral).  {{spl_plan->split_sel}} is computed as {{best_rec_per_key / unsplit_card}} (opt_split.cc:1119) and {{best_rec_per_key}} ultimately comes from {{key_info->actual_rec_per_key(keyuse_ext->keypart)}} where the keypart is zero.  If we inspect {{key_info}} during that computation, we see its table is t1.  But during {{best_extension_by_limited_search}}, as demonstrated above, the calculations end up with row estimates attributed to DT, the derived table, not t1, so perhaps that is a source of the mis-estimation.  Shouldn't the estimate be based on numbers computed for the derived table, regardless of splitting, during {{best_extension_by_limited_search}} rather than the base table?  During {{JOIN::add_keyuses_for_splitting}}, the {{spl_opt_info->unsplit_card}} (used in the {{split_sel}} and {{choose_best_splitting}} computations) is derived from {{select_lex->master_unit()->derived->table->stat_records()}}, and {{select_lex->master_unit()->derived->table}} is "DT" in this case.  Interesting that, during {{JOIN_TAB::choose_best_splittin}}g, the left multiplier ({{unsplit_card}}) of records is based on the derived table while the right multiplier ({{split_sel}}) is based on the base table.

Repeating the analysis without lateral derived (split materialization) optimization enabled.
{{best_extension_by_limited_search}} computes {{current_record_count}} to be 499.2 by {{COST_MULT(record_count, position->records_out)}}.  Here, {{position->records_out=99.84}} and {{record_count=5}}.  The current position concerns the derived table DT.  {{record_coun}}t was passed in by the caller, by recursion also {{best_extension_by_limited_search}}, and was computed by taking {{record_count * position->records}} out in the caller's context.  As before, {{best_access_path}} populates the position structure from the best plan, so {{position->records_out}} is copied from {{best.records_out}}.  {{best.records_out}} is computed when {{records= keyinfo->actual_rec_per_key(key_parts-1)}} produces zero (see note on {{generate_derived_keys_for_table below}}), relying on{{ s->records / rec}} and scaled by the {{key_length}} ratio described above.  In this case, {{s->records=9984}} and {{rec=100}}, and the overall result sets records to 99.84 (seen as 99 in the explain output).  {{rec = s->records/MATCHING_ROWS_IN_OTHER_TABLE}}.  However, unlike in the split materialized case, the table share's record count ({{s->records}}) is computed during {{JOIN_TAB::estimate_scan_time}} by reading {{table->stat_records()}} (the table in this case is the derived table DT).  The return value of {{table->stats_records()}}, {{used_stat_records}}, is computed during {{set_statistics_for_table}} (called by {{make_join_statistics}}) and is based on {{table->file->stats.records}} (which again in this case is the derived table DT and the {{table->file}} is a heap, for the temporary table).

{{generate_derived_keys_for_table}} invokes {{TABLE::check_tmp_key}} and, on success, {{TABLE::add_tmp_key}} both of which don't consider the cost of the key added.  It's this added key that returns 0 during the {{records= keyinfo->actual_rec_per_key(key_parts-1)}} during {{best_access_path}}, for both split materialized and no split materialized cases above.  This seems to be a candidate for change: supply the row estimate for the given key during {{TABLE::add_tmp_key}}, perhaps updating {{keyinfo->rec_per_key}}?  A comment for that field says that "For temporary heap tables this member is NULL" so it is unused.  During {{TABLE::add_tmp_key}}, {{this->reginfo}} has a reference to a {{JOIN_TAB}} and {{JOIN}}, perhaps key estimates could be computed from that context.

"rows" output in the explain is computed during {{JOIN_TAB::get_examined_rows}} and for derived table DT is taken from {{JOIN_TAB::records_init}}.

Changing the example query to use straight_join, or any combination of disabling derived_with_keys or split_materialized optimizations did not improve the estimates.
Attached analysis as a markdown file which is easier to read.

[~Johnston] please check out review input at :
{code}
commit 60d4d712bbc0d0cf78d787b190295824ac9fd513 (HEAD -> bb-11.4-MDEV-36321-review-input, origin/bb-11.4-MDEV-36321-review-input, bb-11.4-MDEV-36321)
Author: Sergei Petrunia <sergey@mariadb.com>
Date:   Sun Aug 24 21:44:26 2025 +0300

    MDEV-36321: add more test  coverage with review input questions
{code}
Please check and address the comments in the .test file.

Also some general comment: 
-  Please consider putting new code into sql/opt_group_by_cardinality.cc  (or even a separate file).

Review input for the intermediate commit  ( 4cd135de80af2e2d66c582dbde6c85b860d57b01) is here:

Q1: why does every function called by infer_derived_key_statistics accept &select->table_list argument?  What is it for?   A: for the future... But then, we don't need it right now.

Q2: Do queries with Split-Materialized  produce correct rows_out with this patch? Looks like yes.  Need to add testcase.

I have removed the table list argument.  Even when we support outer references in derived tables i can't imagine it will be needed to ensure it is local.

As for the test cases, we have a bit of an issue here.
Tracing the setting and usage of *recs_per_key[n-1]* we see that if it is zero when entering best_access_path() it is updated here

{code:c++}
│     8953               if (!(records= keyinfo->actual_rec_per_key(key_parts-1)))            
│     8954               {                                   /* Prefer longer keys */        
│     8955                 trace_access_idx.add("rec_per_key_stats_missing", true);         
│     8956                 records=                                                        
│  >  8957                   ((double) s->records / (double) rec *                             
│     8958                    (1.0 +                                                          
│     8959                     ((double) (table->s->max_key_length-keyinfo->key_length) /    
│     8960                      (double) table->s->max_key_length)));                       
│     8961                 set_if_smaller(records, (double)s->records);                    
│     8962                 if (records < 1.0)                                             
│     8963                   records= 1.0;     /* Can't be as good as a unique */       
│     8964               }
{code}

Now those last 2 lines were added by Monty in 3fa99f0c0e29 dated 2022-12-27, so since then, the tests added by Varun have not been testing the function of his code.
Nor can i add any meaningful test that sets rec_per_key[n-1] to 1.
I'll investigate use of the optimizer trace to test this next.

[~Johnston], ouch, I've missed the above comment and just did a review pass of what's commited.
Please look at these commits in the bb-11.4-MDEV-36321-review-input:

For the first three, please add into your patch unless there are any notes/ objections. 
The last one is not for adding into the patch, please check the comments in it.

{code}
commit d07c03c440d1bd22130ad3116399901e4f42889c (HEAD -> bb-11.4-MDEV-36321-review-input, origin/bb-11.4-MDEV-36321-review-input)
Author: Sergei Petrunia <sergey@mariadb.com>
Date:   Wed Aug 27 13:14:10 2025 +0300

Author: Sergei Petrunia <sergey@mariadb.com>
Date:   Wed Aug 27 11:46:56 2025 +0300

    MDEV-36321: Review input part 3: Remove key_parts_match
    
    The same logic is achieved by:
    -          key_parts_match(keyinfo, key_parts, &select->item_list))
    +          key_parts == select->item_list.elements)
    
    In infer_derived_key_statistics(), see the code above this one.
    It already uses the "key_parts==..." check.

commit f7b1e4f2630fa1a3cfbb3a2149a074fd8c9dc846
Author: Sergei Petrunia <sergey@mariadb.com>
Date:   Wed Aug 27 11:44:04 2025 +0300

    MDEV-36321: Review input part 2: remove is_item_in_key()
    
    item_index_in_key() does the same thing.

commit bab33ad43edcef1437e698e2e6f0b59e35801990
Author: Sergei Petrunia <sergey@mariadb.com>
Date:   Wed Aug 27 11:27:28 2025 +0300

    MDEV-36321: Trivial review input: code cleanup .

{code}

[~Johnston] your query is a good example.
Pretty-printing it:
{code:sql}
explain 
select * 
from t2, 
  (select distinct grp_id from t1 -- SUBQ1
  UNION ALL
  select distinct value from t1) -- SUBQ2
  DT 
where
  t2.a= DT.grp_id;
{code}

I denoted the subselects as SUBQ1 and SUBQ2.  It is clear that both of them produce output with rec_per_key=1.
Yet, in the current code

{code:cpp}
      /*
        This is a SELECT DISTINCT list where the list matches the key,
        this select will produce one record per full key value
      */
      if (key_parts_match(keyinfo, key_parts, &select->item_list) &&
          (select->options & SELECT_DISTINCT || distinct))
{code}

the call to key_parts_match() will return false for SUBQ2 , because 
- the name of the column in temptable DT is "grp_id".
- the name of the column in SUBQ2's SELECT list is "value".

I hope this example makes it clear that checking column names is not relevant :-)
What is sufficient is to check that the derived table index is using  all the columns from SELECT DISTINCT list (and not a subset).
Just like my patch suggested:
{code:cpp}
        if ((select->options & SELECT_DISTINCT || distinct) &&
            key_parts == select->item_list.elements)
{code}
Do you agree? 

(BTW, if I put this into the current patch, I see the tests pass.  Please add test coverage showing the difference.)

[~Johnston] Please also apply code cleanup changes from bab33ad43edcef1437e698e2e6f0b59e35801990 : 

Move declaration of
{code}
double estimate_post_group_cardinality(JOIN *join, double join_output_card);
{code}
from sql_select.h into opt_group_by_cardinality.h
this requires adding #include in sql_select.h
Also add this comment
{code:diff}
diff --git a/sql/opt_group_by_cardinality.cc b/sql/opt_group_by_cardinality.cc
index 85392612168..5abf85b8a32 100644
--- a/sql/opt_group_by_cardinality.cc
+++ b/sql/opt_group_by_cardinality.cc
@@ -17,8 +17,13 @@
 /**
   @file
 
-    Contains estimate_post_group_cardinality() which estimates cardinality
-    after GROUP BY operation is applied.
+    Contains
+    - estimate_post_group_cardinality() which estimates cardinality
+      after GROUP BY operation is applied.
+
+    - infer_derived_key_statistics() to infer index statistics for
+      potential indexes on derived tables that have data produced with
+      a GROUP BY operation.
 */
 
 #include "mariadb.h"
{code}

[~Johnston],

Optimizer tracing is missing the derived table alias.  If a query uses multiple derived tables with GROUP BY, it might be hard to understand which one the trace is covering.  Please fix this.

I also think just the final rec_per_key estimate would be sufficient, but I don't have a strong opinion there, can also have details about individual SELECTs.

Other than that, we're close to finish. 
Please also rebase on top of the current "main" branch.

Please review
https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4274
The patch is good, ready for testing.

[~Johnston], [~psergei] I'm not sure it is a bug or not, but the view query plan does not match the table query plan, although the queries are ultimately interpreted the same way:

*Case:*
{code:sql}
--source include/have_sequence.inc

create table t1 (
  grp_id int,
  value int,
  index (grp_id asc)
);

insert into t1 select
  A.seq, B.seq
from
  seq_1_to_100 A,
  seq_1_to_100 B;

create table t2 (a int);
insert into t2 select seq from seq_1_to_5;

analyze table t1,t2;

explain extended
select * from
  t2,
  (select max(value), grp_id from t1 group by grp_id) DT
where
  t2.a= DT.grp_id;


create view v1 as select * from t1 ;

explain extended
select * from
  t2,
  (select max(value), grp_id from v1 group by grp_id) DT
where
  t2.a= DT.grp_id;


drop view v1;
drop table t1, t2;
{code}

*Results:*
{code:sql}

explain extended
select * from
t2,
(select max(value), grp_id from t1 group by grp_id) DT
where
t2.a= DT.grp_id;

1	PRIMARY	t2	ALL	NULL	NULL	NULL	NULL	5	100.00	Using where
1	PRIMARY	<derived2>	ref	key0	key0	5	test.t2.a	1	100.00	
2	DERIVED	t1	ALL	grp_id	NULL	NULL	NULL	10000	100.00	Using temporary; Using filesort
Warnings:
Note	1003	/* select#1 */ select `test`.`t2`.`a` AS `a`,`DT`.`max(value)` AS `max(value)`,`DT`.`grp_id` AS `grp_id` from `test`.`t2` join (/* select#2 */ select max(`test`.`t1`.`value`) AS `max(value)`,`test`.`t1`.`grp_id` AS `grp_id` from `test`.`t1` group by `test`.`t1`.`grp_id`) `DT` where `DT`.`grp_id` = `test`.`t2`.`a`


explain extended
select * from
t2,
(select max(value), grp_id from v1 group by grp_id) DT
where
t2.a= DT.grp_id;
id	select_type	table	type	possible_keys	key	key_len	ref	rows	filtered	Extra
1	PRIMARY	t2	ALL	NULL	NULL	NULL	NULL	5	100.00	Using where
1	PRIMARY	<derived2>	ref	key0	key0	5	test.t2.a	10	100.00	
2	DERIVED	t1	ALL	grp_id	NULL	NULL	NULL	10000	100.00	Using temporary; Using filesort
Warnings:
Note	1003	/* select#1 */ select `test`.`t2`.`a` AS `a`,`DT`.`max(value)` AS `max(value)`,`DT`.`grp_id` AS `grp_id` from `test`.`t2` join (/* select#2 */ select max(`test`.`t1`.`value`) AS `max(value)`,`test`.`t1`.`grp_id` AS `grp_id` from `test`.`t1` group by `test`.`t1`.`grp_id`) `DT` where `DT`.`grp_id` = `test`.`t2`.`a`
{code}

I have updated the code and tests and pushed the result to branch 12.2-MDEV-36321.

fields.description:
Add column to INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLLATIONS that shows whether collation is PAD SPACE or NOPAD. For compatibility let's use same values and same column name as in MYSQL

h2. INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLLATIONS
Let's add the new column after SORTLEN (before COMMENT), so the new structure looks like this:
{noformat}
MariaDB [test]> desc information_schema.collations;
+--------------------+----------------------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
| Field              | Type                       | Null | Key | Default | Extra |
+--------------------+----------------------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
| COLLATION_NAME     | varchar(64)                | NO   |     | NULL    |       |
| CHARACTER_SET_NAME | varchar(32)                | YES  |     | NULL    |       |
| ID                 | bigint(11)                 | YES  |     | NULL    |       |
| IS_DEFAULT         | varchar(3)                 | YES  |     | NULL    |       |
| IS_COMPILED        | varchar(3)                 | NO   |     | NULL    |       |
| SORTLEN            | bigint(3)                  | NO   |     | NULL    |       |
| PAD_ATTRIBUTE      | enum('PAD SPACE','NO PAD') | NO   |     | NULL    |       |
| COMMENT            | varchar(80)                | NO   |     | NULL    |       |
+--------------------+----------------------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
{noformat}

The above order will be compatible with MySQL-8.0 order  (with the exception that MariaDB has an extra last column COMMENT):
{noformat}
+--------------------+----------------------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
| Field              | Type                       | Null | Key | Default | Extra |
+--------------------+----------------------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
| COLLATION_NAME     | varchar(64)                | NO   |     | NULL    |       |
| CHARACTER_SET_NAME | varchar(64)                | NO   |     | NULL    |       |
| ID                 | bigint unsigned            | NO   |     | 0       |       |
| IS_DEFAULT         | varchar(3)                 | NO   |     |         |       |
| IS_COMPILED        | varchar(3)                 | NO   |     |         |       |
| SORTLEN            | int unsigned               | NO   |     | NULL    |       |
| PAD_ATTRIBUTE      | enum('PAD SPACE','NO PAD') | NO   |     | NULL    |       |
+--------------------+----------------------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
{noformat}

h2. SHOW COLLATION
Let's also add this new column to {{SHOW COLLATION}} as the last column, as follows:
{noformat}
MariaDB [test]> show collation like 'utf8mb4_bin';
+-------------+---------+------+---------+----------+---------+---------------+
| Collation   | Charset | Id   | Default | Compiled | Sortlen | Pad_attribute |
+-------------+---------+------+---------+----------+---------+---------------+
| utf8mb4_bin | utf8mb4 |   46 |         | Yes      |       1 | PAD SPACE     |
+-------------+---------+------+---------+----------+---------+---------------+
{noformat}

This will be compatible with MySQL's {{SHOW COLLATION}}:
{noformat}
+-------------+---------+----+---------+----------+---------+---------------+
| Collation   | Charset | Id | Default | Compiled | Sortlen | Pad_attribute |
+-------------+---------+----+---------+----------+---------+---------------+
| utf8mb4_bin | utf8mb4 | 46 |         | Yes      |       1 | PAD SPACE     |
+-------------+---------+----+---------+----------+---------+---------------+
{noformat}

issuetype.description: A new feature of the product, which has yet to be developed.
issuetype.name: New Feature

fields.description:
Dump the table statistics into a JSON section in optimizer trace:

- number of rows in the table
- used index statistics, for all key parts in each index.
- all records_in_range() calls that optimizer has made and their return values.
- constant lookups the optimizer has made and their results.

(Note that the above list is not exhaustive. It will need to be enhanced to provide exact same execution. But these variables form a good-enough first step).

All values should be in user-readable format.

*NOTE*: This MDEV doesn't provide the whole optimizer state capture/replay feature, but it's usable on its own so can go into 12.1

(Further continuation is MDEV-36523)

h2. Implementation

A list of things to capture:

h4. Used Histograms and EITS statistics. 

TODO: do we capture all histograms available or  just those that were used? 

h4. records_in_range calls

SQL layer makes two kinds of calls:
- multi_range_read_info_const()
- records_in_range().

Should we capture both? 

h4.  Constant table row reads.

Just capture what rows were read from the table (right?)
(Q: or, should we also capture the fact that some rows were read but not found?)

h4. Optimizer settings in system variables.

Capture the values of system variables controlling the optimizer:
- join_cache_level
- optimizer_prune_level
- optimizer_search_depth
- optimizer_switch
- optimizer_use_condition_selectivity
- 

h2. MS1 - Dump basic stats

The goal is to produce JSON like this:

{code:js}
  "records": 123,
  "indexes" : [
    {
      "index_name": "IDX1",
      "rec_per_key": [123, 1230, 123000],
    }
    ...
  ]
}
{code}

The records should come from {{table->stat_records()}}
the rec_per_key from:
{code}
  for each index IDX
    write array of key parts:
    for each i
      table->keyinfo[IDX].actual_rec_per_key(i)
{code}

h2. MS2 - scan_time()
TODO: which call to make

h2. MS3: records_in_range ?

comments.body: I am putting an estimated work as 7 days. However, this is a ball-park figure, and producing exact estimates will itself take time.
status update - The cost estimates for index, and rows for ranges are captured and stored as a JSON-object now, instead of an array (which was done in the last dev-sprint)

The optimizer_context now includes records of keyread_time calls.

Uploaded these changes to the PR https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4255

No new stats are dumped into the context. So, not much work has been done during the last week.

However, EITS information would be added to the context as well. So, need to finalize on the implementation details.

- number of rows in the table
- used index statistics, for all key parts in each index.

Note: one can use a storage engine (i.e. an object derived from class handler) to capture or fake the statistics, but is this a  good approach? Inheriting from class handler (or, e.g. ha_innobase) seems to be quite complex.

fields.summary: Optimizer Trace replay step #3: load basic statistics back

issuetype.description: A new feature of the product, which has yet to be developed.
issuetype.name: New Feature

fields.description:
Continuation of MDEV-36511.
Assuming the user has extracted the JSON section from MDEV-36511 and has provided its contents in  a variable, create code to parse it back.

Then, use the hooks to replace the statistics fed into the optimizer.

Note: one can use a storage engine (i.e. an object derived from class handler) to capture or fake the statistics, but is this a good approach? Inheriting from class handler (or, e.g. ha_innobase) seems to be quite complex.

comments.body:
This task loads the stats of the tables that are used in a query, from the trace into the optimizer.
This feature is also controlled by optimizer_record_context, and is not enabled by default. The stats
such as num_of_records present in the table, indexes if present then their names, along with the average number of records_per_key with in each index are loaded from the trace. Additionally, stats from range analysis i.e. ranges, and the corresponding number of records are also loaded from the trace.

The trace context which is in JSON format is firstly set into the session variable optimizer_trace_stored_context. Later, when a user issues a query, the contents of optimizer_trace_stored_context variable is parsed and an in memory representation is build using the class Optimizer_Trace_Stored_Context_Extractor. This class is then used by the optimizer to update and save original values of the tables, indexes, and range stats in the methods "set_statistics_for_table()" of sql_statistics.cc, and "check_quick_select()" of opt_range.cc. After the query gets finished, the statistics that were updated in the optimizer are restored back to the saved original values.

The entry point for parsing the json structure is in "mysql_execute_command()" of sql_parse.cc, and similarly exit point i.e. to restore the saved stats of the optimizer is at the end of the same method.
https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4255
I am putting an estimated work as 7 days. However, this is a ball-park figure, and producing exact estimates will itself take time.

Status Update:
Replaying non-constant ref access did not produce the same cost.  

This is because cost functions called from {{cost_for_index_read()}} did not get traced/replayed.  Those are handler->keyread_time(), row_blocks(), index_blocks(key).

Discussion take-aways:

h2. Optimizer Context capture should include records of keyread_time calls.
{code:js}
"key_read_time_call" : { 
   -- index and table name are not stored because this JSON object will be located
   -- in the JSON document where it is clear which tablename.index_name the call was made for
   "ranges" : NNN,
   "rows" : NNN,
   "blocks" : "NNN",
   "return_value": { 
      -- an object describing IO_AND_CPU_COST components
   }
}
{code}
Calls to h->keyread_time() could be made multiple times for same or different values of parameters.
Current solution is to just store all the calls in the context.
When replaying the context, take the first call with the matching parameter values.

Q: do all calls with the same parameter values have the same return value?    A: this should be the case.   It would be nice to detect the case where this is violated, handling such case is low priority.

h2. Size of optimizer context

The size of sysvar value is currently limited to 8k.
Optimizer context will probably go larger than that.
It is also not nice to have sysvars with very long values.

Immediate solution 0:  current examples we work with will fit in 8K  (increase to eg. 16K if necessary).
Solution 1: for the release:  store the context in the user variable  (which has no limits),  store the user variable name in sys. variable.
Solution 2: We could also explore writable I_S tables (with different content for each session)  but that has not been done yet.

h2. Json schema for context

Try to come up with a JSON schema describing the saved optimizer context.
(Want to have JSON Schema for the EXPLAIN output as well but within this MDEV)
(We probably don't want to have schema for the optimizer trace).

Create the schema manually, put it into .json file.  Then we could use MTR to validate the captured context.    It will also serve as documentation.

Created JSON_SCHEMA for the optimizer_context section of the trace. It uses array of objects. However, JSON_SCHEMA_VALID(@schema, @opt_context) is always returning FALSE, as there seems to be a bug in recognising array of objects. Created https://jira.mariadb.org/browse/MDEV-38033 for the same. Although tests are added to use JSON_SCHEMA_VALID, but it is disabled/commented. Added a TO-DO comment in the test to use reenable using the function in the tests, once the bug is resolved.

Also, the optimizer_context now includes records of keyread_time calls. 

Size of 8k for the optimizer context still suffices for the current set of test cases.

Uploaded these changes to the PR https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4255

In addition to the range stats being reused successfully, added more cases.

Used tables and indexes with the following properties: -
1. Table having 1 or more indexes
2. Index having primary keys, unique and non-unique keys with one or more columns.

Join equality, and predicate equality queries using above tables/indexes are added. So, the access types that are tested included: -
1. ref
2. index_scan
3. eq_ref
4. all
5. index_merge

The existing solution works with non-eits cases. However, when eits stats are used in the queries, then using captured context is not able to generate the same plan cost after modifying the table by inserting/deleting data.

So, the stats that are captured into the context should also be containing EITS information so that they can be infused into the query planning, even after tables are modified. This is the next item to be implemented.

Additionally, working on polishing the code to reduce duplicate code pieces. The PR https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4255 has the all the new changes.

Here are the following items that are planned after having a discussion with [~psergei]: -
# make optimizer_replay_context store reference to user var:  optimizer_replay_context='@var'; 
# Rebase on a branch that has the "move the code from opt-histogram"  patch i.e. MDEV-38120. However, there is a pending issue that is preventing the merge.
# After above point is done, move basic JSON readers into sql_json_lib.*
# Check if JSON parsing, as well as other areas that needs further fixes to reduce code duplication or polish

First point is already take care of.

Second and third points from above comment are also taken care. Fourth point is WIP.

In addition to these, added logic in the tests to use round_cost() function, so that there is no diff in the explain plan output across builds.

worked on
# reducing the number of classes for reading different types of values from JSON, by using Template classes.
# added OOM checks
# Changed the type of optimizer_replay_context variable to SESSION_ONLY from SESSION.
# Moved reading primitive values from json code to sql_json_lib.h, and sql_json_lib.cc
Worked on fixing the crashes, and result mismatch failures that happened due to the previous commit made on Dec 5, 2025.
Working on https://jira.mariadb.org/browse/MDEV-38805.

fields.summary: Remove some markers that variable is not going to be used uninitalized in clang

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done.
issuetype.name: Task

fields.description:
There are a number of compiler defines that marks variables as 'will not be used uninitialized'. 
This is to around issues with compilers that wrongly conclude that a variable will be used uninitialized.
The macros that makes this possible are LINT_INIT and UNINIT_VAR for example.

With modern static analysers and the current usage, these are very shallow path to determine the initialisation did happen.  They however still do mistakes.

While we want to have optimal code, we still want to be able to catch uninitialised values usage in the code.

The {{UNINIT_VAR\(x) x= x}} construct was causing UBSAN issues like:

{noformat}
sql/sql_view.cc:1299:8: runtime error: load of value 16, which is not a valid value for type 'bool'
{noformat}

However vallgrind and other memory checkers does not have this issue.
When compling with UBSAN we should use the -DWITH_UBSAN option, like we do in the BUILD scripts. 

The fix for this would be to change:
{noformat}
#if defined(__GNUC__)
/* GCC specific self-initialization which inhibits the warning. */
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x= x
#elif defined(_lint) || defined(FORCE_INIT_OF_VARS)
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x= 0
#else
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x
#endif

to

#if defined(__GNUC__) && !defined(WITH_UBSAN)
/* GCC specific self-initialization which inhibits the warning. */
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x= x
#elif defined(FORCE_INIT_OF_VARS)
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x= 0
#else
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x
#endif
{noformat}
(I removed _lint as this is not used anymore)

comments.body: Monty, can I get a review of https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/3961 please.

The problem is that people want to compile with options like -Wall -Werror, and compilers want to warn with false positives about uninitialized variables.

And without a mechanism to deal with this, people will then add random initializations to variables just to prevent those compiler warnings (->errors), regardless of whether that initial value is actually correct.

And then this in turn hides real bugs from tools like Valgrind and MSAN (just as you mentioned in the bug description), when a variable that should not be referenced is accessed incorrectly.

Remember, just because a variable is initialized at the definition of it, doesn't mean it has a valid value!

Maybe the UNINIT_VAR() macro could be extended so it takes also an initial value, but then marks the variable as undefined memory to Valgrind and MSAN?

> and compilers want to warn with false positives about uninitialized variables

I think the assumption of an abundance of warnings isn't the case, perhaps due to over initialisation:

{noformat}
$ cmake -DCMAKE_C{,XX}_FLAGS='-Wall' .
$ b
[256/1577] Building CXX object tpool/CMakeFiles/tpool.dir/tpool_generic.cc.o
/home/dan/repos/mariadb-server-rebase/tpool/tpool_generic.cc:221:22: warning: private field 'm_group_enqueued' is not used [-Wunused-private-field]
  221 |   unsigned long long m_group_enqueued;
      |                      ^
1 warning generated.
[794/1577] [BISON][gen_oracle_cc_hh] Building parser with bison 3.8.2
/home/dan/repos/build-mariadb-server-rebase-debug/sql/yy_oracle.cc:35313: warning: suspicious sequence in the output: b4_bin [-Wother]
[1533/1577] Generating user.t
troff: fatal error: unable to open macro file for -m argument 'm'
[1535/1577] Generating user.ps
troff: fatal error: unable to open macro file for -m argument 'm'
[1577/1577] Linking CXX executable sql/mariadbd
{noformat}

> Maybe the UNINIT_VAR() macro could be extended so it takes also an initial value

Why?

There's no need for such an abstracted fakery. If you want an uninitialised variable just declare that way. Plenty are already, and they aren't generating warnings or MSAN errors.

The point of valgrind and MSAN is to run instrumented but unmodified code, once you run modified code, you're testing a different product.

[~danblack], m_group_enqueued warning is genuine, this variable it is not used anywhere, and it is remainder after something I've tried. But there was never a warning that it is not used, or not initialized, or anything

Going to apply some gcc and clang version based upper limits to the code so the really old buildbot works have the same number of warnings however anyone using a modern compiler effectively has a UNINITVAR no-op to catch the real warnings around uninitialised variables and the other odd thing or so like what [~wlad] saw.

So quite clear so far that clang has no warnings on uninit vars and much later gcc has to be tested.

||builder||compiler||uninit warnings pr at c735a931b4||uninit warnings on 10.6-47e687b109||
|aarch64 centostream8|gcc 11.5.0|[~170|https://buildbot.mariadb.org/#/builders/493/builds/18230/steps/5/logs/warnings__181_]|
|aarch64 debian 11|gcc  10.2.1|][134|https://buildbot.mariadb.org/#/builders/313/builds/28593/steps/5/logs/warnings__138_]|
|aarch64 macos|AppleClang 15.0.0.15000309|[0|https://buildbot.mariadb.org/#/builders/590/builds/13909]|
|aarch64 openeuler 2403|gcc 12.3.1|[172|https://buildbot.mariadb.org/#/builders/830/builds/3585]|
|aarch64 rhel8|gcc 8.5.0|[136|https://buildbot.mariadb.org/#/builders/75/builds/39171]|
|aarch64 rhel9|gcc 11.4.1|[173|https://buildbot.mariadb.org/#/builders/482/builds/23797]|
|aarch64 ubuntu 2004 (and debug)|gcc 9.4.0|[135|https://buildbot.mariadb.org/#/builders/98/builds/36784]|
|aarch64 ubuntu 2204|gcc  11.4.0|[173|https://buildbot.mariadb.org/#/builders/351/builds/19461/steps/5/logs/stdio]|
|amd64 centos 7 bintar|gcc  4.8.5|[0|https://buildbot.mariadb.org/#/builders/577/builds/18545/steps/5/logs/stdio]|
|amd64 debian 11 clang 16|Clang 16.0.6|0|
|amd64-ubuntu-2404-clang18-asan|clang 18.0|0|

tested gcc 14.2.0 / 14.2.1 and its still has uninitialized in many places.

Excluded clang from the false identification as its proved reliable for a very long time. This will enable the UBSAN builders not to error hence blocking MDBF-741.

Added some corrections to connect engine to remove some of its initialisation errors.

example 10.6- debug test failure that this fixes:

{noformat}
mariabackup.xb_rocksdb_datadir_debug     w3 [ fail ]  Found warnings/errors in server log file!
        Test ended at 2025-05-09 01:31:53
line
/source/sql/sql_view.cc:1299:8: runtime error: load of value 42, which is not a valid value for type 'bool'
SUMMARY: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: invalid-bool-load /source/sql/sql_view.cc:1299:8 
^ Found warnings in /build/mysql-test/var/3/log/mysqld.1.err
{noformat}

The main idea with UNINIT_VAR() is that one can silence the compiler when it wrongly thinks that something can be used uninitialized when it is note the case.  We want to preserve this functionality also in the future.
Valgrind builds should use -UFORCE_INIT_OF_VARS. This helps to that it will find all cases where variables using UNINIT_VAR() are used uninitialized.

x=x does not cause any issues for Valgrind; The variable is still regarded as uninitiated by valgrind.
Apparently we have to do some adjustments for UBSAN as it cannot properly handle the x=x construct

Some changes required for both patches.
Please provide a new pull request and I will review again.

PR updated and force pushed. Review comments posted inline with pervious review.

As UNINIT_VAR is about silencing compile warnings and Clang never issues a false uninitialised warning, I've just remove its effect except under the FORCE_INIT_OF_VARS. I've enforced this case of clang being right with -Werror=uninitialized* for clang. PR updated, and it includes a few other errors that show up in clang/debug testing because of stack size and other warnings. Hope that's ok.

The reason this is targetting the 10.6 branch is to deploy a much improved ASAN/UBSAN tester into BB (MDBF-741) and this is the main blocker to achieve this. The MDEV-36708 could be crudely worked around. Without this at least on 10.6 (or at least 10.11) the errors that are discovered won't be identified until they are merged up the the branch that contains this fix. The set of test cases that are affected by this are rather broad an ineffective to mask.

I would be fine with this change:

#if defined(__GNUC__) && !defined(WITH_UBSAN)
/* GCC specific self-initialization which inhibits the warning. */
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x= x
#elif defined(FORCE_INIT_OF_VARS) &&  !defined(WITH_UBSAN)
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x= 0
#else
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x
#endif

This way, one have to only set WITH_UBSAN to get what you want

Just a note regarding "The point of valgrind and MSAN is to run instrumented but unmodified code, once you run modified code, you're testing a different product."

When using valgrind or MSAN, one should always use -UFORCE_INIT_OF_VARS -Wno-uninitialized, like we do in
the BUILD scripts. This ensures that we do should find all variables that are wrongly marked with
UNINIT_VAR().

Regarding Kristian's comment about wrong usage of UNINIT_VAR():
- The macro is not there to allow people an easy way to silence compiler warnings.  It is there to be used when the developer has got and checked the compiler warning about uninitialized memory and he is 100% sure the variable is not used uninitialized and the code is in a critical place where we get a gain by not initializing the variable for no good reason.

Valgrind and MSAN  are there to check that the developers assessment is right.
Note that setting a variable to 0 and later assuming it was set to a proper value when it was not can as easily introduce bugs and in this case using UNINIT_VAR() can be a safer option than setting it to 0.

As we are not setting a value to zero when using valgrind or UBSAN should solve Kristian's concern that we should mark the value as 'undefined' as we are already doing that (at least for valgrind, as x=x will keep the variable marked as undefined.

items.toString:
There are a number of compiler defines that marks variables as 'will not be used uninitialized'. 
This is to around issues with compilers that wrongly conclude that a variable will be used uninitialized.
The macros that makes this possible are LINT_INIT and UNINIT_VAR for example.

With modern static analysers and the current usage, these are very shallow path to determine the initialisation did happen.  They however still do mistakes.

While we want to have optimal code, we still want to be able to catch uninitialised values usage in the code.

The {{UNINIT_VAR\(x) x= x}} construct was causing UBSAN issues like:

{noformat}
sql/sql_view.cc:1299:8: runtime error: load of value 16, which is not a valid value for type 'bool'
{noformat}

However vallgrind and other memory checkers does not have this issue.
When compling with UBSAN we should use the -DWITH_UBSAN option, like we do in the BUILD scripts. 

The fix for this would be to change:

#if defined(__GNUC__)
/* GCC specific self-initialization which inhibits the warning. */
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x= x
#elif defined(_lint) || defined(FORCE_INIT_OF_VARS)
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x= 0
#else
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x
#endif

to

#if defined(__GNUC__) && !defined(WITH_UBSAN)
/* GCC specific self-initialization which inhibits the warning. */
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x= x
#elif defined(FORCE_INIT_OF_VARS)
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x= 0
#else
#define UNINIT_VAR(x) x
#endif

(I removed _lint as this is not used anymore)

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done.
issuetype.name: Task

fields.description:
MDEV-24625 showcases that problems in opening the binary log lead to debug assertions that may indicate the server running in an invalid state.

This ticket is a sub-task of the overall problem to perform an initial manual static-analysis (i.e. code-level analysis) of the issue. This analysis will be used in a future task to create MTR tests which verify the expectations set out by the report. The report should track:

1. The functions that open binary logs
  1a. What errors can be reported by these functions?
  1b. Are there calls that should have error handling but don't?
  1c. Are all functions consistent in how they report these errors?

2. What contexts/use cases call into these functions that open binary logs?
  2a. How are these errors handled?
  2b. Are these errors ever overriden/discarded? 
  2c. Is error handling consistent between these different use cases?
  2d. What are the expected server/transaction states before opening new binary logs?
  2e. What are the expected server/transaction states after opening new binary logs?
  2f. What are the expected server/transaction states after *failing* to open a new binary log?

fields.summary: Langchain mariadb lazy init

issuetype.description: A technical task.
issuetype.name: Technical task

fields.description:
The primary motivation for this patch is that, in a client-server application (e.g., RAG), the developer might not or isn't required to know the embedding_length in advance.
Without lazy init and no prior knowledge of the embedding_length, the developer would be stuck with the default of 1536, which might differ from what the model actual value is.

Of course, from_texts() will determine the dimension at runtime but we need to consider that
in some cases one would like to get an instance of MariaDBStore first and then perform any other operations later.

Thus, we need to add support lazy initialization of the store, which will establish the embedding dimension
and create the tables on either the first search or the first insert, whichever comes first.

comments.body:
With respect to binlog, check this commit which is part of on-going MDEV-34705:

{noformat}
commit 7a306564d7f281e978da9e8998cd011c9dd544f4
Author: Kristian Nielsen <knielsen@knielsen-hq.org>
Date:   Fri Apr 25 12:47:30 2025 +0200

    MDEV-34705: Binlog-in-engine: mariadb-backup integration
{noformat}

https://github.com/MariaDB/server/commit/7a306564d7f281e978da9e8998cd011c9dd544f4

One of the advantages of the new binlog is that it can be cloned in a similar way to other InnoDB tablespaces, as implemented in the above commit. Then the cloning of the binlog GTID position is handled automatically (since the binlog is cloned consistently with the data).

It should be ensured that the design of the CLONE feature can integrate seamlessly with the design of the new binlog (even if the coding may initially be easier to do independently until merged into a common tree).
This is based on [MySQL WL#9209: InnoDB: Clone local replica|https://dev.mysql.com/worklog/task/?id=9209].

This comment is about some future improvement that I think will be necessary at some point of time.

According to [~knielsen], the current {{mariadb-backup}} does nothing about binlog files. Users are expected to rely on something obscure stored by InnoDB for determining the binlog position. See MDEV-22351 for some details. 

In https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/3775/ (MDEV-34705) there is some code for covering the new-format binlog files. I think that for the clone interface to be usable, it must eventually cover the binlog as well. I think that it would be reasonable to support only the MDEV-34705 format.

Both RocksDB LSM trees and the MDEV-34705 binlog files are append-only. This means that instead of copying files, we can (and should) just create hard links and let the recovery logic ignore any excess content. If we are doing a local clone, we should eventually "materialize" the hard linked binlog files by copying them in the traditional or the reflink (MDEV-23947) way. To a remote clone, we can just stream from the hard-linked binlog file and let the remote recovery trim the content that is ahead of the final LSN.

I went through {{cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DENABLE_GCOV=ON}}. There seems to be quite a bit of code that is beyond the current scope (remote clone, incremental clone, parallel clone). This has to be simplified down to the essentials before it can be really reviewed.

The MySQL Clone plugin interface does not allow to leverage the properties of append-only or immutable files, or file systems that support data block sharing (MDEV-23947).

I believe that instead of porting the MySQL Clone interface, we’d better implement the actual low-level copying of files in the server executable and have a ‘dumb’ backup client. That is being tracked in MDEV-14992.

fields.summary: Add VIDEX as storage engine for MariaDB

issuetype.description: A new feature of the product, which has yet to be developed.
issuetype.name: New Feature

fields.description:
VIDEX (Virtual Index for MySQL) is an open-source virtual index storage engine developed by ByteDance, designed to simulate the impact of indexes on query plans without requiring real data. It supports what-if analysis for index strategies, integrates AI-based cardinality and NDV (number of distinct values) estimation algorithms, and has been validated with benchmarks like TPC-H. VIDEX is currently implemented for MySQL 8.0 and deployed at scale, optimizing thousands of MySQL instances daily.

ByteDance has expressed interest in adapting VIDEX for MariaDB compatibility, seeking collaboration with the MariaDB community due to differences between MySQL 8.0 and the MariaDB codebase. This feature story requests research and estimation to identify the technical requirements, challenges, and effort needed to integrate VIDEX in MariaDB Server, enabling MariaDB users to benefit from advanced query optimization capabilities.

*Objectives*

Understand the architectural differences between MySQL 8.0 and MariaDB that impact VIDEX compatibility.

Identify modifications needed in the MariaDB Server codebase to support VIDEX as a storage engine plugin.

Estimate the effort required for development.

*Acceptance Criteria*

A Jira story report documenting:

Key differences between MySQL 8.0 and MariaDB affecting VIDEX integration.

Specific changes required in MariaDB Server to support VIDEX (e.g., plugin interfaces, statistical metadata handling).

Estimated effort for implementation.

Recommendations for collaboration with ByteDance to streamline adaptation.

Validation that the proposed changes align with MariaDB’s architecture and performance goals.

A plan for testing VIDEX integration using benchmarks like TPC-H and JOB to ensure simulation accuracy.

*Background*

VIDEX Overview: VIDEX simulates query plans by providing statistical information (e.g., NDV, cardinality) via a RESTful algorithm service, supporting AI-driven estimation models. It skips index query interfaces (e.g., index_first, index_read) and focuses on optimizer interactions (ha_engine::info, ha_engine::records_in_range).

VIDEX Architecture: VIDEX uses a three-layer disaggregated design (production database, VIDEX-Optimizer, VIDEX-Statistic-Server), allowing lightweight statistical replication and AI model integration (VIDEX paper, arXiv:2503.23776).

items.fromString:
*Description*

VIDEX (Virtual Index for MySQL) is an open-source virtual index storage engine developed by ByteDance, designed to simulate the impact of indexes on query plans without requiring real data. It supports what-if analysis for index strategies, integrates AI-based cardinality and NDV (number of distinct values) estimation algorithms, and has been validated with benchmarks like TPC-H. VIDEX is currently implemented for MySQL 8.0 and deployed at scale, optimizing thousands of MySQL instances daily.

ByteDance has expressed interest in adapting VIDEX for MariaDB compatibility, seeking collaboration with the MariaDB community due to differences between MySQL 8.0 and the MariaDB codebase. This feature story requests research and estimation to identify the technical requirements, challenges, and effort needed to integrate VIDEX in MariaDB Server, enabling MariaDB users to benefit from advanced query optimization capabilities.

*Objectives*

Understand the architectural differences between MySQL 8.0 and MariaDB that impact VIDEX compatibility.

Identify modifications needed in the MariaDB Server codebase to support VIDEX as a storage engine plugin.

Estimate the effort required for development.

*Acceptance Criteria*

A Jira story report documenting:

Key differences between MySQL 8.0 and MariaDB affecting VIDEX integration.

Specific changes required in MariaDB Server to support VIDEX (e.g., plugin interfaces, statistical metadata handling).

Estimated effort for implementation.

Recommendations for collaboration with ByteDance to streamline adaptation.

Validation that the proposed changes align with MariaDB’s architecture and performance goals.

A plan for testing VIDEX integration using benchmarks like TPC-H and JOB to ensure simulation accuracy.

*Background*

VIDEX Overview: VIDEX simulates query plans by providing statistical information (e.g., NDV, cardinality) via a RESTful algorithm service, supporting AI-driven estimation models. It skips index query interfaces (e.g., index_first, index_read) and focuses on optimizer interactions (ha_engine::info, ha_engine::records_in_range).

VIDEX Architecture: VIDEX uses a three-layer disaggregated design (production database, VIDEX-Optimizer, VIDEX-Statistic-Server), allowing lightweight statistical replication and AI model integration (VIDEX paper, arXiv:2503.23776).

Hi Sergey,

Thanks for the positive update and the team's discussion. We are glad to hear MariaDB is interested in adopting VIDEX as a community server plugin.

Regarding the timeline and packaging concerns, we would appreciate your advice on the following:

1. Timeline and Jira tag:
We fully understand that resolving packaging issues properly may take a prolonged period. We are committed to the long-term success of this project and are willing to move forward at a steady pace. We are eager for feedback and will fully cooperate on necessary changes, aiming to complete the VIDEX merge according to the JIRA schedule (by Q2 2026, jira.mariadb.org/browse/MDEV-36737<http://jira.mariadb.org/browse/MDEV-36737>).

I noticed the Jira is tagged with "Fix Version/s: 12.3 [ 30147 ]". Could you help me understand what that means? Does this imply that the team is targeting MariaDB 12.3 as the release version for merging VIDEX?

2. Clarification on "Packaging" Issue:
To help us prepare, could you clarify if the "packaging concerns" are primarily related to the Python-side Statistic Server and its dependencies?

We are keen to follow MariaDB guidance. If needed, we can prepare a bundled pip package for a one-line installation. Alternatively, if absolutely necessary, we could rewrite this component in C++, though that would require significant effort.

3. Merge Strategy:
Since we have a longer timeline, I’d value your advice on merge strategy. Is the goal to solve all packaging issues first and then merge everything as a single large update? Or, could we merge the core C++ plugin first (perhaps marked as "Experimental" and disabled by default), while we work on the Python packaging logic in parallel?

4. Communication with Daniel:
I am ready to work with Daniel Black. Should I wait for him to reach out, or should I contact him directly via Zulip, Jira, or the PR?

Thank you again, Sergey.

Best regards,

Rong

fields.description:
MaxGUI should automatically redirect to the `/login` endpoint to perform SSO login when accessed via MemaGUI.
This allows users to access MaxGUI from MemaGUI without needing to log in again.

comments.body:
Hi @Thien Ly,

Is it feasible to integrate this with OKTA?
If Okta supports OpenID Connect then it should be compatible with it. I've at least tested it with Auth0 and it works with that.

Thanks, Markus, for the confirmation.


Just curious, this is for Maxscale GUI login, right? We've been waiting for this feature for a very long time.
Yes, this is for the MaxScale GUI.

Markus, thank you for clarifying.

So, we can add all the okta settings like ClientID, secret, URL's ...etc in the GUI itself or backend config file?

The next MaxScale version will support OpenID Connect code and implicit authentication flows and it the client ID and secret can be configured in maxscale.cnf. Currently the only supported authentication mechanism is the basic authentication where the client ID and secret are delivered in the Authorization header. This should be supported by at least Auth0 and Keycloak.
So, you mean after 25,10 version only we can use OKTA integration? I mean 25.10.1 version it will be available or not?
Yes, the fixVersion is set to the upcoming 25.10 series of MaxScale.
Oh, Thanks Markus.

Hi Markus,

Following up on our earlier discussion — Do you have any update on the OKTA SSO integration timeline?
MXS-5998 was closed with a fix version of 25.10.1 so that'll be the release that will most likely include it.

Thanks, Markus, for the update.

Can the OKTA settings be configured directly in MaxScale, and are they only for the MaxScale GUI login? Or do we need to configure them through the MariaDB Enterprise Manager?

Do I need MariaDB Enterprise Manager to log in to MaxScale using Okta SSO?
Does MaxScale SSO work only when Enterprise Manager is used, or can I use SSO directly in MaxScale without Enterprise Manager?

Also, can we have documentation for setting up OKTA with MaxScale?

MaxScale 25.10 supports logging in via [OpenID Connect|https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-docs/blob/maxscale-sso/maxscale/reference/maxscale-rest-api/maxscale-rest-api.md#openid-connect] but the exact method of setting up Okta to set the custom claims in the JWTs isn't currently documented by MariaDB.

Thanks, Markus, for the update.

Can we have the document ready along with the 25.10.1 release? We are not sure which settings need to be configured for SSO.

fields.description:
Python dependencies of burza are installed using Poetry, but all the other parts (like MariaDB connector/node exporter/flame graphs/perf and its kernel modules) are not covered by any automated process. 
There is also a buildbot task that runs burza on hetzner servers, but there are some problems with it:
* allocation of VMs and their provisioning is inseparable. You cannot allocate VMs once and then develop on them, updating the sources
* there is no direct access to these VMs, only thru jump hosts, which complicates the development
* task itself is run in Buildbot. So for every change one has to create a PR, wait for review, then run it
* buildbot tasks are not a standard tech. It is not available outside of the company. So for example Tempesta had to implement their own Ansible provisioning. If burza becomes open source in the future, we'll also need some standard tech for deployment

So I propose using https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/columnstore-ansible-aws (Terraform + Ansible, the project is open) as a base to add deployment of burza using Ansible

fields.description:
After MDEV-34551 one can specify a column list in the UPDATE trigger definition.
These columns should be visible in the standard INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TRIGGERED_UPDATE_COLUMNS table.

comments.body: Please review this feature in [bb-main-mdev-36996|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/tree/bb-main-mdev-36996].
If no column mentioned for trigger, the trigger will work for all columns, should that columns be present in the table?

No. The standard says

bq. The TRIGGERED_UPDATE_COLUMNS base table has one row for each column identified by a <column name> in a <trigger column list> of a <trigger definition>.

According to the SQL Standard, a user must have any non-SELECT privilege on the column to view it in the {{INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TRIGGERED_UPDATE_COLUMNS}} table. 
Unlike {{INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TRIGGERS}} table, which in MariaDB requires the user to have {{TRIGGER}} privilege for the table, {{INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TRIGGERED_UPDATE_COLUMNS}} table does not require any table-level privilege for the columns to be shown.
OK send for tests
testing looks good, okay to push
Documented here: https://mariadb.com/docs/server/reference/system-tables/information-schema/information-schema-tables/information-schema-triggered_update_columns

We already have awesome https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/columnstore-ansible-aws project that allows one to create a Columnstore cluster in AWS and provision it using Ansible. But we need to make it a little bit more developer-friendly, because right now there are some issues that block many developers from using it for development.

What has to be done:
* Simplify AWS setup: currenly user has to create security groups/VPCs/etc by hand in AWS console, which is tedious (and not really needed later for development work), these resources can be set up automatically
* Support sharing of Columnstore sources between developer's own VM in AWS and cluster nodes. We need it because Drone builds are very slow (>30 minutes), so after changing one line of code developer has to wait for a very long time. It would be much faster if we could share sources between the hosts and build/install using bootstrap_mcs
* (optional) automate generating passwords, obtaining AWS credentials and choosing/generating SSH keys to connect to the cluster nodes

fields.summary: Implement table and index options to enable/disable ADAPTIVE_HASH_INDEX

issuetype.description: A new feature of the product, which has yet to be developed.
issuetype.name: New Feature

fields.description:
Note: The scope of this MDEV has been updated to exclusively cover {{ADAPTIVE_HASH_INDEX}} options. The {{QUERY_CACHE}} and {{BINLOG_ROW}} per-table options have been split into MDEV-39949 and MDEV-39950.

Some of the features in MariaDB are only usable (from performance point of view) in special circumstances:
- (Moved to MDEV-39949) QUERY_CACHE should no be used with tables that changes values *very* frequently
- InnoDB adaptive_hash_index does not work well if there is changes in the rows that are part if an active adaptive_hash
- (Moved to MDEV-39950) Statement based binary logging  is not optimal for tables that does updates where the master has to scan a lot but only updates a few or inserts of many rows with generated auto-increments.

This MDEV is about fixing this issue by adding new table specific options where the user can enable/disable the options per table.

All table optimization should have the 3 values: ON, OFF and DEFAULT.  'DEFAULT' is needed to be able to remove the option from being stored in the table definition.

The suggested new table options are:
||Option|Effect|
|-QUERY_CACHE-|(Moved to MDEV-39949) -Having this option OFF is the same as using SELECT SQL_NO_CACHE for any query using this table. Having this option ON is same as using SELECT SQL_CACHE for this table and the query will be cached if no other table has QUERY_CACHE=OFF-|
|ADAPTIVE_HASH_INDEX |Having this option OFF will disable InnoDB adaptive hash index for this table. Having it ON will enable adaptive hash index for the table if adaptive hash indexes are enabled at all|
|-BINLOG_ROW-|(Moved to MDEV-39950) -If this option is ON for any table, row based binary logging will be used-|

comments.body:
First one should be auto-detected, it's not user's job to decide what it's being changed frequently

Second is InnoDB specific, *must* be implemented inside InnoDB.

Third must be auto-detected based per statement, it's not a table property.

Could there also be an option to disable the automatic creation of virtual columns (MDEV-371)? And one to enforce the existence of a primary key (MDEV-21181)?

An {{adaptive_hash_index}} option would best be an index-level option ({{HA_IOPTION_BOOL}}) that is applicable to B-tree indexes (not {{SPATIAL}} or {{FULLTEXT}} or other special types).

There is no way I can think of to reliable auto-detect any of the above options.
I do not understand what you mean with "Third must be auto-detected based per statement, it's not a table property."  The specification already is clear of how it should work.  If you find something unclear, please update the task description.

MDEV-21181 is an independent task not related to this one.
Sorry, I do not what "option to disable the automatic creation of virtual columns" would mean or how it could work.  MDEV-371 is a feature that requires a virtual column to be created. It is up to the user to decide if he uses the feature or not. Adding an option to disable things like MDEV-371 is not constructive.

This MDEV is to allow users to specify per table what optimizations and features the server can use with the table. It is not for changing other options that the user has already specified for the table.

Regarding innodb, I thought it would be good to have the option on both table and index level.
This way one can easily enable AHI for all indexes or just for one index.  The table level option would affect all index that does not have an index specific option

h2. how to
just rough ideas
h3. QUERY_CACHE
* {{Query_cache_query::hit_count}} already exists
* two atomic counters per {{TABLE_SHARE}} counting qc hits and invalidations:
** every time qc entry is invalidated by a table change, this table's {{TABLE_SHARE::invalidations}} gets incremented and for all tables of the {{Query_cache_query}}, {{TABLE_SHARE::hit_count}} is increased by {{Query_cache_query::hit_count}}. This all can be generally done lock-free.
* if for a specific table number of invalidations is large, compared to number of hits (say, about the same, or at least half), stop caching queries that use this table
* would be good to start caching table again when it stops being constantly updated. but it's not necesary, {{FLUSH}} will serve as a workaround.

h3. ADAPTIVE_HASH_INDEX
* this is internal InnoDB feature, can be done completely inside InnoDB, needs no server changes
* cannot say right now how to do it automatically, this needs to discussed with innodb developers

h3. BINLOG_ROW
* optimizer knows whether a query will scan a lot of rows but the result set will be small. And when a lot of rows are going to be inserted. In some cases optimizer doesn't — and in that case better to switch to ROW for that table. But it's not a per table property, written in CREATE TABLE. It's a sysvar, like {{@@rpl_optimized_mixed_mode}} or something, where the server lets optimizer decide whether it'd be faster to do SBR or RBR, per statement (if binlog_mode=MIXED).

I just pushed to the 11.8 branch [an adjustment to the regression test suite|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/commit/311b4445c59caa36ed031f5499eae79d07b68c0c] that not only allows all tests to pass, but also demonstrates smaller {{pages_accessed}} counts for the test {{main.rowid_filter_innodb}} when using the non-default setting {{innodb_adaptive_hash_index=ON}}. A variation of this could be used for testing the option {{adaptive_hash_index}}.

Instead of just having an option to enable or disable the adaptive hash index for a particular index, I think that it could be more useful to have a means to pin a specific value of {{index->search_info.left_bytes_fields}}. [~alessandro.vetere] shared some data from a test where the adaptive hash index is being rebuilt between a 1-field prefix of an index record, or 1-byte prefix. For such cases, it would be useful if the DBA could pin one of the parameter. Side note: We might also hard-code the minimum prefix to 2 or 3 bytes, because a 1-byte prefix would limit us to at most 256 unique hash values, which would not be very useful.

Internally, if an adaptive hash index exists for an InnoDB B-tree index, it will have the following parameters:
# *Number of complete fields* (0 to the number of columns the key is defined on; MariaDB allows up to 32 {{KEY_PART}} per B-tree index)
# *Number of bytes* to include in the first incomplete fields, or 0.
#* This is only usable for {{memcmp()}} comparable index fields, such as {{VARBINARY}} or {{INT}}.
#* For example, a 3-byte prefix on an {{INT}} will return an identical hash value for 0‥255, another one for 256‥511, and so on.
# When multiple adjacent records have the same hash value: Will the AHI point to the *first or last* record?
#* Usually it is the first, known as {{left_side}} in the code.
#* Example: we have an {{INT}} column with the values 1,4,10 and {{bytes=3}}, will that hash value point to the record 1 or the record 10?
#* Note: all values will necessarily have the same hash value computed on the big endian byte prefix 0x800000, for all of the values 0x80000001, 0x80000004, 0x8000000a. InnoDB inverts the sign bit in order to have {{memcmp()}} compatible comparison.

For a multi-column index that are serving very different queries, it can make sense to *disable the auto-configuration logic by explicitly specifying the parameters*. My suggestion would be to use the combination {{fields=0}}, {{bytes=0}} to indicate that auto-configuration is preferred. Maybe, let’s declare the Boolean parameter {{last}} (the opposite of {{left_side}}) so that we can conveniently declare all attributes to be 0 or {{OFF}} by default, to have the auto-configuration enabled by default.

"FLUSH will serve as a workaround." is unexceptionable.  We cannot assume users will actively monitor the database and adjust things when it gets things wrong (like wrong decided when disabling query cache).
I have got numerous requests from users to allow them to permanently enable or disable QUERY CACHE per table.
This MDEV is to honor these requests for the cases when the user KNOWS when QUERY CACHE works or does not work.

Same goes for adaptive hash indexes.

Having things automated would mean that we would need several new variables to allow the user to tune when to use query cache (to turn things one, turn things off, monitoring), which would requires more resources and put a penalty on tables for which the user knows the features does not apply.  We also do not have resources to implement these things, especially as it is very hard to get them right.

Implementation to allow one to turn of adaptive indexes per table and per index is now pushed to bb-ahi-monty.

Here follows the commit message for this commit:

    Changed the innodb_adaptive_hash_index from a bool to an enum with
    values ON, OFF and TABLE. TABLE means that adaptive hash indexes are
    only used by tables that uses the ADAPTIVE_HASH_INDEX=YES|NO table or
    index options.
    
    Added ADAPTIVE_HASH_INDEX=YES|NO table and index option to InnoDB.
    The table and index options only have an effect if InnoDB adaptive hash
    index feature is enabled.
    
    - Having the ADAPTIVE_HASH_INDEX TABLE option set to NO will disable
      adaptive hash index for all indexes in the table that does not have
      the index option adaptive_hash_index=yes.
    - Having the ADAPTIVE_HASH_INDEX TABLE option set to YES will enable the
      adaptive hash index for all indexes in the table that does not have
      the index option adaptive_hash_index=no.
    - Using adaptive_hash_index=default deletes the old setting.
    - One can also use OFF/ON as the options. This is to make it work similar
      as other existing options.
    - Added the following new index options for tuning adaptive_hash_index:
      - ADAPTIVE_HASH_COMPLETE_COLUMNS
      - ADAPTIVE_HASH_BYTES_IN_FIRST_INCOMPLETE
      - ADAPTIVE_HASH_ON_MATCH_LAST

    Example:
    CREATE TABLE t1 (a int primary key, b varchar(100), c int,
    index (b) adaptive_hash_index=no, index (c))
    engine=innodb, adaptive_hash_index=yes;

There is only two values for adaptive_hash_index, 0, 1   (0 = off, 1 = on).
DEFAULT is used to remove the explicit setting of adaptive_hash_index for a table or index.
This is how things works for all table and index engine options.

The values 0,1 is are what the engine gets from ALTER TABLE t1 adaptive_hash_index=ON|OFF
This is used in innobase_copy_frm_flags_from_table_share
To set the ahi_enabled for the table or index to 0, 1, 2.
These values represents:
0, ahi explicitly disabled by the user.  There should be no ahi for the specified table or index.  If table has ahi disabled, all index that does not have ahi explictely enabled will also be disabled.
1, ahi enabled if ahi is globally enabled (what we had before). This is corresponds to innodb.adaptive_hash_index=ON
2, ahi is explicitly requested by the end user.  Ahi is enabled if  innodb.adaptive_hash_index=ON or  innodb.adaptive_hash_index=IF_SPECIFIED

items.fromString:
Some of the features in MariaDB are only usable (from performance point of view) in special circumstances:
- QUERY_CACHE should no be used with tables that changes values *very* frequently
- InnoDB adaptive_hash_index does not work well if there is changes in the rows that are part if an active adaptive_hash
- Statement based binary logging  is not optimal for tables that does updates where the master has to scan a lot but only updates a few or inserts of many rows with generated auto-increments.

This MDEV is about fixing this issue by adding new table specific options where the user can enable/disable the options per table.

All table optimization should have the 3 values: ON, OFF and DEFAULT.  'DEFAULT' is needed to be able to remove the option from being stored in the table definition.

The suggested new table options are:
{noformat}
- QUERY_CACHE                    ;  Having this option OFF is the same as using SELECT SQL_NO_CACHE for any query using this table. Having this option ON is same as using SELECT SQL_CACHE for this table and the query will be cached if no other table has QUERY_CACHE=OFF.
- ADAPTIVE_HASH_INDEX   ; Having this option OFF will disable adaptive hash index for this table. Having it ON will enable adaptive hash index for the table if adaptive hash index are enabled at all.  
- BINLOG_ROW                    ; If this option is ON for any table, row based logging will be used.
{noformat}

items.fromString:
Some of the features in MariaDB are only usable (from performance point of view) in special circumstances:
- QUERY_CACHE should no be used with tables that changes values *very* frequently
- InnoDB adaptive_hash_index does not work well if there is changes in the rows that are part if an active adaptive_hash
- Statement based binary logging  is not optimal for tables that does updates where the master has to scan a lot but only updates a few or inserts of many rows with generated auto-increments.

This MDEV is about fixing this issue by adding new table specific options where the user can enable/disable the options per table.

All table optimization should have the 3 values: ON, OFF and DEFAULT.  'DEFAULT' is needed to be able to remove the option from being stored in the table definition.

The suggested new table options are:
||Option|Effect|
|QUERY_CACHE|Having this option OFF is the same as using SELECT SQL_NO_CACHE for any query using this table. Having this option ON is same as using SELECT SQL_CACHE for this table and the query will be cached if no other table has QUERY_CACHE=OFF|
|ADAPTIVE_HASH_INDEX |Having this option OFF will disable InnoDB adaptive hash index for this table. Having it ON will enable adaptive hash index for the table if adaptive hash indexes are enabled at all|
|BINLOG_ROW|If this option is ON for any table, row based binary logging will be used|

|Comprehensive Testing (Regression/Edge-case)|5–6 Days| To Do|
|Final Polish & Merge|1 Day|To Do|
|*Total Estimated Effort*|*~10 Days*| |

{{SELECT ... FROM information_schema.SLAVE_STATUS}} is an alternative to {{SHOW SLAVE STATUS}} that supports {{WHERE}} and column selection.
Utilizing this server-side feature allows {{mariadb-dump --dump-slave}} to iterate only the required data on the client side.

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done.
