comments.body:
See below for a test that uses unordered scan in a nontrivial way (triggering the second assert added in the comment above[1]), simplified from the "Bug #24186" testcase in main.partition. Note that if the "BETWEEN @ff AND @tt" is substituted with the actual values, then the assertion does not get tripped. I looked into it and for some reason using constants instead of the the uservars causes a different (semi) join order (t2-t1) to be chosen because loosescan is considered.

[1] https://jira.mariadb.org/browse/MDEV-37330?focusedCommentId=310635&page=com.atlassian.jira.plugin.system.issuetabpanels%3Acomment-tabpanel#comment-310635

{code:sql}
CREATE TABLE t1 (
  id int(8),
  PRIMARY KEY (id)
);

INSERT INTO t1 VALUES (11), (22), (33);

CREATE TABLE t2 (
  taken int,
  id int,
  PRIMARY KEY (id,taken),
  KEY taken (taken)
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (taken)
(
  PARTITION p1 VALUES LESS THAN (50),
  PARTITION p2 VALUES LESS THAN (60),
  PARTITION p3 VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE
);

INSERT INTO t2 VALUES
  (51,11), /* p2 */
  (63,11), /* p3 */
  (51,22), /* p2 */
  (53,22), /* p2 */
  (55,22), /* p2 */
  (57,22), /* p2 */
  (61,22), /* p3 */
  (63,22), /* p3 */
  (51,33), /* p2 */
  (55,33); /* p2 */

set @ff=53;
set @tt=64;

SELECT t1.id
FROM t1
WHERE t1.id IN (
    SELECT distinct id
    FROM t2
    WHERE taken BETWEEN @ff AND @tt)
ORDER BY t1.id;

drop table t1, t2;
{code}
[~ycp], please checkout this MDEV description, the *Suggestions* section.  Does it make it clear what/why I'd like to be changed in the patch?

[~ycp], good question.   Indeed, if we pick a method for every range there could be multiple methods...  I think accumulating a list of what was used would not be a good idea... Let me get back on this.

Looking at
{code}
commit 0f4bce48761df2f86fef883e69dbea2373722806
Author: Yuchen Pei <ycp@mariadb.com>
Date:   Mon Oct 27 23:35:34 2025 +1100

    MDEV-37330 Add a field in ANALYZE FORMAT=JSON for partitioned table to indicate what kind of index scan method has been used  
{code}

* In partition_info, add enum data member pi_scan_method.
* in Explain_table_access, add {{partition_index_scan_method *pi_scan_method}}.
* in JOIN_TAB::save_explain_data(), set it to point to the member in partition_info.
  Note that this is done next to make_used_partitions_str() call.
* In ha_partition::handle_ordered_index_scan(), set m_part_info->pi_scan_method  to the method used.

Some objections:
Initially, "Explain Data structures" were introduced to be self-contained. See the comment in sql_explain.h
Note the call to make_used_partitions_str(). It was added exactly so that we could print EXPLAIN/ANALYZE output without touching the handlers.
Since then, Explain_table_access::handler_for_stats was added which broke this.
Do we continue with breaking the "self-containment" rule?

What is the reason to have pi_scan_method in partition_info and not in ha_partition?

Hi [~psergei], ptal at the new patches that have addressed all comments:

{noformat}
abb45436680 bb-main-mdev-37330 MDEV-37330 [to-squash] Support reverse index
7d7d552b036 MDEV-37330 Allow unordered index scan for tables partitioned by range when a priority queue is not needed
6065d0ddecf MDEV-37330 Indicate in ANALYZE FORMAT=JSON index scan method used for partitioned tables
{noformat}

Addressed comments, with some extra questions that I will also think about myself:

*For the main commit*:
- Check prefix values in read_range/multi_read_range agree: done
- Support MRR: done. Question: do we still want to support read_range, given it is only done in loose index scan?
- Support ORDER BY ... DESC: done. Question: do we want to support reverse index for this MDEV? *UPDATE on [2025-11-24 Mon]: pushed an extra commit that supports reverse index and updated the commit list above.*
- Support PARTITION BY RANGE over multiple columns in Case 1.1 (new addition in the issue description): not sure it makes sense to do so - see example below
- Add comments / rename method: done

Consider the following example with PARTITION BY RANGE over multiple columns, the partition reading order is circular (p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p1, p2, ...) rather than linear (p1, p2, p3, p4, p5), so it would be less efficient doing unordered scan / scan iterating over partitions:

PARTITION `p1` VALUES LESS THAN (3, 2),

- change output from "ordered"/"unorderd" to "merge_ordered_scans"/"iterate_over_partitions": done. also added "both" when both have been used
- move pi_scan_method from partition_info to ha_partition: done - now print only when the index scan method is not NONE and handler_for_stats is not NULL, so not breaking the "self_containment" further

Aside from a few suggested comments and a potential (later) refinement, this looks good to me.

The potential (later) refinement is to support multi-column range for Case 2 / (1.2 in the description)

items.fromString:
Consider a table partitioned by date:

{code:sql}
CREATE TABLE t1 (
  date_created DATETIME
   user_id INT,
   ...
  INDEX idx1(user_id, date_created)
) PARTITION BY RANGE COLUMNS(date_created) (
 PARTITION `p_first`  VALUES LESS THAN ('2022-02-24 00:00:00'),
  ... 
 PARTITION `p_2025_02` VALUES LESS THAN ('2025-03-01 00:00:00'),
  ...
  PARTITION `p_last` VALUES LESS THAN ...
);
{code}

And a query looking to get the last row describing a given user.
{code:sql}
select * from t1
where user_id=1234
ORDER BY date_created DESC LIMIT 1
{code}

The index  {{idx1(user_id, date_created)}} will allow to use ref access and SQL layer will make one index lookup.

However, ha_partition has only two algorithms:
* unordered index scan
* ordered index scan

Here, ordered index scan will be used.  ha_partition will read a row from each partition and put that into the priority queue, then it will get the last one.
When there are many partitions, this will have a lot of overhead.  Why can't we just read the row from partition p_last ?  And after we've exhausted that, read the row from partition before the p_last and so forth? 
(This is actually similar to what "unordered index scan" code does except that code starts from partitions with smaller number and continues to partitions with larger number)

h2. Looking at the current patch

So, the current patch does this:

In ha_partition::partition_scan_set_up(), if we are using PARTITION BY RANGE($part_range_expr),

then we check if the table's SELECT_LEX has an ORDER BY expression and one of the following holds:

1. the ORDER BY expression is a field reference and it matches the $part_range_expr (which must also be a field reference)

2. the ORDER BY expression (not necessarily a field reference) matches  $part_range_expr.

One thing that looks bad is is that ha_partition examines the SELECT and checks the ORDER BY clause.  This breaks any conceivable API contract in the SE interface.

1. the ORDER BY expression is a field reference and it matches the $part_range_expr (which must also be a field reference)

2. the ORDER BY expression (not necessarily a field reference) matches  $part_range_expr.

One thing that looks bad is is that ha_partition examines the SELECT and checks the ORDER BY clause.  This breaks any conceivable API contract in the SE interface.
items.toString:
Consider a table partitioned by date:

{code:sql}
CREATE TABLE t1 (
  date_created DATETIME
   user_id INT,
   ...
  INDEX idx1(user_id, date_created)
) PARTITION BY RANGE COLUMNS(date_created) (
 PARTITION `p_first`  VALUES LESS THAN ('2022-02-24 00:00:00'),
  ... 
 PARTITION `p_2025_02` VALUES LESS THAN ('2025-03-01 00:00:00'),
  ...
  PARTITION `p_last` VALUES LESS THAN ...
);
{code}

And a query looking to get the last row describing a given user.
{code:sql}
select * from t1
where user_id=1234
ORDER BY date_created DESC LIMIT 1
{code}

The index  {{idx1(user_id, date_created)}} will allow to use ref access and SQL layer will make one index lookup.

However, ha_partition has only two algorithms:
* unordered index scan
* ordered index scan

Here, ordered index scan will be used.  ha_partition will read a row from each partition and put that into the priority queue, then it will get the last one.
When there are many partitions, this will have a lot of overhead.  Why can't we just read the row from partition p_last ?  And after we've exhausted that, read the row from partition before the p_last and so forth? 
(This is actually similar to what "unordered index scan" code does except that code starts from partitions with smaller number and continues to partitions with larger number)

In ha_partition::partition_scan_set_up(), if we are using PARTITION BY RANGE($part_range_expr),

then we check if the table's SELECT_LEX has an ORDER BY expression and one of the following holds:

1. the ORDER BY expression is a field reference and it matches the $part_range_expr (which must also be a field reference)

2. the ORDER BY expression (not necessarily a field reference) matches  $part_range_expr.

One thing that looks bad is is that ha_partition examines the SELECT and checks the ORDER BY clause.  This breaks any conceivable API contract in the SE interface.

fields.summary: Improve MaxScale Query Statistics

issuetype.description: A new feature of the product, which has yet to be developed.
issuetype.name: New Feature

fields.description:
Currently the TPM filter is unsuable, and the TOP filter is elementary. As a user I want detailed statistics of my queries going through maxscale.

Min, max, average, sum time execution (sum_time), total number of executions per query digest (count_star).

Some nice to haves for the first version would be by schema name, username, first seen and last seen timestamps. In the future, we'd like to cache by digest, or route queries by digest using the data learned/found from this query stats filter. Ideally some way to measure the latency maxscale is adding would be great too. so that users can better understand the latency overhead of a proxy, filter processing.

comments.body:
# MXS-5768: Query Statistics

# Important Metrics

The "four golden metrics" are:

- Latency (how long a query takes)
- Throughput (QPS or TPS)
- Error rate (errors versus resultsets/ok packets)
- Saturation (e.g. how much memory is left, how much CPU is used)

Out of these, throughput and error rate are the easiest metrics to calculate as they're simply counters. Throughput is already calculated in MaxScale as queries per second and in readwritesplit as transactions per second. Error rate is not tracked but tracking it would be easy as it's just another counter. Saturation is tracked by how busy each thread is which translates to overall CPU usage. Network throughput is also tracked as bytes sent which could be used to measure network saturation. Memory usage is auto-sized and limited via configuration settings so tracking these in MaxScale isn't as relevant.

This leaves latency which is currently only measured via averages per each query canonical form and log10 histograms (bins of 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10 100 etc.) for each server for read and write latency.

Averages are simple to calculate but are not a terribly good metric for characterizing the actual behavior of a system (see [DDSketch paper](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol12/p2195-masson.pdf) for a good visualization). 

The [Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/) and [this New Relic blog post](https://newrelic.com/blog/apm/monitoring-golden-signals) have some good explanations on why averages are not great. For example, from the Google SRE book:

> If 1% of your requests are 50x the average, it means that the rest of your requests are about twice as fast as the average. But if you’re not measuring your distribution, the idea that most of your requests are near the mean is just hopeful thinking.

Values at specific quantiles appear to be a widely used metric to track system health. The 95th and 99th quantile both appear quite often. Producing quantiles is difficult which is why they're nearly always generated via approximations of some sorts. Histograms are one way of tracking the distribution of values and they can be used to generated an approximate quantile value e.g. with linear interpolation within the boundaries of a bucket.

The log10 histograms that are in MaxScale currently are a bit too coarse for this and they do not implement quantile estimations (easy to add). With the log10 histogram, detecting a slowdown of 2s to 8s is not possible as they both fall into the 1s-10s bucket. Using a log2 histogram would detect this change but the accuracy still suffers once we're in the tens of seconds range. For example, a slowdown from about 30s to 60s with a log2 histogram still puts the values into the same bucket which makes it less accurate. For values less than 10 seconds, the resolution of a log2 histogram in milliseconds is adequate for coarse estimations but it still falls short of the accuracy of quantile sketch data structures.

# Quantile Sketches

## HdrHistogram

Implemented a bit like a log2 histogram but with linear sub-histograms inside the buckets that use a fixed part of the value for the sub-bucket index. Behaves a bit like a floating point number in that it retains a relative error guarantee across the whole range.

Some versions of the same data structure appear in e.g. librdkafka: https://github.com/confluentinc/librdkafka/blob/master/src/rdhdrhistogram.c

Pros:
* Configurable relative value error, accurate to within N digits
* Public domain C implementation: https://github.com/HdrHistogram/HdrHistogram_c
* Fast, one {{__builtin_clz}} call and integer arithmetic with some bit shifts and integer increments
* Supports multi-threaded access as everything is pre-allocated
* Relatively understandable algorithm
* Available as a package on RHEL 8, 9 and 10
* Mergeable

Cons:
* Uses up a lot of memory
* Fixed range and precision
* Merging histograms is somewhat slow
* No "official" published papers on the implementation or proofs of the algorithm, the best available one is this: https://www.david-andrzejewski.com/publications/hdr.pdf
* Needs to be built from source on Ubuntu, Debian and SLES

Size in memory with a range of 1ms-9h:

1 digit:  2KiB, 10% accuracy
2 digits: 20KiB, 1% accuracy
3 digits: 120Kib, 0.1% accuracy
4 digits: 1.4MiB, 0.01% accuracy

Resolutions with given digits:

| Digits    |    1s-2s    |    1min-2min    |    30min-1h    |
|-----------|-------------|-----------------|----------------|
|2          | 0.063s      | 4.000s          | 2min    11s    |
|3          | 0.007s      | 0.500s          | 16s            |
|4          | 0.001s      | 0.063s          | 2s             |
|5          | 0.001s      | 0.003s          | 0.127s         |

## DDSketch

Fully-mergeable, relative-error quantile sketching algorithm with formal guarantees. Uses {{logγ\(x\)}} as the bucket index where {{γ := (1+α)/(1−α)}} and {{α}} is the accuracy of the sketch. For example with 1% accurate quantiles, this ends up as an odd {{log1.02020202}} histogram. This histogram is unbounded and converting it into a fixed size one is done by always merging the smallest bucket into the next smallest one.

Pros:
* Unbounded input
* Fixed size that is smaller than the HdrHistogram (around 5KiB)
* Formal guarantees according to [this paper](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol12/p2195-masson.pdf)
* Mergeable and faster to merge than the HdrHistogram

Cons:
* No C or C++ implementations available. Java, Go, C#, Javascript and Python implementations are available that could be used for reference.
* Uses "relatively heavy" operations for the logarithm calculations in the naive case, logarithm approximations reduce this.
* Size increases if logarithm approximations are used.

## T-Digest

Another sketch data structure that has very accurate results at extreme quantiles like q99.99: https://github.com/tdunning/t-digest

Pros:
* Popular
* Handful of C/C++ implementations (e.g. [Folly](https://github.com/facebook/folly/blob/master/folly/stats/TDigest.h), [Apache Arrow](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/master/cpp/src/arrow/util/tdigest.h))

Cons:
* Not really suitable for direct histogram visualization

*TL;DR:*
# Export query latency metrics via OpenTelemetry
# Add configuration options to filter which queries and how many to send
# No need to make the percentiles configurable at this point
# Add a configuration setting for disabling all of the statistics gathering and sending.

The commits that add the statistics tracking and switch the cache to a global one are done, the next step is to expose the statistics as metrics via OpenTelemetry. This is a slightly more vague problem to solve as there's no right number of queries to export and the types of queries being exported is not going to always be the same for all users.

The current ordering of the query cache contents uses the cache hit count as the sorting order meaning that queries which have been most frequently used will be returned. This is different from the cache eviction policy which uses a LRU replacement policy but the frequency should provide relatively stable output while also automatically aging out obsolete queries over time.

There is still a need to control how many queries are returned and what types of queries are returned. An easy approach is to combine a regular expression for filtering the entries with a fixed limit on how many query patterns to send as metrics. By default the top 50 most used queries could be sent as metrics.

Another aspect that may have to be controlled is which percentile values are used. Each percentile sent increases the amount of data transmitted. Industry standard values like 95th and 99th percentile are most likely good default values and values like the median can also be useful. Other percentiles like the 75th can be useful for less rigorous SLAs like is mentioned in the Google SRE book. Percentiles below the median seem to rarely appear in blog posts and other online resources. The default percentiles to export thus could be set to 50, 75, 95 and 99. Making them configurable is most likely not necessary at this point.

To be able to measure the overhead of this, we'll need a way to disable the latency measurements. This'll also be a useful way to reduce memory usage for those scenarios where the latency statistics are not of interest as not gathering them lowers the memory usage.

!example-graphs.png|thumbnail! 

Some prototype graphs of TPC-C workloads with various modifications to the indexes of the tables. The p70 panel is actually the p50 latency.

fields.summary: Create an ExasolRouter

issuetype.description: A new feature of the product, which has yet to be developed.
issuetype.name: New Feature

fields.description:
The purpose of the {{ODBCRouter}} is to send SQL to the server specified with an ODBC connection string in the configuration of the router. The {{ODBCRouter}} is a _sink_, in the sense that it will *not* route queries forward to some target but handle the query as is. In a sense it is a MariaDB Protocol <-> ODBC translator that on the one hand takes MariaDB Protocol request packets and converts them to the appropriate ODBC calls and, on the other hand, takes ODBC responses and converts them to MariaDB Protocol response packets. MaxScale components before the {{ODBCRouter}} will not be aware of the ODBC conversion taking place, but will only deal with MariaDB protocol packets.

The intended use of {{ODBCRouter}} is to have it as one target of some other router that based on some criteria sends some queries to the {{ODBCRouter}} and some queries to some other target. 

In the MaxScale configuration file, the ODBCRouter will be configured something like:
{code}
[ODBC-Service]
type=service
router=odbcrouter
connection_string=DRIVER=libmaodbc.so;SERVER=my-server;PORT=3306;UID=my-user;PWD={my-password}
...
{code}

Initial limitations:
* The connection to the ODBC server will always be done using explicitly specified credentials, irrespective of the client connecting.
* All queries assumed to be SELECTs.

fields.summary: Refactor Master & Relay Log info to iterable tuples

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done.
issuetype.name: Task

fields.description:
Currently,
* Loose and repeated code provides the loading of the info files as well as te saving of the {{@@relay_log_info_file}}.
* One single hard-to-track text formatting drives the saving of the {{@@master_info_file}}. 

By iterating through collections of polymorphic instances, we not only avoid both issues for both operations, but can also expect the loops to be more performant.

Since all of the saved info is visible in SHOW REPLICA STATUS, the command can also optionally use a polymorphic method for writing its fields.
The same can't be guaranteed for the lexing/parsing for CHANGE MASTER currently, but it would nonetheless help with eventually eliminating repetitions in the code for evaluating.

By iterating through collections of polymorphic instances, we not only avoid both issues for both operations, but can also expect the loops to be more performant.

Since all of the saved info is visible in SHOW REPLICA STATUS, the command can also optionally use a polymorphic method for writing its fields.
The same can't be guaranteed for the lexing/parsing for CHANGE MASTER currently, but it would nonetheless help with eventually eliminating repetitions in the code for evaluating.

fields.summary: Implement innodb_log_archive

issuetype.description: A new feature of the product, which has yet to be developed.
issuetype.name: New Feature

fields.description:
The InnoDB write-ahead log file ({{ib_logfile0}}) is pre-allocated to {{innodb_log_file_size}} and written as a ring buffer. This is good for write performance and space management, but unsuitable for arbitrary point-in-time recovery or for facilitating incremental backup.

As noted in MDEV-14992, it would be better if the server took care of saving a sufficient amount of InnoDB write-ahead log to support backup. The SQL interface with a backup program would be something like the following:
{code:sql}
-- At the start of the backup, we check if log archiving is already running.
SELECT @@GLOBAL.innodb_log_archive, variable_value
FROM information_schema.global_status
WHERE variable_name = 'INNODB_LSN_ARCHIVED';
-- If BETWEEN 1 AND the LSN of the previous backup, skip copying InnoDB files (incremental backup)
-- Else if necessary, request the log to be archived from the current LSN onwards.
SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=ON;
-- In this case, at the end of the backup, we would disable the log archiving again:
SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=OFF;
{code}
Log archiving could also be enabled indefinitely, to facilitate arbitrary point-in-time recovery of anything that is covered by the InnoDB write-ahead log. When MDEV-34705 is implemented and enabled, this would include the binlog. However, point-in-time recovery of DDL operations would not work without limitations even for an InnoDB-only deployment, because part of the data dictionary is stored in {{.frm}} files, whose creation is covered by a separate log (see MDEV-17567).

The default value of {{innodb_log_archive}} is OFF, meaning that the log archiving is disabled by default.

When {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}, changes of the parameter {{innodb_log_file_size}} will take place when the current log file is about to be filled up and a new file is being created and allocated. The log resizing logic (MDEV-27812) as well as the creation of a redundant log file {{ib_logfile101}} will remain in use when {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}}.

When {{innodb_log_archiving=ON}}, the server will write log to files like the following:
{noformat}
ib_0000000000003000.log
ib_0000000000400000.log
ib_00000000007fd000.log
ib_0000000000bfa000.log
ib_0000000000ff7000.log
ib_00000000013f4000.log
{noformat}
The above example is with the minimum {{innodb_log_file_size=4M}} (0x400000 bytes in hexadecimal). The file names will refer to the log sequence number corresponding to offset 12288 (0x3000) in the file. At the start of each file, there will be a 12288-byte header that contains 64-bit offsets into checkpoint mini-transactions that end in {{FILE_CHECKPOINT}} records that point to the checkpoints.

-For {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}, we will impose a maximum {{innodb_log_file_size=4G}}, to keep the log file sizes manageable and to allow the format of 32-bit offsets to work.- Edit: we will use 64-bit offsets as per MDEV-39162.

For efficient recovery from archived log files instead of {{ib_logfile0}}, two further start-up parameters will be introduced:
||parameter||meaning||
|{{innodb_log_recovery_start}}|LSN to start recovery from (instead of the LSN of the mini-transaction that point to the latest available checkpoint); at the LSN we expect to find an optional sequence of {{FILE_MODIFY}} records and a {{FILE_CHECKPOINT}} record.
|{{innodb_log_recovery_target}}|recovery point objective (end LSN of a backup)|
An implementation of backup may write these parameters into a {{.cnf}} file or pass these in a command line when invoking {{mariadbd}}. The idea of these parameters is to limit the scope of recovery and to avoid replaying an archived log from the very beginning to the very end.

We must keep in mind that the creation and modification of some files, such as {{.frm}} files that form part of the data dictionary, are not covered by the InnoDB write-ahead log. Therefore, it is important to be able to stop the recovery at a specific LSN.

h2. Testing considerations
{{mariadb-backup}} will assume {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}}. It will not attempt to read any other log files than {{ib_logfile0}}.

We must keep in mind that there are several log I/O implementations:
* on Linux {{/dev/shm}} or PMEM unless {{cmake -DWITH_INNODB_PMEM=OFF}}: memory-mapped reads and writes
* else:
** parsing during recovery is either via {{pread}} or memory-mapped, according to the {{innodb_log_file_mmap}} setting
** writes are via {{pwrite}}

All combinations must be covered in testing. I have made use of the regression test suite like this:
{code:bash}
# data directory stored outside /dev/shm, or server compiled WITH_INNODB_PMEM=OFF
mysql-test/mtr --parallel=auto --big-test --force --mysqld=--loose-innodb-log-{archive,recovery-start=12288,file-size=4m,file-mmap=OFF} --skip-test=mariabackup
mysql-test/mtr --parallel=auto --big-test --force --mysqld=--loose-innodb-log-{archive,recovery-start=12288,file-size=4m,file-mmap=ON} --skip-test=mariabackup
# data directory in /dev/shm and server built WITH_INNODB_PMEM=ON
mysql-test/mtr --parallel=auto --big-test --force --mysqld=--loose-innodb-log-{archive,recovery-start=12288,file-size=4m} --skip-test=mariabackup
{code}
It would be beneficial extend our stress tests as follows:
# Cover both {{innodb_encrypt_log=OFF}} and {{innodb_encrypt_log=ON}}. Note that this parameter cannot be changed (at server restart) while {{innodb_log_archive=ON}} is set.
# Kill the server and determine the final LSN. This can be done by attempting startup with impossible {{innodb_log_recovery_target=12288}} and checking the error message.
# Start the server with {{innodb_log_recovery_target}} set to the final LSN.
# Expect everything to work, except any writes to persistent tables. Some transactions, such as any reads at {{TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE}} may be blocked by locks that are held by recovered incomplete transactions.

comments.body:
h2. Object file system considerations
Amazon S3 as well as https://github.com/minio/minio seem to support atomic multi-part uploads, including ones that are partly based on duplicating existing objects (files). This would seem to facilitate appending contents to old objects ("files"), such as the individual log snippet files, as well as atomically updating a copy of an archived log to a newer version. All the individual append-only log files as well as the "manifest" would be updated in one atomic operation. If I understood correctly, the maximum size of an upload is some gigabytes, but a multi-part upload may be used to construct larger objects, up to some terabytes.

It would seem reasonable to configure {{innodb_log_file_size}} (the size of individual preallocated log snippets) to some gigabytes. Any NUL bytes at the end of the preallocated file will be readily ignored by the log parser, which will expect each mini-transaction to end in 0x01 and a CRC-32C.

MariaDB Server would not write any log files (archived or not) to remote storage. An external program could do that. Older archived log files will not be accessed by the server under normal operation. Even crash recovery will not access them unless the main {{ib_logfile0}} is unavailable.
h2. Switching log files
The fuzzy or sliding-window log checkpoints makes the splitting of the archived log files somewhat of a challenge. Similar to a new log file that is being created during {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_file_size}} (MDEV-27812), we typically must start writing an archived log file at an arbitrary LSN somewhere between log checkpoint LSNs.

Upon reaching the preallocated size of the current file, the archived log writer would create and preallocate a new file of {{innodb_log_file_size}} and resume writing at byte offset 12288 of that file. Until the next log checkpoint is made, the new file would contain no checkpoint and could not be used by itself for recovery.

The name of a log archive file will be {{ib_%016x.log}}, containing its start LSN in hexadecimal. If log archiving is available from the very beginning, the first log archive file name would be {{ib_00003000.log}}, corresponding to {{log_sys.FIRST_LSN}} (12288).
h2. Log checkpoint
On each log checkpoint, a checkpoint header in the applicable log file will be updated. If {{innodb_lsn_archived}} is between 1 and the checkpoint LSN, a record will be appended to the {{ib_manifest.log}} file. If it is the first checkpoint of a recently created archived log file, then the previous {{ib_logfile0}} will be renamed to an archived log file and the current log file renamed to {{ib_logfile0}}, so that it can be used as a basis for normal recovery.
h2. Recovery
On startup, if no {{ib_logfile0}} is available and {{innodb_force_recovery=6}} is not specified (MDEV-27199), InnoDB will read the {{ib_manifest.log}} if available and start from the earliest applicable archive file. If the file {{ib_manifest.log}} is missing, then we will read checkpoint information from each available {{ib_%016x.log}} file.

If both {{ib_logfile0}} and an archived log exists, and {{innodb_log_archive}} had been set to a nonzero value on startup, the checkpoint will be validated with the archived log. If there is a mismatch, startup will fail, suggesting the DBA to restart with the default setting {{innodb_log_archive=0}}. Else, the value of {{innodb_log_archive}} will be adjusted to the earliest available archived checkpoint LSN. Any log records since the latest checkpoint in {{ib_logfile0}} that are missing from the archived log will be replicated.
h2. What to do if space allocation fails
InnoDB recovery will read records from one or more log files. Only after the log-based recovery is completed, may InnoDB start writing log records, just like under normal operation.

It is safest to *block any InnoDB writes when we fail to allocate space for a log file* when {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}, and simplest to *crash the server*. This is very disruptive, but a situation that InnoDB would be guaranteed to recover from.

If we silently executed {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=OFF}}, that could ruin a "perfect streak" and prevent point-in-time recovery. I do not want to introduce a difficult-to-handle regression, such as the open bug MDEV-27803 which involves a failure to allocate space for the binlog.

Allowing {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive_path}} would appear to be rather complicated, because there is no special interface for parameters that are file names. The maximum length of a string parameter would appear to be {{STRING_BUFFER_USUAL_SIZE}}, or 80 octets, possibly including a NUL terminator. That is much less than the maximum length of a path name. We seem to be a little inconsistent on validating path names. There exist functions {{is_secure_file_path()}} and the Microsoft Windows specific {{is_filename_allowed()}}, which are not being invoked on every parameter.

To start with, I would allow {{innodb_log_archive_path}} to be only changed at server startup, similar to {{innodb_log_group_home_dir}}. Interestingly, there is no {{is_filename_allowed()}} check for {{innodb_log_group_home_dir}}. For some reason, semicolons ({{;}}) are being disallowed in that parameter. For {{innodb_log_archive_path}} I am not planning to implement any restrictions beyond those that the underlying file system would impose. If the parameter is unspecified, it would default to {{datadir}}. This would be similar to {{innodb_log_group_home_dir}}, whose default value is {{NULL}}.

There is a way to simplify the process of enabling or disabling log archiving:
# Just add a single Boolean parameter {{innodb_log_archive}}; all files will be created in {{innodb_log_group_home_dir}}.
# As long as {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}, changes of {{innodb_log_file_size}} will affect the creation of subsequent log files once the current one is filled up.
# The active log file will be named {{ib_logfile0}} ({{innodb_log_archive=OFF}}, default) or {{ib_%016u.log}} ({{innodb_log_file_archive=ON}}, with the LSN corresponding to file offset 12288).
#* {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive}} will convert and rename the last log file between {{ib_logfile0}} and {{ib_%016u.log}}.
#* MDEV-27812 uses {{ib_logfile0}} and a redundant file {{ib_logfile101}} during {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_file_size}}; recovery will only refer to {{ib_logfile0}}
#* {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive}} is not allowed when MDEV-27812 resizing is in progress.
#* When {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}, the last two {{ib_%016u.log}} may be needed for recovery, and there is no redundancy during {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_file_size}}.
# On the completion of a log checkpoint, the previous {{ib_%016u.log}} file may be made read-only, to indicate that it can be safely moved.
#* The idea is that a DBA may *safely (re)move read-only files* {{ib_*.log}} from the {{datadir}} or {{innodb_log_group_home_dir}}
#* Any files {{ib_logfile*}} would be “off limits” just like they have always been.

The status variable {{innodb_lsn_archived}} will report the earliest LSN for which recovery history is available. By default ({{innodb_log_archive_start=0}}), it will reflect the {{ib_*.log}} files, or the last checkpoint of {{ib_logfile0}}.

The new Boolean parameter {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive}} will be protected by both {{LOCK_global_system_variables}} and a shared {{lock_sys.latch}}. In InnoDB, the parameter *will have effect when the current log file is about to fill up*, as follows:
* If {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}}:
** The current {{ib_logfile0}} will simply wrap around.
* If {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}:
** A file {{ib_%016u.log}} will be created and allocated to {{innodb_log_file_size}}.
** *If creating the log file fails, InnoDB will crash!*

In recovery with {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}, the value of the sequence bit at the end of each mini-transaction will be assumed to be always 1, because no wrap-around will be possible. Ignoring the bit will allow a simplified transition between an archived log and a circular {{ib_logfile0}}.

Because {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_file_size}} will release {{LOCK_global_system_variables}} while waiting for a log checkpoint (see MDEV-36828 for suggestions to improve this), we must implement some additional logic to prevent race conditions:
* After {{log_t::resize_start()}} has invoked {{log_resize_acquire()}} and checked for {{resize_in_progress()}}, it must implement a special fast path if {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}: just adjust the desired file size for the next {{ib_logfile_new}}.
* In {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive}}, after acquiring {{lock_sys.latch}} we must ignore the request (and report an error) if {{log_sys.resize_in_progress()}} holds, that is, a {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_file_size}} is in progress.

For a backup client that relies on hard-linking log files, things will be complicated a little:
# {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archiving=ON;}}
# Read the value of the status variable {{innodb_lsn_archived}}.
# Copy the data files as needed (see MDEV-14992).
# Hard-link any {{ib_*.log}} files as needed.
# If {{innodb_log_achiving}} was {{OFF}}, {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archiving=OFF}}, which shall delete any {{ib_*.log}} files from the data directory.
# Unlink any {{ib_*.log}} file that are past the backup end LSN.
# Unless the last hard-linked {{ib_*.log}} file is read-only, copy or block-clone the necessary part of it, until the backup end LSN.

Instead of or in addition to creating a separate {{ib_manifest.log}} file that contains checkpoint LSNs and file names, it may be simplest to use the largely unused 12KiB spare area at the start of each log file to record a history of all checkpoints. In the current circular {{ib_logfile0}} ({{innodb_log_archive=OFF}}), the format is as follows:
||offset||size||purpose||
|0|512|log file format identification (48 bytes), followed by 460 bytes of padding and a 4-byte CRC-32C|
|4096|64|log checkpoint|
|8192|64|log checkpoint|
|12288| |start of log payload|

In the header, we have 12288-48-4-64-64 = 12108 padding bytes (NUL) that could be repurposed for storing additional checkpoint LSNs. In the circular file, the two log checkpoint headers are being written in an alternating fashion, and recovery will be using the newest one.

In a sequential file ({{innodb_log_archive=ON}}), we only need to write the first available checkpoint LSN, which in the current format would be written to the first block at offset 4096. Everything else is basically redundant. We could go as far as define a completely new header format for {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}, optimized for space efficiency. An in-place conversion to {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} would be possible by durably overwriting the first checkpoint block (at 4096), followed by overwriting the log file identification block.

The header format of {{innodb_log_archive=ON}} could be something like the following:
||offset||size||purpose||
|0|4|format identifier|
|4|4|CRC-32C of the first 32 bytes|
|8|8|{{log_sys.first_lsn}}, an LSN corresponding to file offset 12288|
|16|8|first checkpoint LSN|
|24|8|checkpoint "end" LSN (pointer to {{FILE_MODIFY}} records and a {{FILE_CHECKPOINT}} record)|
|32| |further checkpoint "end" LSNs|
|12288| |start of log record data|
After the fixed header, we would store further "end" LSN in some variable-length or compressed encoding. For example, if we guaranteed that log checkpoints will never be more than 4 GiB apart, we could use 4 bytes per further checkpoint LSN. At each encoded "end" LSN we expect to find a possibly nonempty sequence of {{FILE_MODIFY}} records and a {{FILE_CHECKPOINT}} record pointing to the actual checkpoint LSN. So, based on this information we should have shortcuts to any LSN. The list of entries would be terminated by the value 0.

It is not strictly necessary to protect the checkpoint array with any additional CRC-32C. If we assume that a hardware power failure will not cause blocks to be corrupted while they are being overwritten, it should be safe to append new entries, without risking breaking anything. The really critical part is what we would store at the very start of the file: the {{log_sys.first_lsn}} and the information of the first available checkpoint. If the rest is corrupted, we will be able to recover by scanning the entire log from the first checkpoint, even though it could be suboptimal. Perhaps we should make that information part of the log file name.

In such a format, we could store (12288-32)/4 = 3064 checkpoints per log file. The maximum log file size would be some 12 TiB if the checkpoints were 4 GiB apart. Currently, the maximum {{innodb_log_file_size}} is "limited" to 2⁶⁴-1 bytes. With log archiving enabled, it could be reasonable to limit individual log files to much less than 1 TiB.

The 3064 log checkpoints could also be only a few hundred or thousand bytes apart from each other. Therefore, we could run out of the log file header space in a log file that is just some megabytes in size. We could mitigate that by applying some filtering: never write pointers to checkpoints if the previous checkpoint is too close or we are shutting down the server. For example, the minimum distance could be derived from the {{innodb_log_file_size}} divided by 3064. With {{innodb_log_file_size=1g}} that should correspond to 342 KiB of log, which should not take too long to parse.

Theoretically, we might also consider writing the actual log payload size somewhere to the 12288-byte header, and appending checkpoint information to the end of the payload area. In this way, the file would be free to grow with as many entries as needed, and a crash-safe in-place conversion between {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} and {{innodb_log_archive=ON}} should still be available. Because checkpoints are expensive operations to begin with, having to extend the log file by a few bytes should not hurt. If that extension operation fails, it is not the end of the world: recovery will still be possible from an earlier LSN. But, I think that we have enough spare space in the file header.

The main motivation for preserving multiple log checkpoint LSNs is to speed up recovery. Recovery, we must parse log records at some known good starting points. Traditionally there has been only one starting point: the latest available checkpoint when the server was killed, or backup started copying log. When applying an "incremental backup" from a log that is in the {{innodb_log_archive=ON}} format, we have to start from an appropriate {{innodb_log_recovery_start}}, which may be much earlier than the latest checkpoint. If we stored a full history of all checkpoints, we could employ *parallel log parsing* by assigning a range of LSN to each log parser thread. Ideally, we should be able to employ all available CPU cores. Each would parse and store the records from one sequential slice of the log.

In fact, only the {{log_sys.first_lsn}} will have to be stored in 64 bits, and all other LSN could be stored in a compressed form, such as 32-bit offset to be applied to the previous LSN. Even the first LSN could be stored as "end" LSN only; the actual checkpoint LSN would be found in the {{FILE_CHECKPOINT}} record:
||offset||size||purpose||
|0|4|format identifier|
|4|4|CRC-32C of the first 16 bytes|
|8|8|{{log_sys.first_lsn}}, an LSN corresponding to file offset 12288|
|16| |"end" LSN of each log checkpoint|
|12288| |start of record payload, at {{log_sys.first_lsn}}|

When using the 32-bit encoding that I mentioned in my earlier comment, this format would be able to hold 3068 log checkpoints. In the special case that no checkpoint has not been written to the file yet, all bytes between 16 and 12288 would be 0.

Assuming that an archived log file would never be recovered with the name {{ib_logfile0}} which MariaDB Server always used for the InnoDB write-ahead log so far, we are completely free to choose the file format. To facilitate an in-place transition between {{innodb_log_archive=ON}} and {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} and to avoid any additional special cases in the log handling, it should be a good idea to reserve an 12288-byte header in the file, to retain common format in the record payload area.

Given that the {{log_sys.first_lsn}} would be part of the archived log file name, it is not strictly necessary to store that information inside the file header. Because we will be scanning the directory for log file names, the file format and the status of {{innodb_encrypt_log}} could be made part of the log file name directly. That is, if the log file format ever has to be changed, the log file name pattern would be adjusted. For now, we can use {{ib_%016x.log}} or {{ib_crypt%016x.log}}. Given this format, the 12288-byte archived log file header may consist of 3,072 checkpoint "end" LSN encoded as an unsigned big-endian 32-bit offset to each previous value, starting from {{log_sys.first_lsn}} that is stored as part of the file name:
||offset||size||purpose||
|0|4|"end" LSN of the first checkpoint, relative to the {{log_sys.first_lsn}}|
|4|4|"end" LSN of the second checkpoint, or 0 if none yet|
|8|4|"end" LSN of the third checkpoint, or 0 if none yet|
|…|4|…|
|12288| |start of the record payload, at {{log_sys.first_lsn}}|
In a disaster scenario where a file system recovery is needed with the consequence that some names of recently created files will be lost, the correct name of the last archived log file can be determined based on the names and sizes ({{innodb_log_file_size}}) of the preceding log archive files.

To accommodate a usage scenario that archived log files will be regularly moved off-site, the read-only start-up parameter {{innodb_log_archive_start}} may specify the initial value of the status value {{innodb_lsn_archived}}. By default ({{innodb_log_archive_start=0}}), the value of {{innodb_lsn_archived}} will be determined from the available log files.

On every log checkpoint when {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} (the default setting), {{innodb_lsn_archived}} will be updated to the latest checkpoint in the circular {{ib_logfile0}}. If {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}, the {{innodb_lsn_archived}} will remain unchanged. Changes of {{innodb_log_archive}} shall rename the last file between {{ib_%016u.log}} and {{ib_logfile0}} as well as rewrite the 12288-byte file header.

Setting nonzero {{innodb_log_recovery_target}} is much like setting {{innodb_read_only=ON}}, with the exception that the data files may be written to by crash recovery, and locking reads will conflict with any incomplete transactions as necessary, and all transaction isolation levels will work normally (not hard-wired to {{READ UNCOMMITTED}}).

The intended purpose of specifying a nonzero {{innodb_log_recovery_target}} is to prepare an incremental backup, as well as to allow data retrieval as of a particular logical point of time.

h3. Crash safety of {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=OFF}}
This operation involves the following steps, with write barriers in between:
# Zerofill the {{ib_%016x.log}} file header byte range 512 to 12288.
# Write an {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} checkpoint block (64 bytes) to offset 4096. This will become accessible after the next step.
# Write a 512-byte {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} header to offset 0, overwriting all {{innodb_log_archive=ON}} information on checkpoints and {{innodb_encrypt_log}} parameters.
# Rename the {{ib_%016x.log}} to {{ib_logfile0}}.

If the server is killed between the execution of {{log_t::header_rewrite(archive=false)}} and renaming the log file to {{ib_logfile0}}, that is, during this part of {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=OFF}}, the following contents in the {{ib_%016x.log}} file can be observed:
# The header between offset 512 and 12288 is zero-filled.
#* This is only observable if more than 128 checkpoints had been written to the file.
#* We will start crash recovery from the latest valid checkpoint available in the header, or whatever is specified by {{innodb_log_recovery_start}}.
# The header between 512 and 12288 is zero-filled, except at offset 4096 there is a 64-byte checkpoint header in the {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} format.
#* This can be recovered in the same way as above. That is, we will retain the {{innodb_log_archive=ON}} format.
# The 512-byte header is in the {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} format (using the MDEV-14425 format tag {{0x50687973}}  or the MDEV-36024 format tag {{0xf09f979d}}), and the rest is zero-filled except the 64-byte checkpoint block at 4096.
#* If {{innodb_log_archive=ON}} was specified at startup, we will fail with an error message, requiring the DBA to configure {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}}. We do not want to clear {{innodb_log_format=ON}} without explicit user intervention.
#* If {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} was specified, rename the file to {{ib_logfile0}} and proceed with the recovery normally.
# The 512-byte header is partly written garbage that starts with a valid format tag:
#* Mostly same as above. If a valid checkpoint is found, correct the header and rename the file.

Furthermore, the logic related to {{log_t::get_sequence_bit(lsn_t)}} needs to be tested. In the {{innodb_log_archive=ON}} format this big is ignored, but in the {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} format it must reliably reflect the number of times the file “wrapped around”. We may have to subtract {{log_sys.capacity()}} from {{log_sys.first_lsn}} to ensure that there will be no discontinuity if the server is killed and restarted soon after {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=OFF}}.
h3. Crash safety of {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=ON}}
This operation involves the following steps, with write barriers in between:
# Rename the {{ib_logfile0}} to {{ib_%016x.log}}.
# Write {{innodb_encrypt_log}} metadata as well encode the latest {{log_sys.end_lsn}} to the file header at offset 0.
# Zero out the rest of the header up to offset 12288, overwriting the {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} checkpoint blocks.

The recovery is very simple:
# We find the file to be in the {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} format
#* As discussed in the previous section, recovery will rename the file back to {{ib_logfile0}}.
# We find at least one valid {{innodb_log_archive=ON}} checkpoint offset
#* We will recover as noted at the start of the previous section.
#* For consistency, we should zero out the file header between the last valid checkpoint and offset 12288. Currently we are missing this, so some debug assertions could fail in {{log_t::write_checkpoint()}}.

I extended the test {{innodb.log_archive}} with the above mentioned crash recovery scenarios. I can think of the following problematic scenario that I did not test yet:
# No log checkpoints will be executed until the server is killed, and we are not near the end of the log file.
#* We have {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}}.
#* {{log_sys.get_sequence_bit(lsn)}} is 0 for all records that had been written since the last checkpoint.
# {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=ON;}} is executed.
#* This will update {{log_sys.first_lsn}} so that the sequence bit will be 1 for any subsequently written records.
#* However, the old log records that had been written since the latest checkpoint have the sequence bit 0.
# {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=OFF;}} is executed.
# The server is killed.
# Recovery will end prematurely because of a discontinuity in the sequence bit.
#* Its purpose is to prevent an "infinite loop" in the {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} format
#* It is supposed to be flipped whenever the file wraps around. But in this scenario there is no wrap-around.

A trivial fix would be to force a log checkpoint during one of {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=ON}} or {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=OFF}}. In {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=ON}} we will need a new checkpoint anyway if the end of the log is at a smaller position than the latest checkpoint, that is, there is a wrap-around in between.

I believe that the simplest way to address the remaining problematic recovery scenarios after {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive}} is to ensure that the latest checkpoint is not before:
# {{get_lsn() - (get_lsn() - first_lsn) % capacity()}}
#* this is only possible if we currently have {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} and the circular log has wrapped around since the previous checkpoint
#* in the {{innodb_log_archive=ON}} format, log records are append-only
# the LSN when {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=ON}} had last been executed
#* this will be enforced in {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=OFF}})
#* log records written while {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=ON}} is in effect will carry the sequence bit 1
#* this rule ensures that any old log records from an earlier {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}} incarnation of the same log file that might carry the sequence bit 0 will be ‘discarded’ by a new checkpoint

The second condition is sufficient but not always necessary. We’d only need it if we have written any log records with the sequence bit value 0 since the previous checkpoint. So, we can just introduce a Boolean flag (without growing {{sizeof log_sys}}) that would be assigned {{!log_sys.get_sequence_bit(checkpoint_lsn)}} in {{log_t::write_checkpoint()}}. If this flag is set in {{log_t::set_archive()}}, we would wait for a new checkpoint.

items.fromString:
The InnoDB write-ahead log file ({{ib_logfile0}}) is pre-allocated to {{innodb_log_file_size}} and written as a ring buffer. This is good for write performance and space management, but unsuitable for arbitrary point-in-time recovery or for facilitating incremental backup.

As noted in MDEV-14992, it would be better if the server took care of saving a sufficient amount of InnoDB write-ahead log to support backup. The SQL interface with a backup program would be something like the following:
{code:sql}
-- At the start of the backup, we check if log archiving is already running.
SELECT @@GLOBAL.innodb_log_archive;
-- If BETWEEN 1 AND the LSN of the previous backup, skip copying InnoDB files (incremental backup)
-- Else, request the log to be archived (from the current LSN onwards).
SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive_path='target_directory',innodb_log_archive=@lsn;
{code}
Log archiving could also be enabled indefinitely, to facilitate arbitrary point-in-time recovery of anything that is covered by the InnoDB write-ahead log. When MDEV-34705 is implemented and enabled, this would include the binlog. However, point-in-time recovery of DDL operations would not work without limitations even for an InnoDB-only deployment, because part of the data dictionary is stored in {{.frm}} files, whose creation is covered by a separate log (see MDEV-17567).

The archived log should probably consist of multiple append-only files, similar to those that {{mariadb-backup --backup}} is generating today. There should additionally be "manifest" and "state" files that maintain some additional information:
* complete list of log checkpoint LSN and the names of corresponding log files
* the desired recovery target LSN (may be before the end of the log)
* the last recovered LSN among the data files (so that recovery can start from the latest available and applicable checkpoint)

These files should be modified and created in a format and way that is inherently crash-safe with local or remote file systems, including object storage such as [Amazon S3|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_S3]. For example, when creating a manifest file, we would create and populate a new file and then atomically overwrite an old manifest file.
items.toString:
The InnoDB write-ahead log file ({{ib_logfile0}}) is pre-allocated to {{innodb_log_file_size}} and written as a ring buffer. This is good for write performance and space management, but unsuitable for arbitrary point-in-time recovery or for facilitating incremental backup.

As noted in MDEV-14992, it would be better if the server took care of saving a sufficient amount of InnoDB write-ahead log to support backup. The SQL interface with a backup program would be something like the following:
{code:sql}
-- At the start of the backup, we check if log archiving is already running.
SELECT @@GLOBAL.innodb_log_archive_file_size, variable_value
FROM information_schema.global_status
WHERE variable_name = 'INNODB_LSN_ARCHIVED';
-- If BETWEEN 1 AND the LSN of the previous backup, skip copying InnoDB files (incremental backup)
-- Else, request the log to be archived (in append-only mode, from the current LSN onwards).
SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive_file_size=12288;
-- In this case, at the end of the backup, we would disable the log archiving again:
SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive_file_size=0;
{code}
Log archiving could also be enabled indefinitely, to facilitate arbitrary point-in-time recovery of anything that is covered by the InnoDB write-ahead log. However, point-in-time recovery of DDL operations would not work without limitations even for an InnoDB-only deployment, because part of the data dictionary is stored in {{.frm}} files, whose creation is covered by a separate log (see MDEV-17567).

|305441471|{{ib_0000000000003000.log}}|
|1074389568|{{ib_0000000040003000.log}}|

To avoid any performance degradation, we’d want to avoid writing multiple logs whenever possible.

{{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_file_archive_size}} will include some special logic:
* Any value smaller than 12288 will disable the log archiving, and any value larger than 12288 will enable the log archiving.
** Similar to {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_file_size}} (MDEV-27812), the operation will block until the switch has been completed.
** During a transition period, we must write to both logs, to guarantee working crash recovery.
** Once the first log checkpoint to the new log (archived or circular) has been written, we may do the switch.
** It could be clearest to delete (unlink) the {{ib_logfile0}} whenever the log archiving has been fully enabled.
* {{SET GLOBAL innodb_log_file_archive_size=12288}} would enable the writing of an append-only log file, of unlimited size.
** I am not sure if it is a good idea to introduce such a special case.
** The only motivation for this was to have something similar to the files that {{mariadb-backup --backup}} is currently producing.

Maybe we should only have preallocated log files, and allow {{innodb_log_file_archive_size}} to be specified in whole megabytes.
* In that case, the only special value would be 0, to disable the log archiving.
* A backup client that wishes to minimize the size of log files copied would set a small but nonzero {{innodb_log_file_archive_size}}.

{code:sql}

-- If BETWEEN 1 AND the LSN of the previous backup, skip copying InnoDB files (incremental backup)
-- Else if necessary, request the log to be archived from the current LSN onwards.
SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=ON;
-- In this case, at the end of the backup, we would disable the log archiving again:
SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=OFF;
{code}
Log archiving could also be enabled indefinitely, to facilitate arbitrary point-in-time recovery of anything that is covered by the InnoDB write-ahead log. When MDEV-34705 is implemented and enabled, this would include the binlog. However, point-in-time recovery of DDL operations would not work without limitations even for an InnoDB-only deployment, because part of the data dictionary is stored in {{.frm}} files, whose creation is covered by a separate log (see MDEV-17567).

The default value of {{innodb_log_archive}} is OFF, meaning that the log archiving is disabled by default.

When {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}, changes of the parameter {{innodb_log_file_size}} will take place when the current log file is about to be filled up and a new file is being created and allocated. The log resizing logic (MDEV-27812) as well as the creation of a redundant log file {{ib_logfile101}} will remain in use when {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}}.

When {{innodb_log_archiving=ON}}, the server will write log to files like the following:
{noformat}
ib_0000000000003000.log
ib_0000000000400000.log
ib_00000000007fd000.log
ib_0000000000bfa000.log
ib_0000000000ff7000.log
ib_00000000013f4000.log
{noformat}
The above example is with the minimum {{innodb_log_file_size=4M}} (0x400000 bytes in hexadecimal). The file names will refer to the log sequence number corresponding to offset 12288 (0x3000) in the file. At the start of each file, there will be a 12288-byte header that contains 32-bit offsets into checkpoint mini-transactions that end in {{FILE_CHECKPOINT}} records that point to the checkpoints.

For {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}, we will impose a maximum {{innodb_log_file_size=4G}}, to keep the log file sizes manageable and to allow the format of 32-bit offsets to work.

For efficient recovery from archived log files instead of {{ib_logfile0}}, two further start-up parameters will be introduced:
||parameter||meaning||
|{{innodb_log_recovery_start}}|LSN to start recovery from (instead of the LSN of the mini-transaction that point to the latest available checkpoint); at the LSN we expect to find an optional sequence of {{FILE_MODIFY}} records and a {{FILE_CHECKPOINT}} record.
|{{innodb_log_recovery_target}}|recovery point objective (end LSN of a backup)|
An implementation of backup may write these parameters into a {{.cnf}} file or pass these in a command line when invoking {{mariadbd}}. The idea of these parameters is to limit the scope of recovery and to avoid replaying an archived log from the very beginning to the very end.

We must keep in mind that the creation and modification of some files, such as {{.frm}} files that form part of the data dictionary, are not covered by the InnoDB write-ahead log. Therefore, it is important to be able to stop the recovery at a specific LSN.

h2. Testing considerations
{{mariadb-backup}} will assume {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}}. It will not attempt to read any other log files than {{ib_logfile0}}.

We must keep in mind that there are several log I/O implementations:
* on Linux {{/dev/shm}} or PMEM unless {{cmake -DWITH_INNODB_PMEM=OFF}}: memory-mapped reads and writes
* else:
** parsing during recovery is either via {{pread}} or memory-mapped, according to the {{innodb_log_file_mmap}} setting
** writes are via {{pwrite}}

All combinations must be covered in testing. I have made use of the regression test suite like this:
{code:bash}
# data directory stored outside /dev/shm, or server compiled WITH_INNODB_PMEM=OFF
mysql-test/mtr --parallel=auto --big-test --force --mysqld=--loose-innodb-log-{archive,recovery-start=12288,file-size=4m,file-mmap=OFF} --skip-test=mariabackup
mysql-test/mtr --parallel=auto --big-test --force --mysqld=--loose-innodb-log-{archive,recovery-start=12288,file-size=4m,file-mmap=ON} --skip-test=mariabackup
# data directory in /dev/shm and server built WITH_INNODB_PMEM=ON
mysql-test/mtr --parallel=auto --big-test --force --mysqld=--loose-innodb-log-{archive,recovery-start=12288,file-size=4m} --skip-test=mariabackup
{code}
It would be beneficial extend our stress tests as follows:
# Cover both {{innodb_encrypt_log=OFF}} and {{innodb_encrypt_log=ON}}. Note that this parameter cannot be changed (at server restart) while {{innodb_log_archive=ON}} is set.
# Kill the server and determine the final LSN. This can be done by attempting startup with impossible {{innodb_log_recovery_target=12288}} and checking the error message.
# Start the server with {{innodb_log_recovery_target}} set to the final LSN.
# Expect everything to work, except any writes to persistent tables. Some transactions, such as any reads at {{TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE}} may be blocked by locks that are held by recovered incomplete transactions.

items.toString:
The InnoDB write-ahead log file ({{ib_logfile0}}) is pre-allocated to {{innodb_log_file_size}} and written as a ring buffer. This is good for write performance and space management, but unsuitable for arbitrary point-in-time recovery or for facilitating incremental backup.

As noted in MDEV-14992, it would be better if the server took care of saving a sufficient amount of InnoDB write-ahead log to support backup. The SQL interface with a backup program would be something like the following:
{code:sql}
-- At the start of the backup, we check if log archiving is already running.
SELECT @@GLOBAL.innodb_log_archive, variable_value
FROM information_schema.global_status
WHERE variable_name = 'INNODB_LSN_ARCHIVED';
-- If BETWEEN 1 AND the LSN of the previous backup, skip copying InnoDB files (incremental backup)
-- Else if necessary, request the log to be archived from the current LSN onwards.
SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=ON;
-- In this case, at the end of the backup, we would disable the log archiving again:
SET GLOBAL innodb_log_archive=OFF;
{code}
Log archiving could also be enabled indefinitely, to facilitate arbitrary point-in-time recovery of anything that is covered by the InnoDB write-ahead log. When MDEV-34705 is implemented and enabled, this would include the binlog. However, point-in-time recovery of DDL operations would not work without limitations even for an InnoDB-only deployment, because part of the data dictionary is stored in {{.frm}} files, whose creation is covered by a separate log (see MDEV-17567).

The default value of {{innodb_log_archive}} is OFF, meaning that the log archiving is disabled by default.

When {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}, changes of the parameter {{innodb_log_file_size}} will take place when the current log file is about to be filled up and a new file is being created and allocated. The log resizing logic (MDEV-27812) as well as the creation of a redundant log file {{ib_logfile101}} will remain in use when {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}}.

When {{innodb_log_archiving=ON}}, the server will write log to files like the following:
{noformat}
ib_0000000000003000.log
ib_0000000000400000.log
ib_00000000007fd000.log
ib_0000000000bfa000.log
ib_0000000000ff7000.log
ib_00000000013f4000.log
{noformat}
The above example is with the minimum {{innodb_log_file_size=4M}} (0x400000 bytes in hexadecimal). The file names will refer to the log sequence number corresponding to offset 12288 (0x3000) in the file. At the start of each file, there will be a 12288-byte header that contains 64-bit offsets into checkpoint mini-transactions that end in {{FILE_CHECKPOINT}} records that point to the checkpoints.

-For {{innodb_log_archive=ON}}, we will impose a maximum {{innodb_log_file_size=4G}}, to keep the log file sizes manageable and to allow the format of 32-bit offsets to work.- Edit: we will use 64-bit offsets as per MDEV-39162.

For efficient recovery from archived log files instead of {{ib_logfile0}}, two further start-up parameters will be introduced:
||parameter||meaning||
|{{innodb_log_recovery_start}}|LSN to start recovery from (instead of the LSN of the mini-transaction that point to the latest available checkpoint); at the LSN we expect to find an optional sequence of {{FILE_MODIFY}} records and a {{FILE_CHECKPOINT}} record.
|{{innodb_log_recovery_target}}|recovery point objective (end LSN of a backup)|
An implementation of backup may write these parameters into a {{.cnf}} file or pass these in a command line when invoking {{mariadbd}}. The idea of these parameters is to limit the scope of recovery and to avoid replaying an archived log from the very beginning to the very end.

We must keep in mind that the creation and modification of some files, such as {{.frm}} files that form part of the data dictionary, are not covered by the InnoDB write-ahead log. Therefore, it is important to be able to stop the recovery at a specific LSN.

h2. Testing considerations
{{mariadb-backup}} will assume {{innodb_log_archive=OFF}}. It will not attempt to read any other log files than {{ib_logfile0}}.

We must keep in mind that there are several log I/O implementations:
* on Linux {{/dev/shm}} or PMEM unless {{cmake -DWITH_INNODB_PMEM=OFF}}: memory-mapped reads and writes
* else:
** parsing during recovery is either via {{pread}} or memory-mapped, according to the {{innodb_log_file_mmap}} setting
** writes are via {{pwrite}}

All combinations must be covered in testing. I have made use of the regression test suite like this:
{code:bash}
# data directory stored outside /dev/shm, or server compiled WITH_INNODB_PMEM=OFF
mysql-test/mtr --parallel=auto --big-test --force --mysqld=--loose-innodb-log-{archive,recovery-start=12288,file-size=4m,file-mmap=OFF} --skip-test=mariabackup
mysql-test/mtr --parallel=auto --big-test --force --mysqld=--loose-innodb-log-{archive,recovery-start=12288,file-size=4m,file-mmap=ON} --skip-test=mariabackup
# data directory in /dev/shm and server built WITH_INNODB_PMEM=ON
mysql-test/mtr --parallel=auto --big-test --force --mysqld=--loose-innodb-log-{archive,recovery-start=12288,file-size=4m} --skip-test=mariabackup
{code}
It would be beneficial extend our stress tests as follows:
# Cover both {{innodb_encrypt_log=OFF}} and {{innodb_encrypt_log=ON}}. Note that this parameter cannot be changed (at server restart) while {{innodb_log_archive=ON}} is set.
# Kill the server and determine the final LSN. This can be done by attempting startup with impossible {{innodb_log_recovery_target=12288}} and checking the error message.
# Start the server with {{innodb_log_recovery_target}} set to the final LSN.
# Expect everything to work, except any writes to persistent tables. Some transactions, such as any reads at {{TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE}} may be blocked by locks that are held by recovered incomplete transactions.
The parameters innodb_log_archive, innodb_log_recovery_start, innodb_log_recovery_target were introduced.

fields.description:
*Idea*
Every view, CTE and derived table participating in a query gets an implicit query block name based on its name or alias. Optimizer hints can be applied to internal objects of view/derived tables/CTE by referencing this implicit query block name.

*Benefits*
Objects inside derived tables and views can be referenced by optimizer hints without explicit addition of the `QB_NAME()` hint

*Example*
{code:sql}
select * from (select * from t1 where a > 10) as DT;   -- `DT` gets an implicit query block name `dt`
-- referencing a table inside a DT by implicit QB name:
select /*+ no_index(t1@dt) */ * from (select * from t1 where a > 10) as DT; 
-- this is an equivalent to:
select /*+ no_index(t1@dt) */ * from (select /*+ qb_name(dt)*/ * from t1 where a > 10) as DT; 

create view v1 as select * from t1 where a > 10 and b > 100;
select * from v1 as vvv, t2 where vvv.a = t2.a;  -- view `vvv` gets an implicit query block name `vvv`
-- referencing a table inside a view by implicit QB name:
select /*+ index_merge(t1@vvv idx_a, idx_b) */ * from v1 as vvv, t2 where vvv.a = t2.a;

with bless100 as (select a from t1 where b <100)
  select * from bless100;    -- The CTE gets an implicit query block name 'bless100'

-- referencing a table inside a CTE by implicit QB name:
with bless100 as (select a from t1 where b <100)
  select /*+ index(t1@bless100) */ * from bless100;
{code}

*Limitations*
# If there is UNION/EXCEPT/INTERSECT inside the implicit QB, it's unclear to which select of the unit a hint should be applied. Such hints are not currenyly supported, and the warning is generated.
# If there is an intersection with explicit QB names, the implicit name is not assigned, for example:
{code:sql}
select /*+ index(t2@DT) */ * from t1,
   (select a from t2 where a < 10) DT, 
   (select /*+ qb_name(DT)*/ a from t2 where a > 100) as DT_big ...
{code}
the hint index(t2@DT) is applied to `t2` from `DT_big`  despite there is another derived table named `DT`.
# If a view, derived table or CTE is referenced more than once with the same alias, the hint cannot be applied. For example,
{code:sql}
select /*+ index(t2@v1) */ * from v1,
   (select a from v1 where b >5) DT  ...
{code}

h2. TiDB-inspired syntax suggestion

h3. Lexical Select Numbering 
Let's define "Lexical Select Numbering" as follows:

- Every VIEW, CTE and derived table has its own local numbering.
- Other than that, SELECTs are numbered "in the order their SELECT keyword occurs in the query text". 

This numeration is similar to select_lex->select_number numeration for basic cases. In complex cases it is apparently different.
It is close to TiDB's SEL_n numbering. The only difference I'm aware of is handling of CTEs.

h3. Locator path
Now, let's describe a way how to address any select in the query.

We can't address selects inside VIEWs or CTEs by their either implicit or explicit qb_name.

We need to assign them a name using "locator QB_NAME" hint, first.
Locator QB_NAME hint looks similar to regular QB_NAME(new_name) hint but it has multiple arguments.

It specifies a "path" to a select and assigns that select a name:
{code}
  QB_NAME(new_name , path)
{code}
The path consists of components:
{code}
  ViewDtCteName1@QbLexNumber1 [ '.' ViewDtCteName2@QbLexNumber2 ...]  '.'  @QbLexNumberN
{code}

All {{QbLexNumberN}}  must be in   {{SEL_n}} form.

We interpret the path as follows:

Start with the root of the query.

Locate the SELECT within the query that has Lexical Select Number QbLexNumber1.

Within that SELECT, locate the TABLE_LIST $TL with ViewCteName1.

(If you are doing this after the derived or semi-join merge has been done, be sure to look at the tables that were originally in that SELECT! There is TABLE_LIST::next_local chain, check if you can use that. Maybe, not)

$TL must be a view, a derived table or a CTE reference.
Enter that CTE, VIEW or DT .
Repeat the above process with QbLexNumber2: locate a SELECT with that Lexical Select Number.
In the SELECT, locate the TABLE_LIST with ViewCteName2.

Eventually, you reach the last "@QbLexNumberN" component of the path.
Again, locate the SELECT with this Lexical Select Number.

This is the SELECT that we need to assign name new_name to.
After the select is assigned a name, one can use other hints to control things in that select.

h4. Abbreviated path step
A  path step can be just  {{.foo}}, that is, have this form
{code}
 ViewDtCteName
{code}
This is equivalent to  
{code}
 ViewCteName @ SEL_1
{code}

Improved (simplified) solution that does not need splitting hint resolution into two stages:
- https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4692 (implicit QB names)
- https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4700 (QB_NAME with path)
Final version: https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4777 (branch name 13.0-MDEV-38045). Both patches are approved by reviewers.

According to [~mariadb-pavithrapandith], this is ready for pushing after the linked bugs are fixed
(And they are either fixed or approved).

select * from v1 as vvv, t2 where vvv.a = t2.a;  -- view `vvv` gets an implicit query block name `vvv`
-- referencing a table inside a view by implicit QB name:
select /*+ index_merge(t1@vvv idx_a, idx_b) */ * from v1 as vvv, t2 where vvv.a = t2.a;

{code:sql}
select /*+ index(t2@DT) */ * from t1,
   (select a from t2 where a < 10) DT, 
   (select /*+ qb_name(DT)*/ a from t2 where a > 100) as DT_big ...
{code}
the hint index(t2@DT) is applied to `t2` from `DT_big`  despite there is another derived table named `DT`.

Let's define "Lexical Select Numbering" as follows:

- Every CTE definition has its own local numbering.

This numeration is similar to select_lex->select_number numeration for basic cases. In complex cases it is apparently different.
It is close to TiDB's SEL_n numbering. The only difference I'm aware of is handling of CTEs.

h3. Locator path
Now, let's describe a way how to address any select in the query.

We can't address selects inside VIEWs or CTEs by their either implicit or explicit qb_name.

We need to assign them a name using "locator QB_NAME" hint, first.
Locator QB_NAME hint looks similar to regular QB_NAME(new_name) hint but it has multiple arguments.

It specifies a "path" to a select and assigns that select a name:
{code}
  QB_NAME(new_name , path)
{code}
The path consists of components:
{code}
  ViewCteName1@QbLexNumber1 [ '.' ViewCteName2@QbLexNumber2 ...]  '.'  @QbLexNumberN
{code}

All {{QbLexNumberN}}  must be in   {{SEL_n}} form.

We interpret the path as follows:

Start with the root of the query.

Locate the SELECT within the query that has Lexical Select Number QbLexNumber1.

Within that SELECT, locate the TABLE_LIST $TL with ViewCteName1.

(If you are doing this after the derived or semi-join merge has been done, be sure to look at the tables that were originally in that SELECT! There is TABLE_LIST::next_local chain, check if you can use that. Maybe, not)

$TL must be a view or a CTE reference.
Enter that CTE or VIEW.
Repeat the above process with QbLexNumber2: locate a SELECT with that Lexical Select Number.
In the SELECT, locate the TABLE_LIST with ViewCteName2.

Eventually, you reach the last "@QbLexNumberN" component of the path.
Again, locate the SELECT with this Lexical Select Number.

This is the SELECT that we need to assign name new_name to.
After the select is assigned a name, one can use other hints to control things in that select.

h4. Abbreviated path step
A  path step can be just  {{.foo}}, that is, have this form
{code}
 ViewCteName
{code}
This is equivalent to  
{code}

{code}

fields.description:
MDEV-9826 adds some xxh use in the server, now we can add an sql function, same as [md5|https://mariadb.com/docs/server/reference/sql-functions/secondary-functions/encryption-hashing-and-compression-functions/md5] and others

After discussion with the team ([~bar],[~serg],[~ycp]), we decided to go with the following function signatures:
{noformat}
XXH32(expr) --> INT UNSIGNED
XXH3(expr) --> BIGINT UNSIGNED
XXH64(expr) --> BIGINT UNSIGNED (will be done in a spearate task)
XXH128(expr) --> BINARY(16)    (will be done in a separate task)
{noformat}

comments.body: I would like to work on this issue

I am looking for feedback on the APIs to be exposed.

Do these look good?
XXH32(expr) --> INT UNSIGNED
XXH64(expr)  --> BIGINT UNSIGNED
XXH3_64(expr) --> BIGINT UNSIGNED

There's an issue with returning numeric types. We do not have a 128 bit numeric type and can't return a value for XXH3_128. We would have to omit it.

The other option is to return a hexadecimal string. 
XXH32(expr) --> CHAR(8)
XXH64(expr)  --> CHAR(16)
XXH3_64(expr) --> CHAR(16)
XXH_128(expr) --> CHAR(32)

Which one of the approaches would you prefer?

Thanks!
[~deo002] Thank you! Please note [~ycp] is on a break. [~nikitamalyavin] & [~serg] FYI, in case either of you has any input on this.

Thanks for the update!
Will wait for feedback.

https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4741/changes/da3353553f7a7ecfa2ee19d8d5b1410fa6a453bc

Both now corrected on PR4741

[DOCS-6169|https://mariadbcorp.atlassian.net/browse/DOCS-6169] Updated.
