fields.description:
h2. Hook records_in_range call
in opt_range.cc  in ror_intersect_add() -> ror_scan_selectivity()
, there is a handler->records_in_range() call.
We need to hook it: save and return back its value. 

Note that  ha_something::multi_range_read_info_const()  as well as handler::multi_range_read_info_const() also  make calls to handler->records_in_range() and we do NOT need to intercept them.

Example query that uses index_merge/intersection and depends on records_in_range() value:

{code:sql}
INDEX i1(a, b)
INDEX i2(a, c) 
select * from t1 where a=1 and b=1 and c=1;
{code}
or try  INDEX(c,a), INDEX(b, a). 

h2. Constant tables 

We need to save the rows we've read from constant tables.
For the moment, let's take the path of least effort: 
We write {{CREATE TABLE ...}} statements into captured context. 
For constant tables, also write {{INSERT INTO tbl VALUES(...)}} statement. 
That way, we won't need any special replay code. 

Use this function for dumping table rows:
{code}
String dbug_format_row(TABLE *table, const uchar *rec, bool print_names)
{code}
Just make it do quoting.

fields.summary: Debugging help: print which MEM_ROOT the object is on

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done.
issuetype.name: Task

fields.description:
This is a debugging help function that was developed when reviewing fix for MDEV-35815. 

Developers agreed that it's generally useful.

Targeting 10.6 as we are still debugging there, too, and this will have no impact on release builds. 

Example of usage:
Where is "pos" located:
{code}
(gdb) p pos
$67 = (Item_direct_view_ref *) 0x7fff58b66a30

(gdb) p dbug_which_mem_root(thd, pos)
$68 = 0x55555703a912 "thd->stmt_arena->mem_root"
{code}
Ok, it is statement-lifetime mem_root.

What about pos->name? Where was it allocated? 
{code}
(gdb) p pos->name.str
$69 = 0x7fff58017f10 "fld"

(gdb) p dbug_which_mem_root(thd, pos->name.str)
$70 = 0x55555703a904 "thd->mem_root"
{code}
On a transient mem_root. This was the bug in MDEV-35815 .

comments.body:
[~Palani] would you be able to asses the severity of this when you have the time? cc [~mariadb-AlexHanshaw] 

Here's my review of the issue:

From https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-43fc-jf86-j433:

{quote}
Impact
Denial of Service - Any application using axios that processes user-controlled JSON and passes it to axios configuration methods is vulnerable. The application will crash when processing the malicious payload.

Affected environments:

Node.js servers using axios for HTTP requests
Any backend that passes parsed JSON to axios configuration
{quote}

The affected component in MaxScale is the maxctrl command line interface. The vulnerability exists only if user-defined JSON is passed to axios which the maxctrl client does not do and thus cannot be affected by this. This means that MaxScale isn't actually affected by the vulnerability and thus it could be closed as _Not Applicable_ but for the sake of not having anything to report, we can upgrade the library version to silence the warnings. My assesment is that the severity of this issue is low considering how the affected code is used in MaxScale.

fields.summary: High rate of index_lock_upgrades due to btr_cur_need_opposite_intention() mostly returning true

issuetype.description: A new feature of the product, which has yet to be developed.
issuetype.name: New Feature

fields.description:
While testing MDEV-34431 using HammerDB TPROC-C (Delivery mix) on a 24 vCPU Intel system (oversubscribed with 88 threads) we observed a strong correlation between ORDER_LINE updates and frequent index lock upgrades.

As an experiment, commenting out the ORDER_LINE update in the Delivery stored procedure significantly reduced index lock upgrades and reduced rd_lock_spin sample percentage.

|| Test || Schema || ORDER_LINE UPDATE || NOPM || index_lock_upgrade() || rd_lock_spin samples (%) ||
| T1 | Partitioned | ON | 586,990 | 14,369,068 | 6.53 |
| T2 | Partitioned | OFF | 654,123 | 3,201,626 | 3.87 |
| T3 | Unpartitioned | ON | 503,278 | 10,220,286 | 19.96 |
| T4 | Unpartitioned | OFF | 653,284 | 3,103,213 | 8.95 |

Counters were added around:
btr_cur_need_opposite_intention()
Entry to pessimistic_search_leaf()
mtr_t::index_lock_upgrade()

For both partitioned and unpartitioned schemas:

btr_cur_need_opposite_intention() returned true for nearly all calls.
The dominant reason was nosib=true.
pessimistic_search_leaf() calls closely tracked the number of true returns.
index_lock_upgrade() calls closely tracked pessimistic_search_leaf() calls.

h4. Example (Partitioned)
{code}
[btr_cur_need_opposite_intention]
calls=14018262 true=14010891
zip=0 nosib=14010891 first=104879 last=121344 small=514079 rightmost=121344 reorg=0

[index_lock_upgrade]
calls=14018262 already_x=0 upgraded=14018262
{code}

{code}
pess@table=tpcc/order_line#P#p7 index=PRIMARY tree_height=3 height=2
pess@table=tpcc/orders index=PRIMARY tree_height=3 height=2
pess@table=tpcc/new_order index=PRIMARY tree_height=3 height=2
{code}

h4. Example (Unpartitioned)
{code}
[btr_cur_need_opposite_intention]
calls=9786751 true=9780023
zip=0 nosib=9780023 first=1 last=2849015 small=471126 rightmost=2849015 reorg=0

[index_lock_upgrade]
calls=9786751 already_x=0 upgraded=9786751
{code}

{code}
pess@table=tpcc_nopart/order_line index=PRIMARY tree_height=4 height=3
pess@table=tpcc_nopart/orders index=PRIMARY tree_height=3 height=2
pess@table=tpcc_nopart/new_order index=PRIMARY tree_height=3 height=2
{code}

This suggests that the update path is almost always escalating to pessimistic search and upgrading the index latch early in the descent (height == tree_height - 1), e.g.:

{code}
calls=14018262 true=14010891 root=14018262 root_true=14010891 lvl0=0 lvlgt0=14018262
{code}

h4. Diagnostic experiment
As a diagnostic experiment, btr_cur_need_opposite_intention() was modified to always return false.

Results:
pessimistic_search_leaf() and index_lock_upgrade() calls dropped from millions to tens.
Unpartitioned throughput improved by ~7.5%.
A small number of pessimistic_search_leaf() calls remained.

{code}
[btr_cur_need_opposite_intention]
calls=41255137 true=0
zip=0 nosib=0 first=0 last=0 small=0 rightmost=0 reorg=0

[index_lock_upgrade]
calls=30 already_x=0 upgraded=30
{code}

When btr_cur_need_opposite_intention() was modified to always return false, instance hangs were observed during schema builds loading the history table. After adding a primary key in our local test schema, the hang did not reproduce.

comments.body: Our fix of MDEV-29835 was to escalate to exclusive index tree latches in cases where the constraints of [MySQL WL#6326|https://dev.mysql.com/worklog/task/?id=6326] could be violated. Before that fix, MariaDB was prone to hang due to lock order inversion. The probability is low but not zero. I expect that MySQL is affected by those hangs; to my knowledge they only fixed MDEV-14637.
[~alessandro.vetere] yes I can re-run the tests. In previous tests the hangs were only observed on inserts into the table without a primary key.

[#4887|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4887] has been opened as a draft targeting 11.8 to get CI coverage and allow initial discussion.
12.3 would be a better target to do performance testing, so I now pushed {{b3a258485a9b87a9c40cdd39f5ef92ead40e4d31}} to the {{bb-12.3-MDEV-38814}} branch to get CI coverage there as well before the testing.

I'm investigating the suspicious {{DB_UNDERFLOW}} error code returned by {{btr_cur_optimistic_update()}} during the test.
It may be that a lot of escalations to pessimistic update are actually unnecessary, therefore the optimization to {{btr_cur_need_opposite_intention()}} could be discarded in favor of something maybe safer that prevents escalations in the first place.

After digging deeper in the unexpected {{DB_UNDERFLOW}} issue, I prepared an alternative draft for addressing this issue at [#4909|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4909].
The rationale behind these changes is to avoid falling back to pessimistic update paths in more cases, to prevent index lock upgrades from happening in the first place.
The two PRs ([#4887|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4887] and [#4909|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4909]) are not mutually exclusive, but I suspect [#4909|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4909] being superior at least in addressing this MDEV's case.

I performed additional testing on top of [#4909|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4909].
The behavior for same-size and shrinking record {{UPDATE}} remains unmodified by the changes. The behavior in 11.8 also matches that of both 10.6 and 10.11, both before and after the modifications.
I back-ported the changes to 10.4 as well and discovered the same consistency before and after. This suggests that [#4909|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4909] affects logic that was already present prior to 10.6.
There is one important difference in 10.4, however: it seems {{UPDATE}} queries there never take an X-lock on the index, but instead always keep the initial SX-lock. There are also differences in root and child node latching during the {{BTR_MODIFY_TREE}} descent prior to pessimistic update handling, which I am still investigating.

I suspect the performance regression in MDEV-39272 (recently linked to this ticket) is mainly related to this difference—caused primarily by the hang fix in MDEV-29835.

Impact of the PRs:

[#4909|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4909] may reduce pessimistic fallbacks for merge attempts and try to split sooner on record-size-increasing {{UPDATE}}, reducing the impact of this difference in newer versions.
I think this type of updates are prominent in the HammerDB TPROC-C (Delivery mix): {{UPDATE order_line SET ol_delivery_d = timestamp ...}}.
But I think the updates of sysbench update-index are same-size updates, since they operate on non-NULL columns (so MDEV-39272 would likely not benefit from this).
Also, since the behavior is there since 10.4, this will not relate to MDEV-39231, which is about a 11.4 vs 10.11 regression.

[#4887|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4887] may reduce upgrade attempts by avoiding the opposite intention check at the root. Without [#4887|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4887], every failed optimistic update escalates to an X-lock on the index for pessimistic handling, since the opposite intention check evaluated at the root will be true (the {{nosib}} condition). This could be beneficial to MDEV-39272 as well.

Similar excessive optimistic-to-pessimistic fallback behavior is seen in purge threads, for deletes.
Since the effort to improve that seems much bigger than that of the record-size-increasing {{UPDATE}} queries, MDEV-39325 has been opened to track this issue.

Testing performed for MDEV-39341 suggests that the 12.3 version of [#4909|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4909] {{bd8724f3d62}} is beneficial for the peak performance (in compatibility with the {{UPDATE}} pattern of the test) while the 12.3 version of [#4887|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4887] {{594cdd2d153}} is not.

I'm already basing MDEV-39325 purge work on [#4909|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4909], extending the monitoring infrastructure and {{index_lock_upgrade.test}}, this time focusing on deletes.

[#4909|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4909] has been updated, a variable that controls the optimizations has been added and a regression fixed.
The default value of the new variable {{INNODB_REDUCE_PESSIMISTIC_UPDATE_FALLBACKS}} is {{OFF}}, so this is safer to merge into 11.8.
The default might be switched to {{ON}} in later versions.

Latest testing in MDEV-39341 confirms that [#4909|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4909] is enough to fix this as the index lock upgrades were almost exclusively not caused by purge activity in HammerDB testing.
This is a brilliant idea with a low risk. However, instead of introducing a global parameter for this, I would suggest to spend some extra effort to introduce an index option.

MySQL 5.7 and MariaDB Server 10.2 already introduced an index-level attribute {{MERGE_THRESHOLD}} that is being parsed from table comments. I wonder if we could use a special value or value range of {{MERGE_THRESHOLD}} to control this.

Thanks [~marko]. I agree the global parameter isn't the final shape for the general release.

I did look into the {{MERGE_THRESHOLD}} idea and it was a good fit for the optimistic part, because of the dependency of {{BTR_CUR_PAGE_COMPRESS_LIMIT}} with the merge threshold:

{code}
#define BTR_CUR_PAGE_COMPRESS_LIMIT(index) \
        ((srv_page_size * (ulint)((index)->merge_threshold)) / 100)
{code}

and because modifying an index comment shall require no index-rebuild, but on the pessimistic side, the gate is a fixed reorganize threshold which which does not depend directly on it:

{code}
#define BTR_CUR_PAGE_REORGANIZE_LIMIT	(srv_page_size / 32)
{code}

So, controlling this feature with {{MERGE_THRESHOLD}} would be too much of a stretch in my opinion, as it would require to repurpose existing metadata on an LTS release.

What I'd propose: keep the global {{innodb_reduce_pessimistic_update_fallbacks}} as it is in [#4909|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4909] for 11.8 (default {{OFF}}), and add the proper per-index control on {{main}} through the MDEV-37070 machinery, instead of repurposing {{MERGE_THRESHOLD}}.
The global flag would stay {{OFF}} by default on {{main}} too, as a coarse fallback, with the per-index option as the granular opt-in.
So rather than flipping the global default to {{ON}} in later versions as I suggested earlier, I'd keep it {{OFF}} everywhere and let the index option carry the opt-in.

I hope this is an acceptable trade-off.

[~alessandro.vetere], thank you, that is a reasonable path forward. Can you please file a ticket for introducing the per-index attribute, and link it here?

Could we use a shorter name for the option? I spotted the term "shrinking a B-tree" in the documentation of one SQL RDBMS. I would suggest  {{innodb_index_shrink}} as the name of the option. When the corresponding per-index option (my proposal: {{shrink}}) is implemented, the variable would become a session variable (to specify a default for subsequent DDL statements).

Thank you again [~marko]. I filed two tickets, MDEV-39851 for adding the per-index option {{shrink}}, MDEV-39852 to enable instant DDL for such per-index options change.
When both will be implemented, one could perform a similar query:

{code:sql}
ALTER TABLE t DROP INDEX idx, ADD INDEX idx (cols) shrink=OFF, ALGORITHM=INSTANT
{code}

and enable the optimization (opt-in) for the specific index (without MDEV-39852, index rebuild is necessary).
The global option {{innodb_index_shrink}} (polarity now inverted, as specified in the PR) remains the only way to enable the optimization until MDEV-39851 is implemented (then, the option will be "declassed" as a session variable, specifying the default value for subsequent DDLs).
I updated the PR as well, ready for your review.
{{e232fc6045e}} merged into {{11.8}}.

You didn't fix the problem, you came up with a workaround that has a cost and removed behavior that used to work. Perhaps I am wrong and someone can show this has no cost WRT table size for write-heavy tables. 

Why should people spend time reporting bugs if this is how they get closed?

Added a variable innodb_index_shrink (default ON matching legacy behavior) to allow disabling the capability of InnoDB of shrinking a B-tree (by merging or reorganizing pages) on record-growing UPDATEs (such as NULL to not-NULL).
The optimization (enabled via setting the option to OFF), reduces index tree latch upgrades and the contention they cause by favoring page splits in such cases, at the cost of slightly sparser pages.

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done.

comments.body: Hey [~nikitamalyavin], can you test with {{-DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS=-march=x86-64-v3 -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS=-march=x86-64-v3}} to ensure we don't get another bug like MDEV-38398.

h1. Foreword
The initial idea was to just use rec_buff_length instead of reclength during memcpy, as rec_buff_length is aligned. Turns out, rec_buff_length is only aligned by 8, as much as our alloc_root aligns its pointers by 8 (sizeof (double)), whereas c++ `new` aligns by 16 on modern intel platforms.

Then I saw we have memcpy_aligned, which feeds a compiler with the alignment assumption.

I tried to use just it, and align the data by 16 bytes. I've seen no feasible results behind the noise in qps, so I had to go deeper.

h2. Setup

I've used my working laptop XMG NEO E23, which has a near-PC performance.
* Processor: 13th Gen Intel® Core™ i9-13900HX, 16 HT cores. Power-saving cores turned off, cpu configured to maximize performance
* Memory: 2x 32 GB (64 GB) DDR5-5200 Corsair Vengeance
* SSD: 1 TB M.2 Western Digital Blue SN580 | PCIe 4.0

All the code for reproduction is available by the link: https://github.com/MariaDB/server/commit/aab26d4087407e526cbed93d83e64a1860d485df


h1. Analysis

h2. Synthetic test
I have coded and vibe-coded a few versions of memcpy. Most of them fallback to memcpy after some threshold (typically 256). 

Layers to consider are: libc memcpy vs __builtin_memcpy, plt call vs just a call, call vs inlined, avx vs sse vs ERMS (rep movsq), alignment impact, gcc assumption and generation capabilities.

Some highlights:
* memcpy_best_aligned/memcpy_best_unaligned: a purely vibe-coded memcpy by gemini by the request like "make me the best optimized memcpy, assuming avx etc..." and all. Aligned puts an assumption on the pointer's 8-byte alignment and unaligned doesn't. Assumption could eliminate a few branches for values below 8. 

* memcpy_threshold_aligned_avx: use the best avx/sse, threshold based, basically assiming the alignment is closest power of 2 for both pointer and size, up to 256 bytes. Tries to generate own instructions for up to that value. Vibe-coded with my intervension.
* memcpy_threshold_unaligned_avx: same but using unaligned avx instructions (vmovdqu vs vmovdqa)

* memcpy_manual_avx_loop_unaligned/memcpy_manual_sse_loop: as it's said, a pure AVX/SSE loop. Vibe-coded.
* memcpy_threshold16,memcpy_switch_inline_aligned other threshold-based funcitons: try to hit into few aligned sizes and call memcpy with now-known constant size and assume-aligned pointers. Some of them are semi-vibe-coded, some are manualy written. We can see if vs switch and memcpy vs builtin generation results.
* memcpy, __builtin_memcpy: a baseline. Also to see memcpy vs __builtin_memcpy difference.
* memcpy_rep_movsq: added as another baseline, pure ERMS.

Benchmark itself: \[[github|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/57eacceff5f851cdf0b08bdf3cce388229468b58/bench_isolated.cpp]\]

h2. Results

By the link, https://jsfiddle.net/sea5k7df/ functions names are clickable. Or  [^index.html] here.
Unclick Rep_movsq and enable Logarithmic Y for comfortable assessment.

First part is alignment: turns out that calling memcpy for unaligned size makes no difference vs aligned. This is not included in the results. Values tried are 3,4,5,6,7,15,31. I saw a smooth line on thechart for memcpy calls.

The rest is mostly as expected: On up to 512 bytes, ERMS is most expensive, then goes memcpy, having the same results as a builtin. The best results come for AVX/SSE loops. 

BM_Switch_NoInline_UnalignedAVX calling a never-inlined my_exact_unaligned_memcpy performs worse than an inlined doppleganger.

Apparently, AI-generated memcpy_best_aligned behaves really well. Same comes for other "thresold-based" functions: both memcpy and __builtin_memcpy were inlined. We can see that options using __builtin_memcpy perfom slightly worse, even though both are inlined to the same code. My conclusion is it's mostly random: __builtin_memcpy had different alignment that memcpy when inlined, or perhaps the funcitons themselves are aligned imperfectly. Gemini agent has made a test with alignment on the code forced and comfirmed this.


Turns out, __builtin_memcpy is not meant to be always inlined. It can the same result in a libc invocation. One quirk I noticed: it makes jmp to plt@memcpy instead of call. -minline-all-stringops is the only way to force this builtin be force-inlined, which is not a widely used or known option, and besides this option cannot be specified in [[gnu::target()]] attribute.


As expected, AVX loop outperforms SSE after 512, and is outperformed by memcpy/ERMS on even higher values.

So this beautiful chart confirms the importance of inlining, alignment, and choosing the best option for the data. We could get up to 0.3-0.4 ns (2-3 cycles for me) But that's a tight loop of memcpy running on the same data, a synthetic test.

h2. Measuring inside mariadbd

Results inside a real sql server could vary. store_record happens a few times per row, but also going into storage engnine, especially innodb, could flush out the cache and give some difference, including branch misprediction.

h3. The approach.
To measure different alignment, I had to change the way records are allocated and introduced TABLE_SHARE::record_alloc. For aligned avx we'd have to align memory and size for 32 bytes.

The baseline stays good old memcpy on reclength (unaligned, vs rec_buff_length, which is aligned.)
We would still want to see if pure memcpy_aligned<> would give any impact.

I used vibe-coded (and then polished significantly) run_mariadb_bench_inlined.py. It:
* loops over memcpy functions
* replaces the macro memcpy_func used exclusively for store/restore_record.
* Adjust record alignment (also by macro replacement)

I'll snap the logic here:
{code:python}
align8 = "8" in func_name or func_name == "memcpy" or "unaligned" in func_name

mult = '4' if 'avx' in func_name else '1' if align8 else '2'
align_val = f"({mult}*ALIGN_MAX_UNIT)"
reclength = 'reclength' if func_name == "memcpy" else 'rec_buff_length'
{code}

The memcpy functions used: \[[github|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/57eacceff5f851cdf0b08bdf3cce388229468b58/include/my_memcpy_bench.h]\]

The measurement approach differs from google benchmark fundamentally. The lapper runs a loop with > 1M iterations, and only measures time before and after the loop. Doing so in mariadbd would result in huge noise, so I had to measure the funciton itself only.

I tried a few options for time including different configs from std::chrono and rdtsc. I stopped at rdtscp for the final result, as it gave the least latency and noise (chrono had 10ns latency and rdtsc is noisy.)

For table t1(id int primary key, c varchar(\{size\})), I iterated over sizes up to 1k. On tmpfs
I stopped at measuring ~50 updates of a 1M rows table. 
I tried system-versioned option, but it was overflowing my tmpfs on 512, and besides it increased the size of record by ~12 bytes, while we'd want to see a performance on smaller records as well.

h2. Results

Innodb: https://jsfiddle.net/j6hrf4vn/ or [^innodb_results.html] 
MyISAM: https://jsfiddle.net/gj62qfra/ or [^myisam_results.html]

Very unexpected. 

Mostly, all the functions gather in one bun. We see a latency of 3ns as a lower baseline for everything.
https://codeberg.org/solarkennedy/latency-numbers-live gives me 
{noformat}
L1 Cache Access ~ 0.4ns
Branch Misprediction ~ 0.8ns
L2 Cache Access ~ 1.1ns
L3 Cache Access ~ 2.1ns.
Main Memory Access (Random) ~ 27.7ns
{noformat}

This means the values are not even in L2 cache, but hopefully are in L3. So it's likely an L2 acces (maybe table->records) + L3 access (table->records[1])
For this case, we see that Enhanced REP MOVSQ gives really close best possible performance starting right from 8 bytes (it used rec_buff_length)!

Memcpy doesn't loose at all as well, meaning that its pointers are likely really well cached, or branch is predicted well to plt@memcpy.

Total of 50M runs and proper warmup would give a good guarantee that any spikes seen are not a noise, but rather some misperforming on corner-sized values, especially when values form the clusters.

h1. Conclusion

Prominent synthetic results show the possible improvement of 0.3-0.4 ns by memcpy substitution. Good candidate could be, apparently, AI-written memcpy_best_aligned, or human-written memcpy_threshold_builtins16. The real-world picture adds a grain of salt: the improvement is over-dominated by L3 cache access, giving a barely distinguishable picture for different mallocs.

I couldn't really categorize the real-world results and conclude the best performer confidently.

Given all circumstances, I think any replacement of memcpy for just storing/restoring poorly cpu-cached is an overkill right now. Perhaps, the first optimization that should come is prefetching the memory, which would theoretically give a 3 ns improvement (10 times more).

For a real performance benefit, it's better to give a go to a row execution plan generation I assessed in MDEV-33219, which gave 3-5% QPS improvement during early tests

{noformat}
1e4ba5ae Generate a sequence of functions (execution plan) to call per each row.
1858ad16 Architecture + extract function ptr from vtable
{noformat}

h1. Update on the cost

1. I added {{__builtin_prefetch(table->record[1], 1);}} before store_record, and saw no difference. This hinted that actual latency comes not from cache access
2. I measured a pair  of rdtscp exclusively with nothing in-between -- it gives a 16-18 cycles latency, roughly 3ns -- corresponds exactly to observed latency

Updated results with subtracted 3.2 ns latency for rdtscp: 
Myisam: https://jsfiddle.net/eutg35fv/ or  [^myisam_results-1.html] 
Innodb: https://jsfiddle.net/oyt8sqfk/ or  [^innodb_results-1.html] 

The picture is more clear now, and still is nothing similar to what we observed around the synthetic benchmark:

Still wee see that:
1. REP MOVSQ is barely dominated, it actually gives a fine performance.
2. memcpy is one of the top performers
3. apparently, memcpy_aligned performs worse, especially on alignment >= 16

This may mean simply the noise, making the results indistinguishable. Anyway, the right conclusion is that to what we observe, the current implementation on {{main}} doesn't stand out.

h1. AVX512 and real Xeon server

I've been suggested to try AVX512. The rationale is that it could avoid an extra read-before-write, and besides real memcpy would use it.
AVX512 became exclusive for Xeons on intel cpus, so my laptop hadn't it. I used Pluto for this test.

Surprisingly, it was slower than my laptop in single thread, it's also 4Ghz max, whereas my cpu is 5ghz, so nanosecond values may be wrongly adjusted.

Myisam: https://jsfiddle.net/c57rhtn1/1/
Innodb: https://jsfiddle.net/w4b9hy6o/

We can see that AVX512 loop behaves almost perfectly for MyISAM up to 133 byte test, whereas for InnoDB it has apparent spikes throughout the chart.
Also we see that unaligned (actually, 8-byte alignement is there) memcpy still has a near-perfect curve everywhere.

fields.summary: Make BACKUP SERVER mutually exclusive with itself and BACKUP STAGE

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done.
issuetype.name: Task

fields.description: Because backing up the data from a server is a very I/O intensive operation, we must allow at most one {{BACKUP SERVER}} operation at a time, and not concurrently with any other backup operations that would invoke {{BACKUP STAGE}} statements, such as {{mariadb-backup}}.

comments.body: As far as I can tell, the currently implemented locking is in part insufficient and unnecessary. This will need to be revised further so that MDEV-39092 can be implemented.

The initial implementation failed to flag {{ER_BACKUP_LOCK_IS_ACTIVE}} if there is an attempt to execute {{BACKUP SERVER}} while a {{BACKUP STAGE}} is active in the same connection. I have now implemented that in the MDEV-14992 branch.

Following changes for review:
- all MTR test cases in one .test file,
- backup lock ticket propagated to plugins so they can upgrade it for specific operations

Can you please demonstrate how a more fine-grained locking than the one that currently exists in the MDEV-14992 branch for InnoDB, can be used to facilitate safe copying of other files, such as {{.frm}} files or {{ENGINE=Aria}} files (MDEV-39092)?

I think that in order to close this ticket, we can incorporate the minimal code changes (adding two {{DEBUG_SYNC}} points) to the current MDEV-14992 branch and have the test cover InnoDB backup.

Now that MDEV-14992 in its current state is copying the InnoDB log, there actually is some room for potential race conditions between a {{BACKUP SERVER}} that has just released the locks, and another {{BACKUP SERVER}} to a different target. This test scenario can be refined further (with attempts to start a server on each backup) as soon as MDEV-39092 and has been fully designed and implemented, including some lock upgrading near the end of the backup.

https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4892 is not currently in a mergeable state. Moreover, I believe that it is more important to refine the locking in MDEV-39092 so that {{ENGINE=Aria}} files can be copied while incurring a minimal amount of disruption to the operation of the server.

Today, I [implemented|https://github.com/MariaDB/server/commit/f257584af9db2d2d435bdb2696515c54311663bc] what I think is necessary and sufficient locking in my MDEV-14992 branch. I don’t think that any significant code changes beyond that are necessary.
This is already part of the MDEV-14992 API, which maps backup lock stages to specific {{backup_phase}}.

fields.summary: Rework MDL enum constants values

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done.
issuetype.name: Task

fields.description:
It is investigation task for check the feasibility of the below changes. The better implementation may be discovered during the work on this ticket.

MDL constants values of 0 assign some default values (MDL_INTENTION_EXCLUSIVE, BACKUP) before MDL_REQUEST_INIT(). That does not make sense if MDL_REQUEST_INIT() was not called. Please rework the values of 0 into (MDL_NOT_INITIALIZED, NOT_INITIALIZED). Described by these comments in the code:

{code:diff}
--- sql/mdl.h
+++ sql/mdl.h
@@ -125,6 +125,11 @@ class MDL_context_owner

 enum enum_mdl_type {
   /* This means that the MDL_request is not initialized */
+  /*
+    TODO (newbie): should be MDL_NOT_INITIALIZED= 0, as it is strange
+    that not-inited request has MDL_INTENTION_EXCLUSIVE.
+    Must fix tests, as at least mysql_rm_table_no_locks() depends on this.
+  */
   MDL_NOT_INITIALIZED= -1,
   /*
     An intention exclusive metadata lock (IX). Used only for scoped locks.
@@ -381,6 +386,10 @@ struct MDL_key
     Note that although there isn't metadata locking on triggers,
     it's necessary to have a separate namespace for them since
     MDL_key is also used outside of the MDL subsystem.
+
+    TODO (newbie): NOT_INITIALIZED=0 as default bzero() sets wrongly type to
+    BACKUP. But dozens switch() cases for NOT_INITIALIZED must be added to
+    pacify the compiler.
   */
   enum enum_mdl_namespace { BACKUP=0,
                             SCHEMA,
{code}

Also after fix this hunk should be reverted:

{code:diff}
--- sql/sql_parse.cc
+++ sql/sql_parse.cc
@@ -8509,6 +8509,8 @@ TABLE_LIST *st_select_lex::add_table_to_list(THD *thd,
     MDL_REQUEST_INIT(&ptr->mdl_request, MDL_key::TABLE, ptr->db.str,
                      ptr->table_name.str, mdl_type, MDL_TRANSACTION);
   }
+  else
+    ptr->mdl_request.type= MDL_NOT_INITIALIZED;
   DBUG_RETURN(ptr);
 }
{code}

comments.body: To fix invalid state for *enum_mdl_type*, shifted enum values so MDL_NOT_INITIALIZED = 0. Adjusted MDL_BIT(A) to 1U << (A-1) to preserve existing bitmask values.
MDL_NOT_INITIALIZED should be left as is as MDL_BIT() does excessive computation. But MDL_BIT() itself should be refactored into inline function (if possible). Sorry, I did not take it into account.
Resolved By PR -  https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/4912
enum_mdl_namespace refactoring should not inflict performance degradation as jump tables are used for switch(enum value).
I'd rather put effort into removing {{MDL_NOT_INITIALIZED}}. {{MDL_request}} is not the right place to track caller state.

[~midenok], in 678b7709e2bb25046bc3205ddac31a19f1ab2f23 you mention only single place that makes use of this value:

{noformat}
    And b) does not update MDL type for pure alias when view is
    initialized, so it is MDL_NOT_INITIALIZED. `lock_table_names()` code
    naturally skips such kind of MDL with (mdl_request.type <
    MDL_SHARED_UPGRADABLE) condition when processing tables list.
{noformat}

If that's the only case, can't you do {{table->is_pure_alias()}} there? Like you did it in {{mysql_make_view()}}.

[~svoj] There is the check for (mdl_request.type < MDL_SHARED_UPGRADABLE). It doesn't need one more condition there. Apart from that having MDL_BACKUP for not initialized is bug prone and misleading in the debugger.

... and yes, that kind of check (mdl_request.type < MDL_SHARED_UPGRADABLE) is not the single one.

[~midenok], right. I see this as a violation of basic encapsulation principles. The caller shouldn't touch {{MDL_request}} guts in the first place.

[~midenok] in 2a8d889b544 you've missed to remove another TODO item that you've added to mdl.h. "Another piece of ugliness for TABLE_LIST constructor" may stay as it still kind of applies, though I don't mind having it removed.

I'm generally fine with the idea introduced in 8039d774161, but {{init_one_tab_r()}} and {{init_one_table_for_prelockn_r()}} are evil. Why don't we just make it right?

comments.body: Work-in-progress branch: https://github.com/MariaDB/server/tree/bb-13.1-MDEV-39491-pqe-chunks. It simulates parallel execution in a single thread: does the splitting into chunks and processes chunks one after another.
[~julien.fritsch], I think at least some of those points are beyond the original scope and should be filed as separate tasks. I just wrote them down not to forget.

The prime suspect of the overhead is the end boundary clamp — `cmp_dtuple_rec(prebuilt->m_pscan_end_tuple, result_rec, …)` which runs for every row in `row_search_mvcc()` on the chunked path.

An idea of optimizing this: records on a leaf page are sorted. So for any chunk-end tuple E:
- if a page's last user record < E  - every record on that page is in range, no per-row checks needed;
- the first page whose last record >= E - the boundary is exactly in this page . Only that page needs per-row checks.

Branch allowing to do a full table scan in chunks, in one thread (pseudo-parallel): bb-13.2-pscan-test-2.
Cleaned-up branch for further development: bb-13.2-MDEV-innodb-chunks.

Branch `bb-13.2-MDEV-innodb-chunks-harness` provides the possibility to verify the splitting logic with this commit:
{code}
commit e462b3e0f8eee5dac367d25ef72e42070cff871d

    MDEV-39491 Add test harness

    This commit implements pseudo-parallel execution of SELECTs
    which allows to test the correctness of parallel algorithms.

    Eligible InnoDB tables that were planned to be full-scanned
    by the clustered index, are switched to the pseudo-parallel execution.
    That means the primary index is split into chunks, and those
    chunks are processed one after another by a single thread.
    This thread mimics the parallel execution by calling the
    parallel handler API and acting as both the coordinator and
    the worker.

    This mode is activated automatically, there is no need to
    set any variables before that. If an InnoDB table is set
    to be fully scanned by primary index, the pseudo-parallel
    mode is employed.

    This harness allows to run MTR tests to catch possible bugs
    in the parallel logic implementation.
{code}

while `bb-13.2-MDEV-innodb-chunks` is a cleaned up branch implementing only the parallel handler API and InnoDB splitting logic.

After the last optimization
{code}
commit bc78ab2c93bf44c0cef5473a1a4db2926f16969f (HEAD -> bb-13.2-MDEV-innodb-chunks)

    MDEV-39491 Parallel Query: cache the chunk-boundary verdict per leaf page
{code}
the overhead of chunked scan of a 10 million-rows table has dropped from 9% to 1.7%:
{code}
+----------+-----------+-----------+-----------+
| mode     | min(time) | max(time) | avg(time) |
+----------+-----------+-----------+-----------+
| parallel |       955 |       962 |   958.375 |
| serial   |       939 |       944 |    942.25 |
+----------+-----------+-----------+-----------+
{code}
958.375 / 942.25 = 1.017 ( +1.7%)

items.toString:
Suppose we want to do a full table/index scan using N parallel workers.

The idea is to split the index into N approximately equal portions, and then give each portion to a separate worker.

This should be a storage-engine call.  Reverse to what  records_in_range() does.  
records_in_range() gets a key (i.e. range endpoint) and produces a percentage "this endpoint is at  0.12345 fraction of the table".
Here, the idea would be to do the reverse:  given a fraction=0.123456, dive into the table and position a read cursor at the specified fraction of the index. 

According to Monty, MySQL has the code to do this?

items.toString: ParallelQuery: split the table/index into chunks to read: Study

Suppose we want to do a full table/index scan using N parallel workers.

The idea is to split the index into N approximately equal portions, and then give each portion to a separate worker.

This should be a storage-engine call.  Reverse to what  records_in_range() does.  
records_in_range() gets a key (i.e. range endpoint) and produces a percentage "this endpoint is at  0.12345 fraction of the table".
Here, the idea would be to do the reverse:  given a fraction=0.123456, dive into the table and position a read cursor at the specified fraction of the index. 

According to Monty, MySQL has the code to do this? 

h2. Example of how to do this.
suppose we want to a parallel full table scan with N=10 workers. 
In InnoDB, full table scan is a full index scan on a [hidden] primary key.

The primary worker requests innodb to provide boundary points for 10%, 20% ... 90% of the table. 
It gets:
{code}
range_endpoints= {  
  pk=val1,   -- this record is located after 10% of the table records
  pk=val2,     -- this record is located after 20% of the table records 
  ...
}
{code}

Then,
* worker1 will be requested to scan the range:  {{-inf < pk < val1}}  
* worker2 will be requested to scan the range: {{val1 <= pk < val2}}   (note the left endpoint is inclusve, the right is non-inclusive)
* ...

worker2 can position at its start location and then scan the rows it needs to scan by doing this:
{code:cpp}
h->index_init(clustered_pk);
h->index_read_map(val2);  // position at 20% of the records.
then it will call
h->index_next();
{code}

h2. What does MySQL do

Their splitting is different. Short: they select "sub-trees" in the BTREE. This is not based on the desired fraction (e.g. give worker#1 10% of table).  This is based on the BTREE shape (e.g. worker #1 will get the first child page of the root page and all its subtrees).

{code}
storage/innobase/include/row0pread.h
storage/innobase/row/row0pread.cc
{code}

MySQL does splitting into chunks ("shards") in two-steps:
1. The user thread creates shards for every subtree (equivalent to a range of keys) in the root node and puts the ranges into the task queue. The first `innodb_parallel_read_threads` shards are not marked, while subsequent are marked as "needs further splitting".
2. When a worker thread fetches a task from the queue, first it checks the flag "needs further splitting". If it's not set, then the range is processed with the worker as is.
3. If the flag is set, the worker doesn't process the range directly but insteads runs the same N-way split of the current subtree as was done for the root node and pushes the new sub-ranges into the task queue.
This eliminates the situation of workers underutilization (for example: 5 root subtrees, 4 workers; after first 4 subtrees are processed, the last one remaining will be processed by a single worker while others will be idle).
The maximum depth of the B-tree lookup is 2 (root node and one level below the root).
The maximum number of pages read during the splitting is 1 for root node + (number of root node children - `innodb_parallel_read_threads`).
(https://www.alibabacloud.com/blog/an-introduction-to-mysql-parallel-query-and-ddl_601920)

Here, the idea would be to do the reverse:  given a fraction=0.123456, dive into the table and position a read cursor at the specified fraction of the index. 

According to Monty, MySQL has the code to do this? 

h2. Example of how to do this.
suppose we want to a parallel full table scan with N=10 workers. 
In InnoDB, full table scan is a full index scan on a [hidden] primary key.

The primary worker requests innodb to provide boundary points for 10%, 20% ... 90% of the table. 
It gets:
{code}
range_endpoints= {  
  pk=val1,   -- this record is located after 10% of the table records
  pk=val2,     -- this record is located after 20% of the table records 
  ...
}
{code}

Then,
* worker1 will be requested to scan the range:  {{-inf < pk < val1}}  
* worker2 will be requested to scan the range: {{val1 <= pk < val2}}   (note the left endpoint is inclusve, the right is non-inclusive)
* ...

worker2 can position at its start location and then scan the rows it needs to scan by doing this:
{code:cpp}
h->index_init(clustered_pk);
h->index_read_map(val2);  // position at 20% of the records.
then it will call
h->index_next();
{code}

h2. What does MySQL do

Their splitting is different. Short: they select "sub-trees" in the BTREE. This is not based on the desired fraction (e.g. give worker#1 10% of table).  This is based on the BTREE shape (e.g. worker #1 will get the first child page of the root page and all its subtrees).

{code}
storage/innobase/include/row0pread.h
storage/innobase/row/row0pread.cc
{code}

MySQL does splitting into chunks ("shards") in two-steps:
1. The user thread creates shards for every subtree (equivalent to a range of keys) in the root node and puts the ranges into the task queue. The first `innodb_parallel_read_threads` shards are not marked, while subsequent are marked as "needs further splitting".
2. When a worker thread fetches a task from the queue, first it checks the flag "needs further splitting". If it's not set, then the range is processed by the worker as is.
3. If the flag is set, the worker doesn't process the range directly but insteads runs the same N-way split of the current subtree as was done for the root node and pushes the new sub-ranges into the task queue.
This eliminates the situation of workers underutilization (for example: 5 root subtrees, 4 workers; after first 4 subtrees are processed, the last one remaining will be processed by a single worker while others will be idle).
The maximum depth of the B-tree lookup is 2 (root node and one level below the root).
The maximum number of pages read during the splitting is 1 for root node + (number of root node children - `innodb_parallel_read_threads`).
(https://www.alibabacloud.com/blog/an-introduction-to-mysql-parallel-query-and-ddl_601920)

h2. Questions

fields.summary: Parallel Query: Open tables for worker threads

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done.
issuetype.name: Task

fields.description:
Worker threads will need their own handler (i.e. ha_innobase, ha_maria, etc) objects.

This is because each worker should have its own "cursor" (i.e. current position in the scan) and table->record[0] (the current record).   The objects should share the same read view of the database.

Should TABLE object itself be shared? 

Should TABLE_LIST object be shared? (probably not as it's a parse tree-level entity)

table->field[0...n] should not be shared, as those have pointers to table->record[0] which
should not be shared.

h2. How to create additional handler objects 

h3. Option 1: open table normally

Open tables "normally" by calling open_table() (or what is the function to get TABLE object
from open table cache).  We will get new TABLE and handler objects.

h3. Option 2: handler::clone

Use handler->clone() to get another handler. 

It is not clear if/how we would get another TABLE object.

fields.description:
Nightly stable-23.10 constantly fails because of slow tests on ASAN and UBSAN builds
It is a false negative because sanitizers just slow down the tests.

Possible solutions:

-Change ec2 types for builds with sanitizers to a bigger ones(via change to columnstore-tooling repo)

-Increase global drone timeout for our nightly

-Leave only basic and bugfixes suites in mtr for ASAN and UBSAN builds(it seems like now mtr tests take most of the time, 4h on the last nightly)

-maybe there are some other solutions for the problem

fields.summary: Parallel query: implement chunked execution in parallel workers

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done.
issuetype.name: Task

fields.description: Port chunked pseudo-parallel execution (MDEV-39491) into multi-threaded execution framework (MDEV-39492, MDEV-39495).

comments.body:
[~Johnston], although the main cause of the slowdown is inefficiency on the InnoDB side, there is also one bottleneck in the parallel framework. A worker fills its batch table and then waits for the manager to drain it sitting idle. Here are some statistics from the performance schema for 4 workers:
{code:sql}
MariaDB [test]> SELECT a.event_name,
    ->        a.count_star      - b.count_star      AS d_count,
    ->       (a.sum_timer_wait  - b.sum_timer_wait)/1e9 AS d_ms
    -> FROM performance_schema.events_waits_summary_global_by_event_name a
    -> JOIN pwt_before b USING (event_name)
    -> WHERE a.event_name LIKE '%pwt%'
    -> ORDER BY d_ms DESC;
+------------------------------------------------------+---------+---------------+
| event_name                                           | d_count | d_ms          |
+------------------------------------------------------+---------+---------------+
| wait/synch/cond/sql/pwt_management::COND_data_avail  |     850 | 191.724825848 |
| wait/synch/cond/sql/pwt_management::COND_data_space  |    2520 | 121.471404546 |
| wait/synch/mutex/sql/pwt_management::LOCK_data       |    5551 |   2.028137518 |
| wait/synch/mutex/sql/pwt_management::LOCK_pwt_thread |       1 |   0.047550786 |
| wait/synch/mutex/sql/pwt_worker::LOCK_worker         |       4 |   0.047503788 |
| wait/synch/cond/sql/pwt_worker::COND_worker          |       0 |             0 |
+------------------------------------------------------+---------+---------------+
{code}

All workers spent 121 ms in total waiting for the manager to drain their batch tables (wait for `COND_data_space` in the statistics). Potential improvement: use two batch tables for each worker. The worker fills table A then passes it to the manager for draining, while immediately starting to fill table B. After the table B is full, pass it to the manager and switch back to table A, and so forth.

By the way, I simplified the sql_select.cc part and moved a couple of functions to sql_parallel_workers.cc, hope you don't mind.

Flame graph   [^flame-single.svg] represents a single-threaded (traditional) execution while [^flame-4.svg] - execution with 4 workers.
Interesting that temp tables handling with ha_write_tmp_row() / ha_delete_all_rows() contributes to roughly 32% of execution time. 22% of the entire profile is memset zeroing HEAP memory. PWT_CHUNK_ROWS = 64 looks too small, I'll try to increase it to reduce the number of the fill/drain cycles .

After increasing PWT_CHUNK_ROWS to 2048 ( [^flame-2048.svg]) the execution time dropped from 3.8 to 2.5 sec (for 1 million rows table) which is still slower than single-threaded (2 sec) but is still a progress. 
Another idea is to replace the temporary batch table with a raw buffer and instead of `copy_field_with_null` + `ha_write_tmp_row` just `memcpy` the record into it. Since the scanned and batched tables are identical, that should probably work. In this scenario we can just reuse the buffer instead of cleaning it up with `ha_delete_all_rows`.

> By the way, I simplified the sql_select.cc part and moved a couple of functions to sql_parallel_workers.cc, hope you don't mind.

Of course not.  You also got rid of choose_parallel_scan(), which was simply me being optimistic/dumb.

> Another idea is to replace the temporary batch table with a raw buffer and instead of `copy_field_with_null` + `ha_write_tmp_row` just `memcpy` the record into it.

I have an early commit with this change and it worked fine.  I'll hack it in and see if it helps.

In fact, the logic in choose_parallel_scan() makes sense, but the idea now is just to make it work for the first non-const table of the join, and then possibly extend the parallelism to other tables of the join or choose the one most appropriate, etc.

Patch containing shipping of raw records vs tmp tables ...
https://github.com/MariaDB/server/commits/bb-13.1-pscan-test-no-tmp/

It certainly is faster, almost as fast as a normal scan in my release build testing.

> In fact, the logic in choose_parallel_scan() makes sense, but the idea now is just to make it work for the first non-const table of the join

There would have to be some serious manipulation of the join execution framework to be able to parallel scan chunks of tables further down the join order.  I think the next step here is try and figure out to make join ordering favour (or at least consider) placing parallelizable scans first (after const tables of course).  Unfortunately everything seems to be calculated backwards, with the join type being the last thing flagged.

[~Johnston], as [~monty] mentioned, with raw buffers instead of temp tables we'll not be able to process BLOBs (however, we are not yet able anyway until MDEV-38975 is merged). We need to remember this limitation. 
One more thing he mentioned is TRUNCATE instead of `ha_delete_all_rows()` should be much faster but currently `handler` doesn't provide this API for some reason.

[~oleg.smirnov]  even after merging MDEV-38975, if blobs are stored as records within the tmp table, we are going to have to implement variable sized chunks to send to the manager, we can't send partial blob.
One thing i noticed in testing here is that the read is only only on committed data.  Would i be right in thinking there isn't any way around this?

With InnoDB pre-fetcher enabled for parallel scans [^flame-prefetch.svg] the performance got much better: 1 million rows table scan executed in 1.3 seconds with 4 workers (against 2.3 seconds before).

On a release build the parallel scan of SELECT * (1M rows) does not scale (87ms serial -> 80/75/83ms at 2/4/8 workers).
Performance-schema wait data shows the cause is not CPU saturation of any thread: 
+------------------------------------------------------+---------+--------------+
| event_name                                           | d_count | d_ms         |
+------------------------------------------------------+---------+--------------+
| wait/synch/cond/sql/pwt_management::COND_data_avail  |     307 | 54.936630408 |
| wait/synch/cond/sql/pwt_management::COND_data_space  |     691 |   50.3352642 |
| wait/synch/mutex/sql/pwt_management::LOCK_data       |    1786 |  0.098478816 |
| wait/synch/mutex/sql/pwt_worker::LOCK_worker         |       4 |  0.000430776 |
| wait/synch/mutex/sql/pwt_management::LOCK_pwt_thread |       1 |  0.000037944 |
+------------------------------------------------------+---------+--------------+

At 4 workers the manager is blocked ~72% of the run waiting for data (COND_data_avail 54.9ms) and the workers are blocked ~22% waiting for the manager to drain (COND_data_space 50ms), with negligible mutex contention (LOCK_data 0.1ms). The worker/manager hand-off is synchronous and single-buffered: a worker fills one batch and then blocks until the manager drains it (handoff_batch), so it cannot scan ahead. Producer and consumer therefore ping-pong instead of overlapping, and adding workers can't close the gap. The fix is to decouple the hand-off — give each worker double buffering (fill buffer B while the manager drains buffer A) and/or let the manager drain without parking the worker — so producers and the consumer run concurrently.

Even more powerful improvement would be pushing down condition evaluation and aggregation to the workers (however, this is out of scope of this task).

Release flame graphs are attached, but they only measure on-CPU time (wait time is not reflected). [^release-2.svg]  [^release-4.svg]  [^release-serial.svg]

h4. Note for myself:  cloning of the read snapshot (similar to MDEV-39489) 
hasn't been yet implemented for this task. It needs to be eventually done too.

fields.description:
In MDEV-37146, {{mariadb-dump}} queries {{information_schema.SLAVE_STATUS}} if the server is MariaDB 11.6+ and {{SHOW ALL SLAVES STATUS}} otherwise.
OTOH, in MDEV-39519, {{mariadb-dump}} always queries {{SHOW REPLICA STATUS}} first and then {{SHOW SLAVE STATUS}} if the former is not supported.

These two conflict, not just in code, but in their approaches.
To temporarily resolve this conflict from the codebase, MDEV-39519 is currently excluded from the 13.x version series and is only present on 11.8 and 12.3.

In [the mailing list|https://lists.mariadb.org/hyperkitty/list/developers@lists.mariadb.org/message/4CZ6ZBN72UDWSZVGFJPRVHQAARFTDE7S/], [~bnestere] recommended to port In MDEV-37146's {{information_schema.SLAVE_STATUS}} to MDEV-39519's attempt-based approach.

[~knielsen] has omitted MDEV-39519’s conflicting part from his merge-up and opened MDEV-40073 about porting that part.

I have dropped the priority a level down as knielsen has “resolved” (by omission) the merge conflict and triaged this as “doesn't seem very important atm”.
[~ParadoxV5] if this was resolved, why is the priority still critical? What's left to do?
[~bnestere] knielsen “resolved” the merge conflict by dropping the incoming feature; that is, MDEV-39519 is present on 11.8 and 12.3, but (temporarily) removed in 13.x.
Thanks [~ParadoxV5]. Please make that clear in the JIRA title.

Let’s try this.

Both your ([~bnestere]) mailing list suggestion and my creation of this task predate knielsen’s “coflict resolution”, hence the task’s theme about a merge conflict.

Thanks [~ParadoxV5], though I mean, someone should be able to read the title and not have to click out to other MDEVs to understand the problem. E.g.

"MySQL Compatibility Nomenclature was Reverted from mariadb-dump Queries in 13.X"
https://github.com/MariaDB/server/pull/5458
Replied to questions

[~susil.behera] The review changes have been made, and the project should be ready for testing (branch {{MDEV\-39880}}).
We are looking for whether {{mariadb-dump --dump-slave}} on this branch can correctly dump from a variety of server versions:
* 10.6 (or 10.6-ES): before {{FOR CHANNEL}}
* 10.11 or 11.4: before {{information_schema.SLAVE_STATUS}}
* 11.8 or above
* _MySQL 8 or above_

[~bnestere] You may want to take a look at the changes in the meantime.
[~sanja_byelkin] FYI on status.

Thanks, all.

\[P.S.]
IIRC, MDEV-39519 had no formal testing.
Susil, if you have time, can you check out MDEV-39519 after as well while here?
See its Release Note Summary for what it’s about.

Thanks [~ParadoxV5]!

I've left one last comment.

bq. But I think it's better we raise a separate ticket to make {{mariadb-dump --dump-slave=}} include {{master_host}} and {{master_port}} as part of the {{CHANGE MASTER TO}} statement. What do you think?
They are behind the {{--include-master-host-port}} switch, which is not on by default.
But what was the purpose of excluding them by default? 🤔

bq. Similarly I ran {{mariadb-dump --dump-slave=1 --gtid}} against a CS 11.8.7 slave but the dump file didn't have the actual {{gtid_slave_pos}} value on the slave server
Well, that’s odd.
MTR test {{main.rpl_mysqldump_slave}} shows that {{SET GLOBAL gtid_slave_pos='…'}} is present in 10.11, 11.8, and this MDEV-39880 branch.

[~susil.behera] there are MariaDB/MySQL incompatibilities in a default {{mariadb-dump}}. We have a guide that gives details on which settings to use: [mysql-to-mariadb-migration-the-master-guide|https://mariadb.com/docs/server/server-management/install-and-upgrade-mariadb/migrating-to-mariadb/moving-from-mysql/mysql-to-mariadb-migration-the-master-guide]. OTOH, in MDEV-39519, {{mariadb-dump}} always queries {{SHOW REPLICA STATUS}} first and then {{SHOW SLAVE STATUS}} if the former is not supported.

These two conflict, not just in code, but in their approaches.
https://www.reddit.com/r/ProgrammerHumor/comments/1r9qy7o/twodevschillinonthesamebranch/

In [the mailing list|https://lists.mariadb.org/hyperkitty/list/developers@lists.mariadb.org/message/4CZ6ZBN72UDWSZVGFJPRVHQAARFTDE7S/], [~bnestere] recommended to port In MDEV-37146's {{information_schema.SLAVE_STATUS}} to MDEV-39519's attempt-based approach.

fields.summary: store read-only sysvars in a read-only root and a read-only segment

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done.
issuetype.name: Task

fields.description: for read-only sysvars: store them in a read-only data segment, their value in a read-only memroot. "read-only" means mprotect after server startup, see {{read_only_root}} in {{mysqld.cc}}

comments.body:
* mseal - Linux (https://docs.kernel.org/next/userspace-api/mseal.html)
* mimmutable - OpenBSD
* VirtualProtect (Windows)
* mprotect (posix)
Or pkeys.

Is {{READ_ONLY_AFTER_INIT}} too verbose?
Maybe {{READ_ONLY_INIT}}/{{INIT_READ_ONLY}}?

As for variable name , I like READ_ONLY_AFTER_INIT , better than both RO_AFTER_INIT and  READ_ONLY_SYSVAR, but I do not mind anything else, as long as it is neutral, i,e not MPROTECTED_ELF_SECTION please :)

[~wlad], please, review 5 top-most commits in bb-10.11-serg:
{noformat}
76803e8cf80 MDEV-40341 store read-only sysvars in a read-only root
e28837a1b9a MDEV-40341 store read-only sysvars in a read-only segment
ceaa90bf794 MDEV-40337 store user vars in a dedicated memroot
fe6f06d33d9 generalize ROOT_FLAG_MPROTECT to work on Windows, rename accordingly
b4f2654a43e cleanup: make my_virtual_mem_reserve() portable, unify buf0buf.cc
{noformat}
Note that READ_ONLY_SYSVAR isn't renamed yet, but support for Windows is there.

* opt_enable_named_pipe is missing READ_ONLY_SYSVAR, fails as
{noformat}
Sysvar 'named_pipe' failed '!is_readonly() || scope() != GLOBAL || offset == 0 || var_is_ro_after_init((char*)global_var_ptr())'
{noformat}

* my_virtual_mem_protect() takes int prot and callers pass PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE - POSIX constants from sys/mman.h (or the compat defines in my_sys.h).  To make it safer, self-contained and coherent API:  use enum type instead of int in the header, and define only 2 constants MY_VMEM_READONLY / MY_VMEM_READWRITE in it, map them to either POSIX or Windows constants in the implementation of my_virtual_mem_protect()
(fe6f06d33d9)

* sys_var::move_charptr_to_root() is a no-op  it seems like 2 conditions cause it to early return always.
!is_struct() skips all non-struct sysvars, amd var_is_ro_after_init(*ptr) (should not the check should be !var_is_ro_after_init(*ptr))?
(76803e8cf80)

* Don't use double-underscore names (__ro_after_init_start, __ro_after_init_end) outside the ELF, where they're unavoidable. Instead of defining them on MSVC and the fallback path, use normal, non-reserved names (e.g. ro_section_low_addr, ro_section_high_addr) and add #define aliases on ELF to map them to the linker-provided symbols. Leading double underscore names [are reserved in C and C++| https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20230109-00/?p=107685]
(e28837a1b9a)

* Please check  mprotect and VirtualProtect return values, there is number of cases it can go wrong, e.g wrong pointer alignment or size. DBUG_ASSERT only is ok.

Also a question - comments suggest that virtual memory allocations on each THD are rather expensive.  Does  it make sense now to precache THDs, with threadpool?Threadpool currently ignores  thread_cache (threadpool reuses OS threads using its own logic, but currently does not cache  connection-related structures like THD) .  Should I write an MDEV about it?

Hi [~serg].
* The return code check from VirtualProtect is incorrect, you might look at https://github.com/MariaDB/server/commit/aea9f957286922243a86d91244526b256eb3da8c , which contains a fix.
* The test case sys_vars.sys_vars_readonly_debug would not run on Windows as-is, i.e it would spit out a crashdump due to a bug in mtr
(windows has core-file=1 as default), and it might bring JIT debugger popup, or actually do Windows error reporting stuff, depending on OS settings. the fix is for that is in https://github.com/MariaDB/server/commit/641d82d891f6f0e9288c79642ab0c94b4ca75f2d (I know, it adds a global variable specifically on Windows, that is not used anywhere else, feel free to either fix, or to disable that test on Windows.
There are faster/better methods to test that variable is readonly (VirtualQuery or SEH try/catch), that do not need a server crash/restart.
* On the naming, and Windows API snark, in comments you added to https://github.com/MariaDB/server/commit/d4d5d2ffd87b21726367b8127502a050c70310d0
{noformat}
 The unfortunate terminology comes from WinAPI, see MEM_* flags below.
 It's rather confusing in the context of a database (and specifically,
 InnoDB, the only user of this functionality), but it's the established
 terminology.
{noformat}
First, it is established terminology, reserve/commit/decommit is used by almost all highly cross-platform,  allocators
(jemalloc, tcmalloc, mimalloc and others), runtimes (JVM, V8, Node.js, .NET). It is notably not used by Linux-only, or Linux-first, or POSIX only allocators, which could describe a something as simple as "reserve" as "anon mmap with PROT_NONE", and "decommit"  as "return memory back to OS".
If anything, the POSIX side is the one requiring unfortunate hacks - see MADV_DONTNEED vs MADV_FREE vs MADV_FREE_REUSABLE vs MADV_PURGE vs disclaim(), with a #warning for unknown platforms. The Windows API handles this with one clean VirtualFree(MEM_DECOMMIT).  It is Innodb, that wanted two-phase virtual memory model, the Windows model, with memory reservation, commit, and decommit. Anyway, I would like to think we're one of the "highly cross-plattform" software, and I gave its naming, which I do not think is very extravagant, given it is used anywhere in portable software.  Thus If possible, I would prefer if snarky comment was corrected.

* thanks, I'll use {{res= !VirtualProtect}} to ifdef as little as possible, but hopefully it'll fix the return code check
* I've seen that too, when I tried it on Windows, but didn't know how to fix it. I'll look into your commit. But we have many crashing tests, are they all disabled on windows? That'd be not good, hopefully your solution will allow to enable them eventually.
* As for this comment, it doesn't say the terminology is generally unfortunate or confusing, it says the terminology is unfortunate and confusing *in the context of databases* (and InnoDB in particular). It took me few minutes to realize it has nothing to do with InnoDB transactions and few more minutes to realize it doesn't make anything "persistent" in transaction-ish kind of sense. Then I had to fight a fleeting urge to rename commit/decommit to alloc/free. The comment says, basically that
** "commit" has a well established meaning in databases (just grep the source code for "commit" and see how many matches you'll get and how many of them will refer to ACID vs MEM_COMMIT)
** it is confusing to introduce an API inside a database where "commit" means something different
** but it's an established terminology and we'll stick to it and will not rename it (I'm sure you can imagine who might want to rename it after seeing it for the first time)
I don't think there three points are controversial and you likely even agree with them, particularly with the last one. So I'm not sure what I shall correct there.

The condition is fixed. Test is fixed and I verified that it passes on Windows.

To simplify review I didn't squash the changes this time.

Hi Serg,
* those crashing mtr-tests on Windows, I guess we run some of them. if it is about DBUG_SUICIDE(), it does not abort or anything, it just terminates current process with TerminateProcess().  This one test however is genuine, expects a crash.  And, there is at least one real abort() in sys_vars suite, something about "Long semaphore wait", it does bring a JIT debugger, I'd need to fix it at some point.
* about commit word being confusing, I dunno, this does not confuse me, never had.   Yes, "virtual memory commit" is not the same as "git commit" nor Windows C runtime _commit() (which is fsync()), nor a transaction commit.  It is a commitment, in sense of making a promise that you could use that memory . Linux also grasps the notion of that, else they would not use Committed_AS , vm.ovecommit_memory etc, but is special as by default it does not give a promise, but lies, and then might punish you with its OOM killer. Traditional Unixes behaved more predictable. But, ok, whatever. I understand that with terminology, everyone might have a personal source of confusion, mine is "Thread" for connection/session/THD and associated vocabulary -  "Thread ID" for connection ID,  "@param thd   Thread handle", flags like MY_THREAD_SPECIFIC, etc.

With that, OK to push.
